speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Coronavirus Disease of 2019 (COVID-19) outbreak is the latest uncertainty to be added to our list of challenges the country faces, even as we grapple with growing stresses in the global trading system, the impending shake-up in the international tax regime, the increasingly difficult geopolitical dynamics that we have to navigate through, to name a few.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are all working against our operating proposition, where, as a small and open state, we thrive on a rules-based multilateral system and where each has its opportunities and livelihood based on competitive advantages.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the midst of navigating these daunting external developments, we have also our domestic challenges to contend with, such as the ageing demographics, peaking of the local labour workforce in the decade ahead, the friction that we saw in jobs matching and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At times like this, it may come across as the world is collapsing upon us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have been hit by external shocks many times in our history.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have had to deal with many existential threats and challenges.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some, we have overcome and some are still out there, like rising sea levels.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And very often, we turned the solutions to our domestic challenges into opportunities and possibilities, like the water story, or how we build physical and non-physical connectivity with the world to make up for our lack of size and hinterland.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore's exceptionalism story has always been about constantly in the mode of preparing and readying for the next crisis to come even as we hope that things can be smooth sailing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And when the crisis does hit us, we respond decisively, purposefully and with ample firepower to make a difference and, thereafter, regroup, build up again and get ready for the next crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, we are already spending more than what we have collected from taxes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The call to spend more, the need to spend more is expected to keep rising.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is understandable for all of us here in this Chamber to push for more spending and subsidies in areas that we feel strongly about.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Finance Minister would then have the unenviable task of allocating the next dollar based on our priorities, and also importantly, based on how these spending commitments can be sustainably funded.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is always tempting to be nice and popular – spend more today and worry about tomorrow later.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fortunately, this is not the case for Singapore's Ministry of Finance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I remember at last year's Budget Statement speech, the Finance Minister said this: "Our fiscal discipline and prudence gave us the resources to respond decisively to unexpected challenges, such as the 2008 Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must not take this for granted." These words said last year may sound like the Finance Minister knew what was to come in 2020.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we know that the good old adage of "Saving for Rainy Days" has never failed Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is our most valuable 20-20 foresight and which so aptly shows up in Budget 2020.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, the first wave impact to the affected businesses, such as tourism, aviation and retail, has been sharp and severe.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some hotels have almost immediately seen a 50% drop in occupancy as travellers deferred their trips and many international conferences and meetings were cancelled.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Air travel has dropped significantly, especially for routes to the affected areas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cinemas, restaurants, taxis have all seen lower patronage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even neighbourhood coffee shops' businesses are affected as more eat at home and do less outings.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Stabilisation and Support Package has rightly focused on tackling two situations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The announced measures of rental waivers, rebates, temporary bridging loans, point-to-to point support package for taxis and private hire car drivers are practical and helpful relief measures to businesses and to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am glad that the Government has also introduced the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS) to provide wage support to companies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It not only helps companies with their cash flow situations but also incentivises employers to hold on to their workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Coupled with the enhanced upskilling measures that were also announced, the message to employers is to tap on these assistance schemes to send workers for training and skills upgrade during this lull period and be ready to seize opportunities again when the recovery comes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, there is this possibility that employers who enjoy this cash grant could still lay off the workers in the months later.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While I believe most employers will be grateful and understand the Government's good intention, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) could eliminate this possibility by adding another condition, which is that the wage support will only be valid for those workers who remain in employment from January to July 2020.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The COVID-19 outbreak and the resulting sudden surge in demand for its related medical services further underscored the critical need to allocate sufficient funding for healthcare services and that we not only need to have the right capacity but also the deep specialisation and expertise to deal with any public health threat of this scale.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As our population ages, the recurring annual costs to provide healthcare services will surely rise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And our expectations for higher subsidies, better quality healthcare and better accessibility will also keep rising over time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, at my constituency, we are building a new 12-storey polyclinic which comes at a cost of more than $100 million and thereafter, millions of dollars in recurring costs to run the centre.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are also looking at sites within our estates to build more senior day-care centres that come with medical facilities to handle long-term chronic illnesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I understand the costs of each such centre is minimally $1 million and, again, the costly recurring expenses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While I dislike seeing the GST rate increase, I do understand that the Finance Minister would need additional funding to help pay for these new expenditures as well as other increased spending in social areas, such as in education, security and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am convinced that our system of GST that is stapled with a massive and almost permanent GST offset package does mitigate its impact on lower- and middle-income households and re-tilt it from a regressive to a progressive tax system.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But those who spend more, especially on more expensive items, will contribute more GST.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These tend to be from the wealthier or the higher-income group.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even foreigners who are here for work, business or leisure also contribute to our GST coffer when they spend in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just like if I travel to Japan, I would also have to pay the 10% consumption tax for my spending there and, in effect, directly helping to fund Japan's budget deficit.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, it would be useful if the Finance Minister can share on the proportion of GST collected that is being contributed by the higher-income groups and foreigners.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are workers in their 40s and 50s.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I am heartened that Finance Minister has pointed out in the Budget speech that in the next bound of SkillsFuture, there will be a dedicated focus on mid-career workers, those in the 40s and 50s.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, many of the workers in their 40s and 50s, especially the Professionals, Managers and Executives (PMEs), are very worried about losing their jobs and they feel a great sense of insecurity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Those who, unfortunately, lose their jobs at this age face an uphill task to find another job that is commensurate with their work experience and expectations, even though they may be prepared to lower their expectations by a few notches.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have met many such jobseekers at my Meet-the-People Session (MPS).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I can fully understand what they are going through.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are often under tremendous pressure to find a new job quickly and the entire family is also impacted as these jobseekers are often also the sole or main breadwinner.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As what the Deputy Prime Minister has related in the Budget speech, for people in their 40s and 50s, when they started work, it was normal to stay with one job, in one or two companies, for life.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They lived through the period when Singapore’s economy experienced high growth, and technology was not changing very fast as to have a major impact on the workplace.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But, now, economic growth is a lot slower and the workplace is undergoing major changes at a rapid pace.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has a direct impact on job market stability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, as our economy transforms, new jobs are created while old jobs disappear and never return.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The issue is that these new positions are often not filled by this age group of jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Reasons often cited are that there is mismatch in skills or expectations from both jobseekers and hirers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are also situations where, even after the training and skills upgrade, employers are still not willing to take on these workers as they have younger ones to choose from.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This trend is particularly worrying, especially when we are now raising the retirement and re-employment age.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We do not want these workers who are still in their prime to prematurely experience unemployment and even stay as long-term unemployed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would be a high social cost to the individual, their families and the society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The economy will also be deprived of a major source of human resource (HR) and talents.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The situation calls for direct interventions from the Government, including more upstream and pre-emptive actions, including stronger retrenchment and job placement support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government saw this problem coming some years ago and that is why we have packages, such as the Adapt and Grow and the Professional Conversion Programme (PCP).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The best way to do this is to help workers stay employable when they still have a job and for them to have the option to move to new jobs and new roles if need be.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to reduce difficulties in job transition and enhance their capabilities to better match jobs so that jobseekers can be re-employed faster.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, I welcome this new SkillsFuture Mid-Career Support Package which aims to do that.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The capacity of our existing reskilling programmes will also be stepped up, such as the PCP, career transition programme and sector-specific programmes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would urge the agencies that run these programmes to also focus more on helping jobseekers to overcome psychological barriers and make mental adjustments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This salary support is equivalent to a negative workers levy and I hope that it will move more employers to consider these experienced workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, we need employers to collaborate and give these jobseekers a chance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister also announced that the Government would review the support package for talent hiring and retention to maximise its impact.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Finance has raised its concerns and views with the Minister for Finance in our Budget engagement and I thank him for hearing us out with this substantial upgrade in package to help our workers in their 40s and 50s, so that they can benefit and have peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, in his Budget speech, Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat also called on Singaporeans to work together in partnership to build the future of our choice.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is in difficult times like this that we need to rally the spirit of SG Together.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At our communities, we have seen spontaneous acts by fellow residents, such as coming together to bottle hand sanitisers and placing them in lifts for residents to use, volunteering at masks distribution centres to distribute masks at Residents Committee (RC) centres or expressing gratitude and cheering on our frontline healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Social organisations, artists, sports persons and many others have also organised various efforts to help vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have also seen commercial organisations like banks, insurance companies, multinational corporations (MNCs) coming up with relief packages to help their clients tide over the difficult period.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Budget 2020 represents a very strong set of decisive actions by the Government to deal with the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But these counter-crisis efforts can be even more effective or powerful if more stakeholders can also facilitate and reinforce the relief measures introduced by the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have just gotten confirmation from the coffee shop operator at my Community Club (CC) who promised me that he will completely pass on half a month's rental waiver to the self-employed stallholders who are impacted by the crisis as well and I would like to urge other coffee shop operators to do the same, especially those in Housing and Development Board (HDB) estates.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Companies that are not adversely affected by the crisis could consider using the wage support received from JSS meaningfully, for example, to invest in their employees' skills upgrade or on their welfare or flow some of it to their clients that may be impacted by the crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Each of us and our businesses can do our part, big or small, each in our own way, to help out fellow businesses that are affected.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: All these efforts add up and go a long way in helping Singapore ride out this difficult period and emerge even stronger.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A young resident came to my MPS some years ago to ask for financial assistance to pay for his Institute of Technical Education (ITE) school fees.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I told him that we would assist him, but I asked that he promise me that he would put in his best effort to do well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I still remember how he, without hesitation, agreed to do so.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: That year, he did come back, showed me his grades and it did reflect him doing well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: After a year, one of my residents came to see me asking for help, saying that he needed help for me to speak to his son.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He explained that his family had financial difficulties and because he was a low-income worker.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He said that his son wanted to quit school to be able to earn an income to help the family with its finances.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He asked if I could convince his son to stay and continue his studies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I told him I would try my best and hope that we could do that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Now, many years later, I recently met this young man.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He now has a promising career and he and his family are doing very well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He said, "I know the importance of opportunity and I am grateful that by continuing my studies, I was able to take the opportunities that came my way".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, he had potential and he would have been able to help his family had he gone and found a job at that time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The fact that he was able to build on the foundation and acquire the skills to enable him to access better opportunities really made the difference for him and he is now clearly able to take on larger opportunities that come his way.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Addressing current challenges and keeping businesses viable are important because, if they fail, Singaporeans who work for these organisations will lose their jobs and their livelihoods will be impacted.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The structural shifts brought about by economic trends, technological disruptions and demographic changes require businesses and workers to transform and this will take time and effort.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the business slowdown, organisations must take the opportunity to execute these transformation plans and reskill their employees.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As the famous quote attributed to Winston Churchhill says: "Never let a good crisis go to waste".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In times of a crisis, it is also time for us to come together to find ways to address the challenges and also see opportunities that present themselves even in these difficult times.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The measures in this Budget support nurturing every Singaporean to achieve his or her full potential.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is a little bit disconcerting sometimes, but I have residents who come and ask me, "Can you get me approval to transfer my SkillsFuture credit to my family members?" The reasons given are that they do not need this to learn new skills because they are too old or just that they do not need it or they think that other members of the family may have more need for training.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The need to continually learn, unlearn and relearn is important for everyone, regardless of age or stage in life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is to build confidence not only for employability but for active participation in life in an economy and society that is more complex and fast-changing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With change comes the need to be agile and to be able to handle ambiguity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Therefore, building relevant skills, picking up new knowledge and the ability to deal with change are key to not only availing oneself of employment opportunities, but also to enabling us to be confident to participate and thrive in society.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will impact an individual's quality of life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The challenge is how we can help as many Singaporeans as possible to understand what training is available, assess what is relevant for them and to make access to learning easy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Today, many more people are taking courses and, while this is encouraging as it shows the willingness to learn, we need to do more to ensure relevancy and the impact of the learning in helping with employability or addressing required lifeskills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Skills are important and we must develop deep skills to play and compete in the areas of new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But we must also recognise that skills and knowledge have a shelf life and do become obsolete.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is equally important is to develop in our people the underlying capability and capacity to learn and relearn to stay relevant, the ability to deal with change, ambiguity and the application of knowledge with the practicality and resolve to make things happen even when there is no charted path.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I particularly like the focus on enhancing the role of enterprises in developing their staff.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will better align training with what businesses require.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will, in turn, drive real productivity and value for both employers and employees.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This learning experience and exposure will better prepare our young to take advantage of new opportunities with the growth of Asia and add value to organisations that they join after they leave school.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The current uncertainties are driving concerns on the implication for businesses and workers, and workers are really worried about keeping their jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But while the support will help, the reliefs are short term.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: No one can tell how long the COVID-19 situation will continue and more help may be required.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We do have to recognise that for some businesses, the impact of the current uncertainties has been quite sharp, and although their business operations have been viable, the drastic drop in business demand and impact on supply chain will have significant short-term operational and cash flow impacts.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Going through the immediate challenges will have to be a priority for them if they are to be able to keep jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While the Stabilisation and Support Package does provide some relief on wage costs and funds training support, they may not be sufficient to help businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Employers will need to take the leadership on cost-management measures as well as partner with employees to help with cost-saving measures to protect jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Perhaps, more can be done to help businesses navigate existing programmes already in place that can complement Budget 2020 to manage this current business impact.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While the number of self-employed workers and freelancers form a small proportion of the workforce, they, too, are experiencing a drop in demand for their services and they may need help with support or maybe even to find an employment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I do hope more can be done for this group of workers as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat had said in the Budget, some in this segment have stayed with one company and have not made career changes since they left school.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the disruptions that we are seeing, the new technologies and the nature of jobs changing, many in this segment do need help to reskill and, more importantly, to adapt to the changes to compete for new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While training and reskilling are important, knowing what the opportunities are and aligning the training to available job opportunities are key for mid-career workers to secure suitable employment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I must tell Members that I do see my residents in this age group struggling with finding suitable employment and this is not because they have not tried.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Anxiety levels are really quite high, not just for them, but also for their families.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am also somewhat concerned with the emphasis on training and reskilling with this Budget because if many are trained and yet they are not able to find suitable employment, we may have a situation where there is even greater frustration and anxiety.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For the PCPs, there is an online listing of roles and industries from different industries – from Precision Engineering, InfoComm, Food Manufacturing, Logistics and many more – outlining the scope of the application criteria and requirements for participating companies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we focus on supporting mid-career workers to develop new skills, we also have to find new pathways to allow these workers to learn new skills and, at the same time, build upon the relevant skills and experience that they have built over the years.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Sometimes, I feel that when we talk about reskilling, we forget that these mid-career workers bring a wealth of knowledge, capabilities and experience that we should leverage while we help them with reskilling.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is something that I hope we can pay some attention to, because otherwise, it will be a waste of opportunities and also wasted skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For example, if data analytics is the area of focus, as we reskill the individual for this, how do we also look at his/her experience, perhaps, say, in marketing or management?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How do they avail themselves of these skills across different industries and roles as they pick up this new skill?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think that is a critical area and it is an important area that we have to focus on.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For organisations, when they look at onboarding their staff, they look at onboarding staff to the new environment in the office, to the company and the company's policies and practices and business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I can tell that to Members personally because I have experienced that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And it can be extremely scary because you suddenly find yourself in situations where you do not even know what questions to ask, because you may not know what you do not know of your new industry.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: That kind of orientation – onboarding and so on – is very important as well as the support systems to be put in place for that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The partnership of our people, businesses and the Government to address social challenges together will help build a more cohesive and resilient Singapore for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Following from the theme of unity, the focus of my speech today is Unity Amidst Disruption.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of all the areas covered by Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat's Budget speech, I was especially interested in the section on Navigating Long-Term Structural Shifts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He acknowledged the global decline in support for globalisation, with protectionism and nativism on the rise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On my part, I have been studying the phenomenon of globalisation for a while, and I would argue that the main debate today is not between those who support or reject globalisation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Instead, it is a more nuanced and constructive debate about the kind of globalisation we should strive for that would improve human welfare in a sustainable way.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Those who advocate such human-centred globalisation are sometimes called "alternative globalisers".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the outset, I should say that Singapore has been a major beneficiary of globalisation, with the Government providing leadership in this endeavour over the years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We have benefited from open trade, foreign investment and becoming a global financial centre.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We are increasingly becoming a global knowledge hub.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While these benefits are undeniable, the question is how the "losers" from globalisation are treated.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In 2006, when Singapore hosted the World Bank meetings, we were met head-on by protestors who came from abroad to make their customary presence felt at these meetings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While some may see them as disruptive and a nuisance, it is increasingly acknowledged that their underlying concerns were valid.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These were concerns about the excesses of global capitalism, such as market destabilisation, exploitation of workers in poorer countries and the destruction of the environment through pollution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Though some far-right groups in the world today seem to reject globalisation outright, this is not constructive, as it is simply not possible to unwind today's world of interconnectedness and multipolar supply chains.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, three decades after globalisation took off, the protestors' core concerns are being recognised in the halls of power.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Climate Change is on the international agenda and in this Budget.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development has sponsored work on subjective well-being and social welfare.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Green financing is gaining momentum, with European Union (EU) law requiring large companies to publish climate-related financial disclosures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: International financial institutions, such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, have had a rethink about their policies, too.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is especially so after the experience of the Asian Financial Crisis and the collapse of Latin American economies that took their advice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is now acknowledged by these institutions that different countries are at different states of readiness, that there can be no universal set of rules for everyone.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, the relative success of China and India in the era of globalisation has been attributed to their opening up of their markets in an incremental manner, giving local enterprises and workers time to adapt.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The lessons from the 1990s show that governments have an important role to play to actively manage globalisation for their respective countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The World Bank highlights that governments need to pay attention to the aspect of human security, such as through targeted poverty reduction and social safety nets.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Though the Government does not label its initiatives in terms of alternative globalisation, some of its policies, including in this Budget, seek to mitigate the harsh impacts of economic liberalisation on Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are various schemes for targeted poverty reduction, for example, through rebates and other financial transfers weighted in favour of the poor.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are also important social safety nets, such as retraining and reskilling efforts, which it is now redoubling on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is useful to unpack the source of such anxiety.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Disruption can come anytime, through industries being off-shored elsewhere, or by being displaced through foreign competition within Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Despite all these efforts, mid-career workers' anxiety will be hard to assuage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There could be mismatch between openings and applicants.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Seeking assistance from Government agencies also positions the citizen as someone applying for help, which can be a humbling experience.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: All this can be a tremendous mental and emotional strain on the whole family.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Every day, he leaves home as usual and comes back at the usual time, while trying to find another job.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In dealing with the long-term structural shifts, the Government has devoted significant resources to enable workers to skill up and transit to other industries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But is it time now to consider other measures too that Singaporeans can tap on more seamlessly, and for security and peace of mind?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It had always been a tenet of this Government to promote self-reliance among Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans, too, prefer to be self-reliant and not have to seek Government assistance at every turn.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With the weak economic outlook and soft job market, it may be the time to re-examine some policy approaches.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, I know of some mid-career employees who had been laid off and turned to Government agencies for assistance, but were unable to secure work for months, a point Ms Jessica Tan alluded to earlier as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some of them wanted to chart their own reskilling towards a professional qualification in another field, which would require a significant cash outlay.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I will speak more about this at the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM's) Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This has been previously debated in this House, with the Government calling it, "not a crazy idea", but preferring its current approach of job creation and reskilling.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How confident is the Government that its existing schemes will be able to find solutions for everyone who applies?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Suffice to say for now, Sir, that the Government would need to reassess its approaches periodically, as economic and technological realities change.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The forces of globalisation also pressure us to constantly up our game, reskill and be prepared to be uprooted to stay relevant.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This transition is not easy, and I appreciate that the Government has poured in resources to support Singaporeans in reskilling and career transition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the anxiety and insecurity aspects will also need to be addressed adequately, in order to shore up the concept of unity which is the theme of this Budget.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Singaporeans ushered in the new year amidst slowing economic growth and geostrategic uncertainties.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With COVID-19, this has further impacted the health of our economy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Although the severity of COVID-19 remains unclear, the Labour Movement will work closely with the Government and businesses to tackle the spread of the disease and protect workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are now much better prepared to tackle an infectious disease outbreak, such as COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our medical infrastructure, public health knowledge and training have improved significantly over the years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, this time round, we are facing a deeper, more wide-ranging impact to our economy than before.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our world is now much more interconnected with China, and the disruption to China's economy is starting to cause far-reaching ripple effects that have affected Singapore as well.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, let us all be mentally prepared and, importantly, ready ourselves, stay strong, and overcome any challenges that come our way.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As Secretary-General of the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), I commend the Government's swift and collected response to the outbreak.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The strong Budget this year reflects the whole-of-Government approach to tackling the virus and maintaining our workers' confidence in the economy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Over the past few weeks, the Labour Movement has been hard at work collecting worker feedback through our union leaders, industrial relations officers and from employer partners.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat has factored this feedback into the Budget.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: During this difficult time, workers are understandably worried for the health of their loved ones, friends and co-workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Additionally, workers in some of the hardest hit sectors are facing daily disruptions and, as Members have said before, they are worried about sustaining a steady income in this uncertain environment.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They do not know if they can keep their jobs and worry about reduced incomes, given less work, less overtime.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As for employer feedback, we are starting to see delays in the supply chain as the reach of COVID-19 deepens.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Also, some companies are suffering from a shortage of labour, while ironically, other sectors have excess capacity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am heartened to see the Budget address these issues and many more.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our workers can take comfort in knowing that the help for businesses will also help them keep their jobs and incomes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: On NTUC's part, we are doing what we can to help and protect our workers and their families.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our union leaders are working hard to help companies manage excess manpower and reduce costs by arranging for subsidised worker training and upskilling through NTUC Learning Hub and the NTUC Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) during this lull period.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In some cases, this is arranged through our Company Training Committees (CTCs) which we launched last year and have proven useful.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are also looking at ways in which we can help workers, in particular PMEs, with their job worries.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Something that could help is a pilot that NTUC is introducing this year, called the NTUC Job Security Council (JSC).

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I will explain more on this shortly, in response also to Ms Jessica Tan and Ms Sylvia Lim's point about worried workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For the self-employed, the Labour Movement is working together with Government agencies to help cushion the financial blow and organise relevant training.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Whilst we work together to overcome today’s challenges, I support the Government's $8.3 billion Transformation and Growth effort to transform our economy and prepare for the realities and opportunities that lie ahead.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Industry 4.0 is changing the nature of many jobs and creating new types of work: from 3D printing of our HDB flats, to friendly chatbots providing 24/7 frontline service to customers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: All these are exciting opportunities which, if we can seize, will bring greater possibilities for our economy and for our workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our resident labour growth is slowing and our workforce is ageing.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There are now more PMEs in the workforce with better education and, in contrast, the proportion of rank-and-file workers is declining.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I know that it can be difficult to think about structural change over the long term while we are facing immediate concerns that seem so much more pressing.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In these circumstances, workers do tell me that they sometimes struggle to keep up with these new realities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They are prepared for transformation and change but, at the same time, these cause them much worry, whether they can adapt to these new realities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But the Labour Movement wants to assure every worker that you matter and we will do our best to support you during this time.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And there is one thing we must do to enhance and, that is, to bring better job security for our workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We believe that job security is the umbrella that protects our workers from passing thunderstorms.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In today's context, job security does not necessarily mean guaranteeing a job for life.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: More and more, job security means providing workers with what they need for skills progression and job placement, which ultimately will improve their work prospects that would bring them more confidence and give themselves, the workers and their families peace of mind in the new economy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our NTUC Labour Members of Parliament will be speaking today on how we are working to ensure job security for every worker: older workers, women in the workforce and, especially the most vulnerable segments of our population, such as the lower-income and the self-employed workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Jessica Tan was almost speaking like a Labour Member of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And given that she has an important appointment as Director in Raffles Medical Group, it is music to my ears to hear an employer speaking in Parliament calling for more to be done for our workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: NTUC introduced the CTCs last year for union leaders and their management partners to work together for the company to drive towards transformation in partnership.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am glad to hear Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat mention the benefits that the CTC platform has brought to our businesses and workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These CTCs enable companies to refresh and deepen workers' skillsets in line with new technologies and, importantly, tap on Government resources, such as the new SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit, to aid with the needed training.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They have also the added benefit of providing a ready-made platform, an avenue for management to discuss more immediate issues with the union, such as manpower and cost concerns arising out of COVID-19 today – not originally intended but necessarily a good tool now for CTCs to enable the discussions between management and workers to think about training in the lull period.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Wildlife Reserves Singapore, which manages the Singapore Zoo, the Jurong Bird Park and other attractions, has, as I said earlier, experienced a significant drop in visitor arrivals because of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Through a recent CTC meeting with the management, and in my discussion with them just this Monday, our unions proposed sending the workers for training and upskilling during this downtime.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will build the company's and the workers' capabilities in tandem and prepare them when the upturn in the economy comes, when more visitors come back to the Singapore Zoo and the Jurong Bird Park.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Such a move will also give their workers the added assurance that they can continue with their jobs – less anxiety.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And I am happy to see that Wildlife Reserves Singapore is fully on board.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These courses will help shape Worker 4.0 actualise the value of technology in the workplace and, equally importantly, help workers improve their work prospects and job security over time.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am pleased to update the House that we are well on our way to meeting this target.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, well done, Wildlife Reserves Singapore and our unions, Attractions, Resorts and Entertainment Union (AREU) and the Singapore Manual and Mercantile Workers' Union (SMMWU).

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There are still some workers who continue to fall through the gaps.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Through my conversations, I have noticed, as many Members have, that there is a growing concern among workers, especially those in their 40s to 50s, and, more often, PMEs, who find themselves displaced or retrenched because their skills have become redundant as technologies evolve.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And if they are retrenched, they can take a long time to get back into a job and one which may not pay as well or may not even fully utilise their skills.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Although these numbers are not large, for the individual worker or PME who has mouths to feed and bills to pay, the situation can cause a lot of fear and anxiety.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: NTUC wants to ease this situation and help these workers and PMEs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While the Labour Movement has already been training and matching workers on an informal basis, we want to formalise this process.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will create an ecosystem of "releasing" companies and "receiving" companies: "receiving" companies being those which can absorb skilled workers and PMEs into their workplace from the "releasing" companies.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: JSC will work with companies to gather information on the job vacancies, jobs that may be phased out and, importantly, jobs that could be redesigned for workers and PMEs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: JSC will then match these workers and PMEs to vacancies within this network and, where needed, identify the new skillsets required and top up workers' and PMEs' skills, where necessary, with the necessary training.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: JSC can also help companies access the many Government schemes, such as the new SkillsFuture Mid-Career Support Package.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: All these schemes are intended to enhance skilling and placement efforts for local workers and PMEs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And NTUC or this JSC can be the conduit to focus workers and companies on accessing the grants to help the workers seek new jobs and upgrade their skills.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These 4,000-plus companies come from a wide range and diverse industries and are of many different sizes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am excited to see MNCs, such as Rolls Royce and General Electric (GE) Aviation, coming on board.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I visited Rolls Royce recently and was impressed by the dedication and commitment of the management to the workforce.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have also some startups, local startups and SMEs, such as Ebenezer Group in the Engineering sector, Blue Ventures Holdings in the Wholesale Trade, as well as Swee Heng Bakery and Montreux Patisserie in the food and beverage (F&B) sector.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Swee Heng Bakery is a household name and has been in the bakery scene for just over 30 years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Their efforts to keep relevant causes them to up technology and, in the process, partnering e2i to up the skills of the workers in using machinery and upping their productivity so that they can remain relevant and do a thriving business.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Companies will also have access to a community of HR personnel and senior management sharing best practices and progressive employment standards.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Through JSC, we want to create a win-win for companies and our workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We hope to lessen the anxiety for workers and PMEs and assure them that NTUC, the Labour Movement, is doing what we can to help them find good jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We look forward to taking this pilot further and we call on companies which may not have yet joined us to contact NTUC to come on board.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, Ms Jessica Tan, I expect a call from Raffles Medical Group soon.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: (In Mandarin):   I have been very concerned about the employment situation of our workers, especially the middle-aged workers and PMEs who are in their 40s to 50s.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many who lost their jobs shared with me that they faced all kinds of difficulties finding a new job.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A year ago, we started exploring ways to help these workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In the past half year, NTUC’s e2i has been in talks with many companies to join the NTUC JSC.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Companies that join JSC, a handful may reduce manpower, but many more want to hire workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And if workers need to have different skills to take on the new jobs, e2i will arrange for them to undergo training and upskill themselves.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will continue to work with companies from more sectors and get them on board JSC so that more workers can benefit.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Around the world, the social compact in many societies is breaking down.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The trust citizens have for their political leaders is eroding.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But in Singapore, we have the trust of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is something that we must never take for granted.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In Singapore, we enjoy the fruits of hard-earned tripartism, which has brought us economic resilience and social stability.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Underpinned by this year's strong Budget, all these will ensure that Singaporeans’ lives are uplifted together.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Labour Movement will continue to work with our Government and employers to improve the social and economic well-being of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To this end, we will continue to strengthen and adapt the uniquely Singapore social compact so that it will stand the test of time.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Today, as we debate Budget 2020, Singapore, as a country, must grapple with the round-the-clock challenge of battling with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is over and above the continued race to keep up with the rise of digitalisation, new technologies and economic transformation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Against the backdrop of these exacting forces, the future of work, workers and workplaces will and must evolve and transform.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Thus far, many union leaders, workers as well as my grassroots leaders and residents have shared positive feedback about this year’s Budget.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On one hand, businesses will receive job and cash flow support to retain and retrain workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On the other hand, our workers – from the young and mid-career to older workers – will get a much-needed boost through the various SkillsFuture Credit schemes to upgrade, upskill and stay employable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What is particularly reassuring is that Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat has also stated affirmatively in his speech that the Government is prepared to do more should the need arise.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This year’s Budget is seen as an expensive as well as expansive one.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am particularly happy and delighted with three items fleshed out in the Budget because it has answered three calls which I have been making in this House.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some Members may not know, but what is particularly beneficial and useful are that freelancers and self-employed individuals can also tap on their SkillsFuture Credits to learn new skills or even develop in their field.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am heartened, therefore, that this top-up will give all Singaporeans aged 25 and above an added push as they make lifelong learning a way of life.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, is the added focus on mid-career workers between the ages of 40 and 60 through the various programmes and policies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Based on labour market statistics and reports, this group continues to be the most vulnerable and affected by retrenchments, with higher skilled, middle-aged PMEs the hardest hit.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Mature and older workers, including PMEs, also face greater difficulty in the job market with the long-term unemployment rate of Singaporeans climbing with age.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For those who are unemployed or retrenched, re-entry into the labour market is also an uphill task.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In my interactions with mature workers, and especially PMEs, they have shared their concerns about being made redundant by younger colleagues or being replaced by technology and job automation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In short, they worry about staying employed and employable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is also something I have suggested in this House.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I hope this credit for employers will serve as a catalyst for companies, especially SMEs, to develop their workforce as they transform their business, by embracing and investing in skills upgrading and training of their workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In particular, the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit will further augment and complement existing efforts by NTUC and our affiliated unions to partner companies in forming CTCs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These efforts, which were introduced last year, aim to equip workers across all sectors and all sizes of companies with the necessary skills, so that they can secure better wages, better welfare and better work prospects.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Notwithstanding a laudable Budget, I have five specific suggestions for consideration.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, to speed up the disbursement of JSS and SkillsFuture Top-up.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the near term, some companies that are directly affected are already feeling the effects of economic fallout brought about by COVID-19 and any immediate relief is welcomed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As I urge the speeding up of disbursements, I also suggest for the Government's support to lengthen and stretch the validity of these schemes should the situation worsen or become prolonged.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second is to expand the Training Support for Mid-Career Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: My second suggestion is not to confine the additional top-up for those aged 40 to 60 only to those 200 career transition programmes offered by the CET centres as outlined in Annex B-2 to the Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I urge for the courses availed to include those recognised under the Industry Transformation Map (ITM) Skills Framework as well as suitable Government and NTUC-run courses and programmes and those of our CTCs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: By the same token, to minimise jobs and skills mismatches, career advisors could look at providing peer-level support for this group and additional support, such as coaching, to identify skills gaps and training intervention that may be needed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third is to restore the Surrogate Employer Programme.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: During the SARS crisis in 2003, I was in NTUC overseeing the Surrogate Employer Programme, where NTUC acted as a surrogate employer and helped many of those affected by the downturn, such as Tour Guides as well as SIA's Cabin Crew who were on unpaid leave, to go for training and upgrading while benefiting from a training allowance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These efforts resulted in a win-win-win for all, in that when the Singapore economy rebounded months later, affected workers who had the training allowance as stipend could now return to their jobs and assignments quickly, to the delight of their employers and customers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: NTUC stands ready to partner the Government to administer the Surrogate Employer Programme so that this group of workers can also benefit from training assistance and incentives.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, to raise the absentee payroll and course fee funding.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Minimally, I submit that this enhanced critical funding can help to address the vulnerabilities of the mature and older workers in this time and space.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Today, the world has changed and continues to change.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Against an increasingly uncertain global environment and an economy that is facing challenges both in the short term and long term, many of our workers are understandably worried that their jobs will be impacted.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As NTUC Secretary-General and Minister Ng Chee Meng has shared, NTUC will be piloting a JSC to pre-emptively match at-risk workers and PMEs into jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Through JSC, NTUC and its affiliated unions will help displaced workers find new jobs within the network and, where necessary, provide the requisite training to help workers smoothly transition from one job to another.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   The COVID-19 outbreak will undoubtedly affect our economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Many workers have told me that they were worried about their jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The new Budget, as announced by Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat, is both assuring and stimulating.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Not only does it address the immediate needs but also focus on long-term planning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With regard to this, I have five suggestions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, allow Singaporeans between 40 and 60 years old to have more courses available to them, including those recognised under the ITM Skills Framework or relevant courses offered by NTUC.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, restore the Surrogate Employer Programme so that freelancers, self-employed persons or certain neglected workers can also receive allowances during their absence so that they can go for courses for upgrading.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, raise the absentee payroll to encourage businesses to send their workers for training.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fifth, at the same time, we must pay attention to job security of our workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As NTUC Secretary-General Ng Chee Meng has announced, NTUC will set up a JSC to help retrenched workers with job matching and necessary training through e2i.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In English): My view is that this is a comprehensive and inclusive Budget, one that will help Singapore overcome our short-term challenges and, at the same time, prepare ourselves for future threats, disruptions and opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I urge our tripartite partners and all of us in Singapore to rally together, stay united and look out for one another.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is so that we can navigate and overcome this rough patch together, and then ride on the wave of change and embrace the upturn thereafter as one Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The COVID-19 crisis is named for the last day of last year on 31 December 2019 when China informed the World Health Organization (WHO) of a novel virus pneumonia in Wuhan.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: On 2 January, the Ministry of Health (MOH) alerted all doctors to identify any patient with pneumonia and a recent travel history to Wuhan.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A day later, we started temperature screening at our airport of all travellers arriving from Wuhan.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: More information starting coming out from China, including the vital fact that the virus could be transmitted from human.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Since then, we have seen the best, and the worst of ourselves.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The heroes in this fight are undoubtedly the healthcare staff – doctors, nurses and all in the healthcare industry – who work under incredible pressures and fears.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Nurses who care for COVID-19 patients are working with cumbersome masks and protective wear.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Those of us who have worn an N95 will know how hard it is to breathe under one of these, even for half an hour.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yet, they have to go through entire working days with these, sometimes doing delicate work, taking blood and other procedures, all the while knowing that these bodily fluids are infected.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And many of these same people would have worked at their jobs when we had SARS.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: When they can finally take off their equipment, clean up and go to lunch, some of them are unfortunately shunned and avoided.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: On trains and buses, their uniforms are a badge for isolation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Unfortunately, there are some who mocked the great who toiled so hard and late.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Prime Minister Lee, our Ministers, our union leaders and community leaders have all made many visits to these workers, openly standing shoulder to shoulder with them, no masks, just smiles.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I also count among these the selfless and courageous grassroots volunteers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the distribution of masks exercises, many volunteers stepped forward to make the whole process seamless and smooth.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There are also others who declined their quota of masks, saying to give them to others as they already have secured their supply of face masks.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Then, there are the students of our universities, which give me hope for the future.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I saw on television a student's union president, Mr Richard Wang, who delivered food to his fellow students regularly and without complaint.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Then, there was the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) Corporal Mohd Shahrom who picked up a patient suspected to have, and later confirmed to have the virus.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And then, there was Mr Keith Aw from MOM who checked on foreign workers on leave of absence, speaking to them for up to 10 minutes a time.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: All these people act, not because they have no fear, but they act in spite of fear.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is no Budget measure that accounts for greatness.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I also want to speak about the wise, the key decision makers, including public health officials, who have acted so quickly and decisively in this crisis.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Contact tracing and quarantine orders were swiftly issued.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We instituted travel declarations and entry restrictions; there were also leave of absence from work and stay-home notices that were instituted.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These are not easy decisions and cause a lot of disruption to people's lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But the price of leadership is to sacrifice the popular for the right.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This again, is the prescience of those who are wise among us.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The leaders who have made all the difficult calls, not just the Cabinet Ministers, but the men and women on the ground who have had to make difficult calls at a time of fear and panic.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And, of course, the opportunists will mock the wise, they will spew untruths and outright lies.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Even in such trying times, some would take the opportunity to spread fake news.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA) office was kept busy during this period, too.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Left unchecked, the spread of deliberate online falsehoods will have serious consequences which society will ultimately have to pay a heavy price for.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I count these measures that we have outlined in this Budget to be among the wise decisions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Overall, there is nothing much that one can find fault with our Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister in this year’s Unity Budget.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, smaller SMEs might have issues understanding Government initiatives and programmes in English and so I suggest such initiatives and programmes be translated into Mandarin, Malay and Tamil so that the wider business communities can understand and embark on such initiatives.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The language gap requires another sort of translation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to make these schemes more accessible by showing SMEs how such Government grants can help them so that they do not miss out on them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Government has also announced COVID-19 relief measures to support SMEs in affected sectors in the form of tax rebates, bridging loans, rental waivers, wage subsidies, higher absentee payroll and training course subsidies, foreign worker levy waivers and so on.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These are certainly appreciated by SMEs and businesses.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I hope the Government will consider and see if these gaps can be addressed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The day that Singapore announced that it was going Disease Outbreak Response System Condition (DORSCON) Orange, there was frenzied buying at the supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But it was not the long queues at the supermarkets but the long queues later for a separate matter that I would like to remember.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Two weeks ago, Red Cross Singapore called for Singaporeans to donate their blood as blood stock levels for some blood types were running critically low.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There were crowds of Singaporeans at the four blood banks around the island.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Meantime, there are other stories of people being incredibly altruistic, leaving sanitisers and masks for their neighbours.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Then, unfortunately, there are those who take advantage of this crisis to do great harm.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Police have also arrested five people for their suspected involvement in five separate e-commerce scams involving the online sale of face masks.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There are those among us who are great and wise and good.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And there will always be those who mock them, those who use fake news or false news, those who are socially irresponsible and those who behave badly.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What about those of us who are neither great, nor wise, nor good?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We, ordinary men and women of Singapore, can be decent.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As Members know, FairPrice was caught up in this panic buying.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As the Group Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of NTUC FairPrice, I witnessed first hand the shopping frenzy by many people on those two days, Friday and Saturday.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This shopping behaviour was quite broad-based, covering all age groups, races and social strata.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To instil calm to all, NTUC FairPrice instituted a variety of measures, including the imposition of purchase limits on some items.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As to be expected, when this was first announced, it attracted quite a lot of noise and there was a minority group that criticised our move.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I would say a large majority were in favour.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, many of them suggested to me that when this episode is over, FairPrice should not allow people who stock up to return their excess goods to us to get a refund.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is so as to teach people a lesson on buying responsibly and not hoard first only to return the stocks later.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think what we will do is to encourage all those who had bought probably a bit too much to consider donating their excess stocks to Food Bank or Food from the Heart.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Maybe I will set up a collection counter for them, too.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, I am also heartened and warmed by the many calls from members of the public who reached out to me to volunteer their services to help out in any crisis, if needed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As I look back over the last one month, I see a Government that has led from the front, been decisive in managing this crisis and coming up with a comprehensive, assuring and caring Budget that takes care of businesses and citizens alike whilst transforming, supporting and building a sustainable Singapore .

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
