speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: And the Government will need to build trust that it is doing what is right for our people, even though it means spending significant resources over a very long-term period to benefit future generations.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: When I asked some residents about the many cameras placed at the void decks and some common areas, they generally believe that the Government is doing so for their safety and security.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: People trust that our Government is using the data captured for good.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: But this is not the case in some other countries.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: In places like San Francisco, the residents have voted against having videos in public places.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: For our own digitalisation efforts to succeed, people must trust that their data is collected solely for the purpose of developing useful services for them.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: By all accounts, we have done well thus far.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: But it is not inconceivable for some to begin to raise the issues of privacy and how their personal data is being used.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe strongly that we must leverage technology, especially on those that will improve our quality of life.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Internet banking, for example, means I do not have to queue up at bank branches anymore.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: So, too, for the many Apps that have been developed by both the private sector and our Government.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: But the flip side of all these new applications of technology are issues of accountability, transparency and trust.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Can our Government protect us from being manipulated by the big tech giants?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Can we trust our Government to use our personal data for the benefit of all Singaporeans and not some political agenda?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: These are questions of trust brought about by the use of technology in our everyday lives.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The trust we have built over the past 60 years or so has given us a quality of life that is the envy of other nations.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Going forward, what more can be done to nurture this trust?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: What can be done to meet the expectations of our people in an increasingly complex world we are living in today?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: We have seen how trust has broken down in other societies leading to the rise of populism.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: And with social media and the rise of misinformation and alternative facts, sometimes, it is unclear whether the lack of trust in Government is an effect of all these developments or it is the cause for the rise of alternative centres of trust.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Our trust in public institutions in Singapore, such as our hospitals, schools, Courts and security agencies, are, indeed, very high.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: This is because these institutions have been well managed, staffed by capable and competent people, and are known to deliver good and fair outcomes.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: We trust that these institutions will do what is right and just.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Similarly, as we digitalise our society, trust that these technologies will be used correctly is important.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: There are ethical issues associated with artificial intelligence (AI) and the use of machine learning algorithms.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Can we trust that these technologies will be deployed in a manner that preserves the best interest of Singaporeans?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Just like the trust we have in our other public institutions, should we not consider similar public institutions that can build trust in our people in dealing with these new technologies?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: If we do not deal with this early, then trust in the Government can be eroded.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope creating an independent Digital Commission to look at these issues can help address these concerns.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: It is time we have a similar committee for the digital revolution.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: But given recent reports of infections in South Korea, Italy and Iran and the warning raised by the US health authorities, it will be sometime before this is over.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Our own teams in Singapore have assured us that we are ready with new measures if the situation worsens.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Our best response is to continue to be vigilant, practise the proposed hygiene practices and make it our way of life and look out for one another in this difficult time.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: How would this moment in our history be remembered?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: After SARS, the then Ministry of Community Development and Sports proposed the Fabric of the Nation project.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: As a nation, including our then Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and his wife, we stitched together patches of fabric to symbolise the coming together of people from all walks of life in overcoming that challenge together.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, that Fabric of the Nation hangs quietly in the lobby of the Ministry of Social and Family Development, a reminder of who we are as a people in times of crisis.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Someone has to keep Singapore clean, keep our transport system moving, ensure there are enough supplies in our markets and supermarkets, and attend to those who are sick and unwell as we battle this crisis.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: These are our fellow Singaporeans and workers who put their lives on the line for the sake of Singapore.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: They, too, have families anxious for the safety of their parents, siblings and loved ones either here or elsewhere.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I am heartened by the responses of Singaporeans towards those at the frontline in this challenge.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: But can this be our way of life when all of this is over?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The kindness and generosity we have shown to our frontline workers should be something history will remember us not just for this moment in our history but for defining who we are as a people.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I am into my 24th year as a Member of Parliament.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps, it is timely for me to thank you, your predecessors and Parliament staff, both past and present, all my colleagues in this Chamber, both past and present.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: It has been an opportunity of a lifetime to be able to serve the people of Singapore as an elected Member of Parliament.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I will always cherish this experience for the rest of my life.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: So, thank you all for a wonderful experience.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am only 14 years in the Chamber, so I am still a junior to the Member.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Budget 2020, as they say, has "something for everyone" from businesses to Singaporeans, young and old.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The original draft must have been in the making for many months before the onset of the unexpected COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I doubt if any other government can pull a focused Budget together like this with such agility and speed.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, kudos to Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat and the team for rising to the occasion!

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Not unexpectedly, the top-of-mind concern of Singaporeans is the "what-if" scenario of a longer-drawn COVID-19 outbreak leading to an extended global and local economic downturn.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What will an extended Stabilisation and Support package look like?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How will it be funded if the impact is even more broad-based than the tourism, retail and transport sectors directly hit by the outbreak when the supply chain continues to be disrupted, when consumer sentiments and demands continue to decline and companies start to shed their local manpower?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The anxiety is real and I seek the Deputy Prime Minister's insights on this concern.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SMEs play an important role in all countries.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The success of Singapore's economic restructuring and industrial transformations hinges plenty on the ability of Singapore's SMEs to reinvent themselves for the long term.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Since 2010, a slew of Government initiatives was launched to help move SMEs up the value chain, streamline and digitalise operations and to venture overseas.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, actions and results, too, lag aspirations and SMEs continue to be challenged, as observed by the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) in December 2019.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Mindsets, talents or the lack of talents, especially in digitalisation and understanding of technology were cited to be key obstacles to business transformation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SMEs now face a more immediate challenge with the negative impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on businesses, except for perhaps the mask, disinfectant, sanitiser or even toilet roll manufacturers and the like.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Besides tourism, the transport sectors and businesses that rely on the People's Republic of China (PRC) supply chain, many businesses that have little to do with China directly are also affected, like smaller businesses in food catering and even event management which are hit by cancellation or postponement of local events.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a general anxiety amongst the SMEs that they may not be able to survive the short term.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Mindsets of many SMEs are still on the "here and now" survival issues.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Training and work system redesigns, work process redesigns are hitherto not corporate habits.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This has been the perennial struggle of SMEs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What is the prognosis that our local SMEs will be strengthened by Budget 2020’s suite of Enterprise Grow and Enterprise Transform Packages?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Will Singapore's economic transformation ever be supported by a very strong base of local innovative SMEs?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Under current circumstances, what more can be done by the Government and the rest of us to ensure that SMEs do come out of this crisis stronger?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Budget 2020 presents a galore of measures to help Singaporeans with cost of living in daily living, such as housing, healthcare, schooling and retirement.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am concerned about three particular groups who are still at risk: one, our low-skilled seniors who still take on jobs, such as cleaners, that challenge them physically; two, our younger Singaporeans who take on low-skilled jobs, such as food delivery and even private hire driving, jobs that offer them short-term gains and some autonomy but sometimes, little long-term prospects; and three, our disabled citizens who are still unemployed or are holding jobs that may disappear as a result of the disruption of technology.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How can the Government and the rest of Singapore better support and uplift the vulnerable amongst us?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can more resources be invested to deep-dive and study their needs, create a spectrum of more suitable jobs and have more effective job placements?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can there be a more impactful and lasting way of signposting to guide them or even to create a jobs clearing house of sorts?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For the disabled, which, thankfully, due to the Government’s eyeballing and ground advocacy, things are improving, but I feel it is still not enough.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Is there a way by which the SkillsFuture movement can include them in a more substantive and systemic way?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Experts are telling us that the difference between the Third Industrial Revolution and the Fourth is the impact of depth and breadth of technological change on everyday life and business.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: From food to retail to banking, you name it, industries are going digital.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore's SkillsFuture movement is a brilliant one, but the speed of change globally and in technology is formidable.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Research shows that innovators, investors and high-skilled IT workers benefit the most in the future economy, and the rest of the population may be at risk of being left out.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To avert this scenario of a "winner-takes-all", how can we develop as many winners as possible amongst our people and businesses?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government has moved several important chess pieces for our workforce to stay relevant and, indeed, of course, it is up to us Singaporeans to respond.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It still calls for a deeper dive, I believe, to remove the income inequality that will surely arise from the advent of technology.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, that is concern four on income inequality.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My last concern in this speech is: SG Together.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I wish to cover the important Singapore Together, or the SG Together, movement – a brainchild of Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat, and very typical of his style – at least to me – of listening and engaging others, including those not in the Cabinet or the Government.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SG Together, indeed, I feel, is a significant and necessary direction.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Issues of the day are so many and so complicated and complex that the Government no longer has the monopoly of ideas and action, and sometimes even resources.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many citizens, myself included, want to be part of the solution to make our society not just successful economically, but also significant in the world.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Besides the concerns I mentioned earlier regarding strengthening SMEs, uplifting our vulnerable and reducing income inequality, I can think of so many other areas in which the Government and Singaporeans can work together: self-sufficiency in food production, impact of the rise of the robot workforce, more inclusive public housing estates, mobile or pop-up healthcare teams and clinics, living within our means in future Budget allocations, lifelong learning schools, grants for not just public housing but for private housing options, feeding the poor in a dignified way and many others.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of us, as enthusiastic advocates, will need to acquire a broader understanding of not just our area of passion and needs, but also an understanding of the ecosystem and how different pieces affect other parts of society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If citizens want to harness resources, there must be a way by which the giver of resources, whether it is the Government or private donors, can count on the track record and reliability of us citizens and partners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, our need to not only demand but to build our competencies and credibility.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But on the part of the Government, I feel there are forces within the Public Service and political system that, if we are not careful, could lead to the SG Together movement becoming tokenistic and not very impactful.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of the changes I would ask the Government to consider to take SG Together to newer heights are these.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can the Government and Statutory Boards cast a wider vision of their role beyond their traditional scopes?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) should be envisioned as the Ministry of Lifelong Learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources should be our Ministry of Sustainability.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On deployment, can we get rid of the possible thinking that only the best executives are the thinkers and remain as the head honchos in the Ministries?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can we deploy more of the best brains to the ground and develop their execution muscles?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I remember the days when I was starting a leadership training firm in China many years ago and I failed miserably at the start.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The business only took off after I sent my best top staff to China and when I regularly worked with my PRC team on the frontlines.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There ought to be a strategy to change the way the Government views and deploys its best.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Station them on the ground to learn, facilitate, forge alliances through personally experiencing the challenges on the frontlines.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Similarly, the Government should be bold enough to appoint good mid-career practitioners to leadership positions in the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Offer them a bridging learning stint if need be.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: That may make a big difference in the complexion and the DNA of SG Together.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, in terms of culture: the culture that will drive SG Together to success will have to be one that learns to be less Ministry-centric and less controlling.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I also thank again the Deputy Prime Minister and the team behind Budget 2020 for their great work.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It would rather be meaningless for the working class to receive top-ups and transfers year after year at every Budget if there is no light at the end of the tunnel for them to realise their retirement dreams.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: A single person on the ComCare Long Term Assistance Scheme receives $600 a month for basic living expenses.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: There is no way for this couple to survive on $570 a month.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The illustration went on to state that this couple has to supplement their retirement needs with family support and their own savings.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: That study has provided some food for thought about retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But the more concerning part of the numbers highlighted in the Budget Annex is the six-in-10 CPF members who could not meet their BRS a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of these Singaporeans are on the old Retirement Sum Scheme and would have reached their PEA by now.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I have met such members who are receiving less than $300 a month in CPF payouts.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some are still working as they do not have extended families or children to support them.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, for those with little or no savings for retirement, the measures announced in Budget 2020 should go some way to alleviate their hardship and uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The couple illustrated in the Annex at the beginning of my speech would receive $1,400 monthly, post-Budget 2020.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Although this is a more meaningful payout per month, at $700 per retiree, it is still predicated on additional family support and their own savings, something policymakers should not presume when formulating policies on retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For Budget 2020, I welcome the Senior Worker Support Package to help keep jobs for our senior workers and to increase their CPF savings for their retirement needs somewhere down the road.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I also welcome the Stabilisation and Support Package to help keep jobs for our workers in general during this period of uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Next, the enhancement to the Silver Support Scheme is also long overdue.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: A number of my residents were shut out of the Silver Support Scheme when it was introduced in 2015 as they had more than $70,000 in their CPF at age 55.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Many of them wondered how long does the Government expect $70,000 in total CPF contributions at age 55 to last when housing alone would have taken a big chunk of it, if not all of it away.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And these people would share that they were low-wage earners to begin with and were living paycheck to paycheck with little savings.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of them would not qualify for the scheme as they are gainfully employed but homeless children are still living with them, for whatever reasons.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The enhancements to the Silver Support Scheme is certainly a welcome move for elderly Singaporeans in these difficult times.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Next, I have a small suggestion to make about the Grocery Vouchers scheme for Singaporeans aged 21 and above, who live in 1-room and 2-room HDB flats and do not own more than one property.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These Singaporeans will receive $100 in Grocery Vouchers for 2020 and 2021.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It was stated in the Budget Annex that these vouchers can be used at participating supermarkets and, to date, NTUC FairPrice, Giant and Sheng Siong have agreed to accept these vouchers.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Grocery Vouchers scheme is expected to cost the Government $16 million.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Would it not make more sense for the Government to avail these vouchers for all the mom-and-pop shops instead, so as to help these small businesses tide over this difficult period at the same time?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The $16 million budgeted for the scheme would go a long way to help these local provision shops but it would only be a drop in the ocean for the three big supermarkets combined.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: NTUC FairPrice alone had reported a group revenue of $3.45 billion for FY2018.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I can understand these big supermarkets would need to agree to accept these vouchers as they would be doing a form of community service.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But for those mom-and-pop shops, I am quietly confident none of them would reject these Government-backed vouchers if presented for use.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I have piloted such a voucher scheme for needy residents in Hougang.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Our vouchers could be exchanged for anything, including cooking oil, detergents, toothpaste, toilet rolls and so on, with the standard restriction on alcohol and tobacco products.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: At the same time, these vouchers would actually benefit two small, owner-operated kiosks in Hougang.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I hope the Government would consider supporting our mom-and-pop shops in a meaningful way in addition to the measures announced in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Extending the Grocery Vouchers scheme to our neighbourhood shops will help bring some buzz and business to the community.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This is a win-win arrangement for needy residents and local provision shop owners.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is certainly not about the grocery run, the hoarding or the hunt for sanitisers and what-have-you.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is about helping a friend in need.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: When China sneezes, the world will catch a flu, whether we like it or not.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The world has to be thankful to China for being able to provide all that for the benefit of consumers everywhere.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, it is imperative that we wish China a speedy recovery.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is also imperative for the world to help China to get back on its feet as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.58 pm until 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Globalisation has redefined the world of technology and innovation, market and competition.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: The implication can be "dua ho, dua pai" in Hokkien or in Chinese, "大好大坏".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Either very good or very bad. "大好", very good for those good enough to move up the economic ladder. "大坏", very bad for those unable to compete as they would be left farther behind.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: We are determined to succeed, to be "大好".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: To beat those who are cheaper than us, we try to be better than them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: To beat those who are better than us, we try to be cheaper than them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: But the cheaper keeps getting better and the better keeps getting cheaper.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: So, we restructure our economy continuously, faster than them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: We stay the course not just in good times, but also in bad.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: During the Global Financial Crisis, other countries cut jobs to save cost.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: So, with an L-shape recovery, many countries took years to recover from their massive job losses.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: But with a V-shape recovery, we took just a few months to return to full employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Not many Singaporeans remember what we did right at a time when so much could have gone wrong for us.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: But for my brothers and sisters in the Labour Movement, we would never forget how much was at stake and how important it was, and always will be, that we get it right every time, including this time round with the Stabilisation and Support package.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: They need meaningful jobs and careers to take care of themselves and their families.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: It is never easy to compete globally for good jobs and investments.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: But because we dare to be different, we never say die, we have created not just over two million jobs for our people.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: In fact, we created more than three million jobs for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Indeed, we have done well as One Singapore Tripartism.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Next, as a society, our challenge is to minimise the downside of globalisation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: It has disunited nations, divided people and broken up societies.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Countries and economies most affected negatively have one thing in common: they pursued economic growth as their end objective at the expense of social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Economic growth is just a means for us to generate the resources we need to improve the lives of our people.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: We also keep strengthening social mobility and people well-being, from upgrading of public housing estates, to the expansion and renewal of public transport, the upgrading of schools and the upscaling of preschool education.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: In a world of growing divides, unrest and disunity, we, in Singapore, continue to live in peace and harmony.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Because from the first generation (1G) to 2G and 3G, we never forget to channel the revenue generated from our competitive economy to take better care of our people.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: With this Unity Budget, our 4G is doing the same, and more.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: It will further strengthen our unity, cohesion and inclusiveness as One Singapore United.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Last but not least, as a nation, we need to strengthen our sustainability for our long-term progress.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Nation-building is a journey with no end. "人无远虑 必有近忧" in Chinese.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: That is, if one generation does not worry for the next generation, our future generations will have much to worry about.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Two-thirds of the world is covered with water, yet the world is short of clean drinking water.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: As an island, we could keep adding to our water supply with desalination.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: But it will be energy-intensive, costly and environmentally unfriendly.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: So, we came up with a same-same but different solution: not just adding, but also multiplying our water supply.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: We closed our water loop and we turned every drop of water into two drops or more with the advances in membrane technology.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: With the support of the entire nation, we achieved something unachievable in other places – the public acceptance of NEWater.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: And we pressed on for more, from NEWater to Green Sand to Zero Landfills.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Indeed, despite our many limitations as a small country, we have done well as One Singapore Unlimited.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: The global environment for trade and investment is changing, becoming more unconducive.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Some countries may choose to continue to pursue globalisation – business as usual.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Social gaps could widen more and the societies could become more divided.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Some may choose to change track, towards deglobalisation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Their economies could become more inward-looking and, eventually, less competitive.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: We want the best of both worlds – a globally competitive economy and a locally cohesive society, both at the same time. "Globalisation" plus "localisation" give us "glocalisation", in short.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: First, for our Future Economy to be globally competitive, we must strive to be a pioneer and leader in the pervasive innovation with AI.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: The concept of thinking machine and machine learning has been around for 60 years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: One of the early applications of AI is language translation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: In the early days, someone keyed in "out of sight, out of mind".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: After being translated into another language and then back into English for verification, what came back was –"a blind idiot".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: AI has come a long way since then, not just in language translation, but in many areas, from banking to medical, engineering, data analytics and more.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Together, AI and human intelligence (HI), "如虎添翼", can be like a tiger with wings, a powerful force to reshape our future for the better.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: The No 1 economy of today and the No 1 economy of tomorrow are competing head on to be the No 1 powerhouse in AI.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: When the First Conference on Innovative Applications of AI was held 31 years ago in 1989 in Stanford University, 30 pioneering AI applications worldwide were selected for presentation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: A group of AI engineers from the Information Technology Institute (ITI) presented the expert system they jointly built with the human experts at our PSA.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: We must run fast and excel in our ability to combine the complementary strengths of AI and HI, so that we can transform our future Singapore economy into one of the smartest in the future world.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Next, for our future society to be locally cohesive, we must turn three growing social divides into social unities.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: The success of a country is not judged by how well the people at the top are doing, but by how well the people at the bottom are helped by the government and treated by the general public.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: A widening income gap can and must be narrowed.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: But I hope much more will be done to transform many more jobs to be ESS – Easier, Safer and Smarter – for our older workers so that they can live more years of Happy and Healthy, Productive and Purposeful (H2P2) life as we live longer.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: At the same time, I hope we will do more to transfer capabilities, especially new and emerging capabilities that are in short global supply from the foreign manpower, both local here and overseas, to our people more systematically and proactively.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: This is one best way to reduce the lose-lose mindset of local versus foreign – two-third versus one-third – and grow the win-win mindset of two-third plus one-third, equals greater than one.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Fifty years ago, we were a pioneer in embracing Clean and Green.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Moving forward, I feel what we need is to create an environment where everyone in Singapore can participate everyday and everywhere in a more active and visible manner as part of our daily life.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: From more use of reusable bag and environmental-friendly car, to the separation of waste for recycling, returning of trays at the F&B outlets and so on, I hope we will strive to be a leading nation in our social behavior to improve our environmental performance and sustainability, so that our future Singapore will truly be a better Singapore in all aspects – more competitive, more cohesive, more socially responsible and more environmentally responsive.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, today, Singapore is a competitive economy, a cohesive society and a nation which can develop sustainably.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: This has been achieved through the collective efforts of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: The question is, why is it that most countries have capable and hardworking people but only a few countries can perform well?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: One of the key factors lies with the quality and style of leadership.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: In some countries, leaders are only concerned with "xiao wo" or self-interest.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: They jostle for power and put their self-interest above that of the country and its people.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: As a result, people’s lives are neglected and the country fails, with nothing being achieved.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: On the other hand, leaders from some countries adopt a "zi wo" or "self-centred" leadership style.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: They can perform well in the short run but are egoistic and lack successors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: As a result, they may do well in the short run, but this success cannot be sustained for long.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Fortunately, leaders from some countries adopt the "da wo" leadership style, or a selfless leadership style that focuses on the greater good.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: When they are in power, they work tirelessly to serve the country and its people.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: At the same time, they focus on the future and continue to groom their successors, because they know that no one can escape death and illness, and this is the law of nature.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Every one of us will become old, but a country's leadership cannot become old.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: This is because nation-building is an endless journey.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Therefore, while these leaders are serving the country and its people, they also spare no efforts in grooming leaders for the next generation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: By doing this generation after generation, the country's leaders can keep up with the times and continue to do good for the people.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Under their leadership, the country can achieve good progress, regardless of short-term or long- term developments.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: I hope the 4G Leaders will uphold the same spirit and prioritise our country's long-term development and our citizens’ long-term interest above everything else.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: I also hope that our people will always treasure this leadership style.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Only by doing this, can Singapore continue to progress and can generations of Singaporeans live better and be happier than their predecessors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, a few months ago, I had a private dinner with Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: He left a deep impression on me – not with his vast knowledge and deep knowledge about nation-building, because that I already knew.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: We shared our views on many topics and many issues.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: But the one that stood out clearly was his passion and commitment in what is known today as "Singapore Together".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: At the dinner, Singapore Together had not been launched yet.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: But later on, the more I heard about Singapore Together, the more I understood what he is trying to do and why that night he was so passionate talking about this.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: Singapore would not be where we are today if not for the tripartite partnership (3P) in our economy and the 3P partnership in our society.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say (East Coast)
text: One that all of us will co-own and all will be proud of.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, firstly, I would like to take this opportunity to thank all the frontline healthcare workers, as well as frontline staff from the Ministry of Defence, the Singapore Civil Defence Force and the various agencies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of course, we must also thank all Singaporeans for their support and cooperation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am confident that we will be able to overcome this COVID-19 outbreak together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): I join my Parliamentary colleagues in supporting this year's very substantial Budget.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The size of the commitment will go a long way to tide us over a challenging and uncertain period.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just as our economy had seen its weakest growth since the 2008 Financial Crisis, the COVID-19 outbreak struck us out of the blue and there is not a single person here who has not felt its impact in one way or another.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Package is well-considered, taking into account the various aspects of employment so that we can help our workers retain their jobs and prepare for the future.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of the smaller companies are already struggling to remain in business and it would be tough for them to wait for another five months.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The timing of the payouts could mean the difference between survival and failure for some.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, we must consider the knock-on effects of company closures on other connected businesses.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The potential chain reaction should not be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, I urge the Minister to consider expediting the assistance.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government's decision to target support for the five sectors directly hit by COVID-19 is understandable.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Suppliers to businesses in these five sectors are suffering, too, as it is common that these five sectors outsource services to vendors and suppliers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Ministry would consider introducing some measures to assist companies which are similarly affected, due to their dealings with firms in these five sectors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a great idea to encourage companies to send their employees for training and reskilling.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, many smaller companies are unable to do so.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of these small companies are almost firefighting every day, they are also stretched for manpower, it is almost impossible to send workers for training.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, they may not have the financial means to do so.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government has committed to work with large anchor enterprises to support training for their sectors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some Singaporeans who were retrenched earlier would have greater difficulty getting jobs now.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They express their desire to continue working, not receiving financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Companies should be incentivised and encouraged with rewards to give these Singaporean jobseekers the highest priority for available jobs in their firms, especially those in their 40s and above who are willing to take part in PCPs, before granting Employment Passes (EPs), S Passes or Work Permits (WPs).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Government determine the scheme’s effectiveness and under what conditions will the Ministry review existing programmes to support the employability of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, I would like to share some suggestions about the support for the point-to-point transport service sector.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For taxi drivers, the hirer will qualify for the $10 per day relief and each hirer, being a full-time taxi driver, typically has to drive 15 to 18 trips per day.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Each hirer typically has a relief driver who also drives about 10 to 15 trips per day but relief drivers do not qualify for the $10 per day relief.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ride-hailing companies, which are asset-light, do not have to pay any such taxes as they are borne by the drivers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, the cost structures of both are different.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Taxi operators are matching the $10 a day relief fund by providing a rental rebate of $10 a day or more.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ride-hailing companies do not need to match $10 a day.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: PHC drivers typically pay 20% commission based on the total fare collection.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For an average day, PHC drivers pay about $36 in commission and the $10 per day relief is equivalent to 27.8% of their expenses.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, taxi rental per day is about $100.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thus, $10 a day relief is equivalent to 10% of the expenses of a taxi driver.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry consider reviewing the Special Relief Fund in view of the different cost structures of both?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government roll out measures to help them find other temporary and part-time jobs?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This group of workers can be redeployed to other tasks, such as temperature-taking.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I saw on television recently there were some who have taken it up.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They would need job counselling and advisory to point them to available temporary jobs or even career changes so that they can continue to secure a livelihood.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, we have benefited from careful and tactical planning which ensure that we accumulate and set aside surpluses for a rainy day.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thus, we are much better prepared to weather this storm of global uncertainty, economic shifts and the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Furthermore, this Budget goes beyond the immediate present and sets aside funds for mid- and long-term goals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, Sir, I would like to focus on assistance for the vulnerable and needy and request for more resources to be committed to help them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our Social Service Offices (SSOs) play an important role in coordinating social assistance for needy residents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They need help with their finances, job seeking, family relationship problems, health issues, care for their children, elderly or disabled family members.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Living from hand to mouth, struggling to just make it through the day, it is daunting for them to figure out where to ask for help, let alone approach different Government agencies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is very helpful that SSO, the coordinating body, provides them with the necessary guidance and help, such as job matching and linking them up with the relevant Government assistance schemes and services and voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs).

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This makes it hard for them to follow up with individuals or families to see if they are doing fine after help has been rendered and the cases considered closed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many social workers and case officers would definitely want to follow up to ensure their cases are okay because, in reality, there are always lingering or recurring problems which pop up as this vulnerable segment goes through the different stages in their recovery or relapse.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, with new cases approaching the SSOs for help, the challenge is having to prioritise with the very limited resources.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Presently, with so many touch and contact points, picking up and identifying cases are not so much of a problem.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Doing a longer and more thorough follow-up is the real challenge.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our social workers and officers need time to build rapport with these families and establish trust.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over a long period, with greater and deeper understanding of their cases, they could be more effective at proposing more long-term solutions and detecting other underlying or potential problems.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is very important, particularly where children or the elderly are involved.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are two groups of people who may not be able to articulate their problems or speak up for themselves.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Protecting and helping children are one of the most important things we should do because we want to enable them to grow up into healthy and well-adjusted individuals who can take care of themselves, break out of the poverty cycle and become contributing members of our community.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Besides providing more funding to hire them, we would also need to train those who are joining these positions mid-career.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Allow me to share my constituency experience about a senior who has been volunteering in my Henderson Dawson welfare committee after his retirement.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Ho Yew Wai, aged 70, is my resident.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He retired three years ago as a senior counsellor in the Family Court.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He visits individuals and families in distress, patiently talks to them and understand their issues, then works with our SSO, various Government agencies and VWOs to ensure these families receive holistic help.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After a couple of months of the case closing, he will get in touch with the families to ensure all is well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This goes on till he is confident that the family is alright.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If something has gone wrong mid-way, he will work with SSO again.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, much time and resources are needed for such a follow-up, and there are just that many cases one can handle.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Investing in resources to take care of our less privileged groups will yield positive results many times over.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The young will break free from the poverty trap, lifting their families with them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Those who are down will not remain down and out for long with many helping hands to pull them up.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Together, we will build a stronger, more unified Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A comparison of the price of EV versions with ICE or hybrid versions of the same car model shows that EV versions currently sells at a significant premium to their ICE or hybrid equivalent.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is mainly because lithium ion batteries are very expensive.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, costs incurred by car distributors to bring in EV models are spread over a small number of cars, thus increasing the per car costs.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The story is the same for plug-in hybrids which allow charging as a source of energy.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A Volvo S60 plug-in hybrid sells for $265,000, a whopping $90,000 over its normal S60 equivalent.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Factoring in the higher road tax for EVs, which will be introduced to compensate for the loss of fuel excise duties, I think EV adoption will continue to be slow.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While car manufacturers have introduced more car models with cleaner engine technologies, local distributors have been slow to bring them in.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, Volkswagen has an EV version of its Golf, called the e-Golf, but it is not available here.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The story is the same for Japanese cars.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Honda has a very cute EV called Honda E, again, not sold here.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last year, the top three car manufacturers are Honda, Toyota and, surprisingly, Mercedes.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Together, they account for more than 28% of total car sales.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Unfortunately, none of them brings in an EV or plug-in hybrid model.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To address this, I would like to suggest the following measures.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While we have a longer-term view for the year 2040, we need short- and medium-term targets as well.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In 10 years' time, by 2030, this will be raised to 20%.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Frankly, if we cannot meet 20% by 2030, there is no way we can meet 100% by 2040.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Without this push, our investment in charging stations will be wasted and the charging stations will become white elephants.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To incentivise car dealers to bring in EV and plug-in hybrid models, there should be double tax deduction for expenses incurred to bring in these car models.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Profits from such sales can also be taxed at a lower corporate income tax rate of 10%.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In order to increase the adoption of cars running on cleaner energy, we need to look at the whole value chain and not just from the car buyers' perspective.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that both MOF and MOT will look into my suggestions.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singaporeans have expressed confidence in the foresight of our Government and its willingness to spare no expense in ensuring that sufficient provisions are made for times of emergency.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Far-sighted and robust contingency planning has allowed us to prevail over crises in times past and will help us to tide over crises in times to come.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Budget 2020 is testimony to the commitment of our Government to help businesses and Singaporeans to overcome the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In particular, I wish to speak on how we can build capabilities in our Government, businesses and the community to ensure that we are prepared for future emergencies or crises.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I would also like to propose some measures that the Government can facilitate to alleviate the strain placed on our nation by COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the government level, the Tourism Authority of Thailand was able to use its BCP to help the Thai tourism industry recover after crises, such as the 2004 tsunami and the 2009 riots.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the business level, Nissan’s contingency planning, which was reviewed and refined multiple times over the years, allowed it to minimise production disruptions following the 2011 Tohoku Earthquake.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Its BCP includes measures, such as establishing a database to keep stock of supplies during an emergency, making its command structure mobile and drawing from a global supply chain made possible with alliances, such as the one with Renault.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To facilitate the effective development of BCP in business, the Government can issue BCP guidelines to the private sector, as the Cabinet Office of Japan did in 2005.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition to the operational benefits this will yield, on a psychological level, this will inspire confidence in our residents that their needs will continue to be taken care of during a crisis.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: With COVID-19, it is patently clear that even the best-designed BCP may be found wanting, especially when global supply chains are disrupted and fear spreads within communities.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is no shortage of literature displaying the dismal effects of COVID-19 on our businesses.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Firms in the aviation, tourism, retail, F&B and transport industries have been hit especially hard.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This can be done by providing matching grants to businesses when they give discount vouchers to consumers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This has caused many businesses to hemorrhage money as there are significant overhead costs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To keep our businesses afloat, it is important that measures which incentivise consumers to consume are implemented.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Businesses can entice consumers by giving them monthly discount coupons on air tickets, hotel stays and shopping vouchers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government can help by giving matching grants to these businesses to help soften the blow of COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This can be done by increasing the frequency of cleaning, disinfecting our surroundings and improving on hygiene.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can ensure that temperature checks are conducted at all shopping centres, hotels and tourist attractions.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These measures will further boost consumer confidence to visit Singapore and our attractions.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: An ill-maintained, dirty restroom is likely to evoke thoughts of disease growth and feelings of repulsion.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As such, the maintenance of clean toilets in Singapore can reduce these unpleasant sentiments and incentivise consumption by boosting confidence that measures to reduce the risk of disease transmission are being taken.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Based on the experience and expertise of various stakeholders, such as architects, interior designers, coffee shop operators and users, we have developed a new benchmark for clean toilets at coffee shops.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: By using the correct designs and materials, toilets can be built to achieve these desired outcomes as follows: first, robust and vandalism-proof; second, easy to maintain; and third, clean and safe for users.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This, together with the professional training of cleaners and continuously educating our users to be kind and gracious when using toilets, can transform the toilet culture in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: At the same time, it will remove potential breeding spots for bacteria and diseases.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will transform our toilets to be clean and safe.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, the South Korean government was able to enact huge and, more importantly, lasting changes within the span of eight years.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should learn from their experiences and start our own Singaporean Restroom Revolution.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I wish to now speak on building capabilities in the community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The community forms the first and last bulwarks against threats.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is likely that members of the public will be the first responders in crises.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As such, community participation should be factored into our contingency plans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Just go to your respective app store as the app is available on both the iphone operating system (iOS) and Android, key in "North West 911" and take the lead in preparing for emergencies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He spoke from the heart and made many instructive points.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He also reminded us that growth is not just for its own sake but it is, ultimately, about making Singapore stronger together as a society, for now and the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His clarion call to work together to progress forever is something all Singaporeans must join in.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Turning to suggestions, on the Stabilisation package, the hon Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Heng Swee Keat expressed gratitude on behalf of the Government to all frontline officers and then he outlined the Stabilisation package.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Many hon Members, including Mr Seah Kian Peng, and Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon today also echoed the sentiments of gratitude to the frontline officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to draw attention not just to these officers but their families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A few weeks ago, I met Mdm Jorah.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She is a nurse with Bukit Batok polyclinic.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She was accompanied by her husband, who is a stroke patient.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Her husband shared with me that on occasions, Mdm Jorah came back and shed tears.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was because she was scolded at the clinic by patients who were demanding surgical masks even though they did not have symptoms.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Her husband was the one who provided emotional support for her and, as a result, Mdm Jorah was able to carry on with her duties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am sure there are many such examples of families supporting frontline officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe these families must be recognised and supported, and to this, I make two suggestions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First is, if they are put to expense because of these deployment requirements, then I think it is only fair for them to be recompensed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One example is if they have to cancel a travel arrangement because leave had to be cancelled.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Alternatively, if there had to be some care arrangement like, for example, Mdm Jorah's husband is stroke-ridden and she had to make arrangements so that he could be taken care of while she goes back to the clinic.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The other thing is, it would be good if we can put together a package of discounts and even gifts for goods and services for the families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We could use perhaps the Courage Fund, with participation from Singaporeans and the private sector.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Government can play a role in providing the funds and funding incentives for organisations to honour our frontline staff and their families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I laud the introduction of this EEC to incentivise employers to employ and retain persons with disabilities (PWDs).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Just a short clarification, I would seek to understand what is the definition of PWD for this scheme?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it, for example, include persons with mental disabilities?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I know voluntary organisations, such as Bizlink, which do good work on this front, would benefit if this is so.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Now, ex-offenders still have a problem in securing decent jobs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I met Mr R who is 66 years old.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He has just been released from prison after serving five years for selling contraband cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He is exceptionally fit and looks much younger than his age.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He has Secondary 2 education and speaks good English.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He told me that he could only secure a part-time job as a coffee shop attendant earning $40 a day.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We can even work the EEC such that it can be crafted to reward ex-offenders if they were to stay on working and fully rehabilitate themselves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That would translate to some level of savings on behalf of the Government as well, because they do not re-offend.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would strengthen the "Unity" element of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Before I go on to seek my clarification, I also want to acknowledge the good work of the Singapore Corporation of Rehabilitative Enterprises (SCORE) in securing employment for ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But we can do our part to help SCORE to do its work to get better jobs for ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The incentives appear to centre on encouraging EV adoption as opposed to other options, such as Hydrogen Fuel Cell Vehicles (HFCVs), which are favoured by countries, such as Japan and South Korea.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister said, and I quote, "The Government is placing a significant bet on EVs." Deputy Prime Minister Heng does not seem to me like a betting person, but may I please ask what is the basis of optimism over EVs as opposed to HFCVs?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, what kind of infrastructural development is required to achieve the aim of 28,000 charges by 2030?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Do we need to build more substations, for example?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would there be cost recovery from users and, if so, how do you do so?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to share one point though from personal experience.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is a potential for municipal issues to creep in during the transition period when you convert parking lots for ICE cars to EVs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have dealt with situations where there have been complaints that EVs take the more accessible parking lots as opposed to ICE cars.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, sometimes, there is scope for such complaints to come up.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I appreciate that fuel excise duties generate revenue and are also imposed to discourage excessive driving.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It also has another element: it promotes less pollution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, I take it that in relation to this lump sum tax that the Deputy Prime Minister contemplates to impose, at least there will be certain savings for EV users because it promotes less pollution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had the chance to gather feedback from residents and committee leaders in Bukit Batok following Deputy Prime Minister Heng's delivery of the Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The observations that were shared were that it was very comprehensive, that it deals with "live" issues on the ground, particularly the fears of mid-career workers, cost of living and, of course, the economic challenge posed by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But we were able to do it without drawing on our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa highlighted this point in his speech and he highlighted that the prudent expenditure policy of the Government helped in this regard.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But one thing which I thought is worth highlighting is that, over the years, this Government had been making a heavy investment to grow the collective capabilities of our people and this, in turn, allowed us to achieve the real income growth as well as the economic growth.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result, operating revenue actually went up.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, that is real growth resulting in revenue increase and I laud the Government for that.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is a clear short-term focus on fighting the impact of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This takes the form of protecting local jobs, lowering corporate cost structures and household stimuli to mitigate the worries concerning the day-to-day expenses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Structural transformation of the workforce continues to be the mid-term focus.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is important that even in the midst of a crisis, we must not lose perspective of the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By recovering faster than the rest, we can leverage on a stronger headstart in the long-term, not to mention the efforts focused on climate change.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first topic is on help for businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Businesses are the bread and butter of our nation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister is right to address the immediate cash flow needs of businesses, and wages are a big part of this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: JSS will certainly help to encourage enterprises to retain their local employees during this period of uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Otherwise, it is almost half a year from now, which may not come in time for SMEs facing liquidity challenges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I urge for efforts to be made to prioritise payouts to companies whose finances are in poorer shape.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another concern is the period that we are basing the wages off.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us say an employer has hired an employee through the months of October to December.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He lays off the said employee in March.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I assume he will still receive his JSS payout.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, does that not defeat the primary purpose of this scheme, which is employee retention?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ultimately, helping businesses is also indirectly helping employees, so I am still glad that there is this scheme.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nevertheless, I hope the Ministry will consider the efficacy and timing issues of such disbursements to ensure they achieve maximum intended results.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, property tax rebates have been a common offering in Budgets in times of uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the intention is for commercial landlords to pass on the savings to their tenants, this is not guaranteed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Time is needed for landlord-tenant discussions to take place and then the administrative work involved to update the tenancy terms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, we can consider increasing the quantum of property tax rebates if the economy is projected to undergo a U-shaped or a slightly deeper U-shaped recovery.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In light of the difficulties experienced across many sectors, we have to ensure that the continued shift away from employment of foreign workers is also conducted in a sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially so for sub-sectors or firms which (a) have a high reliance on foreign workers, (b) are facing external headwinds from the earlier global economic tensions, and (c) are now further burdened by COVID-19 pressure on margins.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also hope more can be done to support sectors directly affected by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: An example is the Temporary Bridging Loan Programme which was introduced to the tourism industry.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we also consider this for the other four directly affected sectors?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I observe that the current measures are focused on retention and retraining of workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But if the business fails to pick up or if businesses are unable to revise their business model, it is only a matter of time before they have little choice but to let go of workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I was extremely delighted to hear the Deputy Prime Minister mention in the Budget that he has introduced a SkillsFuture Mid-Career Support Package for locals in their 40s and 50s to help them stay employable and move on to new jobs or new roles.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am in this 40 to 50 age group.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, hopefully, I will benefit from some of this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is good to know also that employers will be supported to recruit, retain and retrain our local mid-career workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I strongly support the effort to increase the capacity of reskilling programmes, such as PSP, by 2025.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This, in my view, is pertinent, because a skills-restructuring exercise is very important for Singapore in this transition phase that we are facing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, can we hasten and intensify the efforts on this and focus a bit more to provide more targeted help for those who are in their 40s and 50s and provide incentives for companies to absorb more of them into the PSPs, which we already had, but we can actually widen a bit more and focus on them in a faster way.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many existing SkillsFuture programmes require employees to be employed and nominated by their employers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For those who are not employed by a participating company, they sign up and hope they are shortlisted.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As with the typical job applications, there is no guarantee.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is not unreasonable to believe most companies will put their interests before anything else and that could mean choosing an applicant who is perceived to have greater potential, someone with better qualifications, younger and so on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This may result in the more vulnerable groups, the ones who need the training and reskilling most, being left in the lurch.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Companies should build their 40s to 50s Singaporean Core through this programme.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
