text: Their experience in the workforce, along with excellent work ethics, make them exemplary employees to invest resources in.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope this can still be considered by the Government, going forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: COVID-19 also underscores the vulnerability of income sustainability for the 40 to 50s gig and contract workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Freelancers across various industries are also affected, from trainers whose class attendances are slashed, to event organisers, emcees, photographers whose events are cancelled and so on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If COVID-19's impact lasts longer than projected, a second round of stimulus may be required to provide more direct help to these individuals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Regardless, job retrenchment and job transitions are inevitable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides current measures, how can we better support in these situations?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How do we develop our people so they seize opportunities in this fast-changing economy?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For every success story of someone who discovered their new calling, there are others who feel discouraged from months of seeking.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Cost of living is a perennial concern even amongst middle-class Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over the years, the Government has come up with new measures, raised income ceilings, provided relief to the sandwich middle-class who have children and elderly to take care of.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But in this climate of uncertainty, the current measures may be insufficient.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore imports more than 90% of our food.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Climate change and natural disasters around the world threaten our food security.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With demand exceeding supply, this drives up food prices everywhere.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Shipping costs, too, are going up due to logistical difficulty in shipping out supplies from China.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And with sudden waves of COVID-19 infection in certain countries resulting in city lockdowns, people are panicking and stockpiling food and necessities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I fear this may also contribute to further price increases in our food and essentials.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In a typical middle-income family, both husband and wife work, so most Singaporeans would dine out and order delivery.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Higher rentals and labour costs as well as increased water and electricity bills have all led to increased operating costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With prices of food and food services going up, a typical sandwich middle-income family can certainly feel the pinch from feeding their children, especially those with larger families.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many parents have shared with me that one of their greatest concerns is paying for their children's tertiary education.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, primary and secondary education in Singapore are, indeed, extremely affordable, but the same cannot be said for universities and polytechnics, where tuition fees and textbooks are hefty.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are bursaries and scholarships, both from the Government and community, but availability and eligibility are limited.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today's sandwich generation are worried about the healthcare costs of their elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is a substantial amount for a large number of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But beyond these, can the Government share how it will mitigate rising living costs or the perception of it, so that Singaporeans will feel assured to build and grow their families?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The asymmetric price adjustments are quite key because, sometimes you adjust prices lower and sometimes you adjust prices higher.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the midst of all the worrying news about COVID-19 and rising economic uncertainties, there is a silver lining.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our key strategy to ensure access to good education opportunities for all has likely contributed significantly to this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There has been heavy investment in education and, more recently, in early education, with a deliberate effort to level the playing field at the early stage.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we must not rest on our laurels.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, there are still vulnerable people who require support to gain access to nutritious food, healthcare and even shelter.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We read about them in the news, we hear about them from social service organisations, we see them at the Meet the People sessions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Labels like "high socioeconomic status (SES)" and "low SES" are being bandied around.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are familiar with the stereotypes applied to different aspects of life in Singapore, from what sport we play to the food that we eat.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our society is becoming increasingly status-conscious, and we need to put a stop to this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to prevent an underclass from forming.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Plenty has been said and done about empowering people through education and skills-upgrading.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The fact remains that there are many amongst the low-income group who are in low-wage jobs with little career prospects and wage growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Due to family circumstances, such as caregiving duties or being in ill-health, some of them are simply unwilling or unable to sink additional time and energy into attending courses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet, the only way forward is through renewed opportunities and upskilling.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One way is to redesign or change these jobs, and this is already done through automation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The other way is to develop workers to switch career paths.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, we need targeted help and handholding to make renewing opportunities possible for the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some social enterprises create job opportunities for the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have no doubt that they, too, are affected by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the nature of their business model, they may be harder hit than other businesses, as are their workers, if they have to be let go during this period.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, in conclusion, the best laid-out plans need a sound and sustainable fiscal strategy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The challenges facing Singapore in the 10 years ahead will grow in complexity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We will need all Singaporeans to come alongside to find solutions to these challenges and chart a new course for the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is reassuring that the Minister has committed expenditures beyond COVID-19 to measures ensuring our sustainability in the short, medium and long term.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am confident that with the Government, businesses and the people working together and playing our part to support one another, we will pull through the challenges together, stronger and better than before.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First, most Singaporeans are heartened by the speed and scale of our initial economic response.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The pressing issue now is effective implementation of the short-term economic package and a dynamic response as the crisis unfolds.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Effective implementation requires all parties to partner one another in the spirit of SG Together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must also respond dynamically as events unfold.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When major societies manage the pandemic in a decisive, clear and transparent way, the economic impact is limited to a short-term supply shock as well as deferred demand, all leading to a V-shape rebound.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: On the other hand, if major economies fail to implement containment and mitigation efforts, widespread fear and uncertainty will trigger a second level economic impact leading to a U-shape scenario.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Governments will need to coordinate economic responses within and beyond their borders.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And if a coordinated economic response fails, in an extreme scenario, global economic contagion could happen.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The global financial markets are starting to price in a U-shape scenario.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Investors are beginning to wonder: in the US, with the upcoming Presidential elections, can the Democrat-held House of Representatives and the Trump administration partner effectively on healthcare and fiscal responses?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And also, if Northern Europe can mitigate a pandemic more effectively than Southern Europe, will the former want to bear the burden of a large EU fiscal response?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, businesses, and many of them from my constituency, would like to contribute ideas on how we can implement effectively and respond dynamically.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Key areas to track include bank lending levels by sector and company size, short-term grant utilisation and efforts to help affected workers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, if companies withhold wage across the board, there could be less take-up on the Enhanced Wage Credit scheme.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Could we then perhaps redeploy funds to other short-term measures so as to achieve the intended positive fiscal impulse?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, some companies in badly affected sectors hope for more assistance in a prolonged downturn.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If we do so, our objective must be to protect the jobs of the Singaporeans in these companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Also, during SARS, the Singapore Tourism Board prepared an excellent marketing campaign so that we were one of the first to pitch for tourism when travel resumed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Even as things look bleak for tourism today, we can do similar preparations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Three, our banks must live up to the social and moral responsibility to lend to viable companies, especially now that the Government has done its part to take on more default risk.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many banks are digitalising their relationship and risk management approach.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, many smaller SMEs told me that they no longer know who are the champions within their banks, which is critical during tough times.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our Singapore banks have a strong reputation of being responsible in supporting viable companies during tough times.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Now is the time for them to earn that reputation for many more years to come.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Four, MAS can consider accelerating the banking licensing process for new entrants, if they can bring different perspectives on credit-worthiness, for example, through supply chain and data analytics so that more viable firms can benefit.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Five, some foreign workers are thinking of returning home.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After the Little India riot, I saw firsthand how our frontbench went systematically to major dormitories to calm the ground.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our TACs, businesses, the Government and unions can consider doing something similar.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Also, if there is an exodus of foreign workers from any particular country, perhaps MOM can consider temporarily expanding the countries our firms hire from.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Could MOF share the likely criterion to determine if a second package is needed, and the considerations and determinations on the scale and scope of further actions?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I also hope the TAC leaders, who are usually respected elders in their industry, play the difficult role to counsel owners, when their businesses are no longer viable and on how to move forward, so that they can seek social assistance early and move quickly to new opportunities, before their finances deteriorate beyond the point of no return.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to speak on MOH's and the taskforce's exceptional response to the coronavirus.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I recently ran into my family general practitioner of many years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Like many Singaporeans, he commended MOH for the excellent response so far.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: He shared that during SARS, we had limited medical resources.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The Communicable Disease Centre (CDC) 1 was a pre-war building and CDC 2 was a converted ward.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, we have an excellent system, with a state-of-the-art NCID at the heart of it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Well-informed foreign investors also shared with me that should a global pandemic happen, Singapore is best placed regionally to weather the storm.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am also heartened to see MOH's additional $800 million of funding, on top of the large post-SARS investments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As a comparison, the US is seeking additional funding of US$1.2 billion for their CDC, for a population of 300 million.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Clearly, our Government spares no expenses when it comes to protecting the lives of Singaporeans!

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With globalisation and climate change, we must expect more pandemics.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And if that is not possible, we can explore prepositioning materials and manufacturing capabilities within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We are making wonderful progress for our seniors to age with purpose and dignity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our urgent task now is to strengthen the employability of mid-career Singaporeans, especially in a protracted downturn.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First, I hope mid-career Singaporeans will fully embrace the SkillsFuture NextCareer Package, now that they have an additional $1,000 credit.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I also hope to see stronger publicity by all for SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Second of all, I hope some industries and TACs can step up.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: A sector is more viable if the companies actively steer industry development.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some industries have yet to come up with compelling visions, despite the additional help that the Government has provided to TACs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Without a compelling vision, Singaporeans will struggle to identify meaningful paths for upskilling within those sectors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If things do not move in some of these sectors, I hope the existing companies and Government can partner to create alternative TACs to drive industry development.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Too many jobs, especially from mid-career Singaporeans, are at risk if we do not do this transformation well.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, in a protracted downturn, I hope the Government can actively work with certain established industries to absorb more mid-career Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These include the construction, engineering services, healthcare, social work, which usually face difficulty recruiting Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Companies can tap on MOM's many excellent initiatives to attract Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I also hope that affected Singaporeans will also keep an open mind for these jobs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But I am confident that Singaporeans will rise to the occasion.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And if things do not move, I hope the Government can consider further DRC reduction for these specific sectors and implement the Fair Consideration Framework vigorously.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Tough actions could be necessary because our sectors that usually absorb mid-career Singaporeans, whether they are heartland enterprises, the Integrated Resorts (IRs), airport, hospitality and private hire transportations, may not be able to do so now.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must give our mid-career Singaporeans the best fighting chance to stay employed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond current concerns, we must also look out for longer-term trends.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I hope our House, as a whole, can start tracking developments in Base Erosion and Profit Sharing (BEPS).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our tax incentives for income within and beyond Singapore are important tools to anchor major investments in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The Group of Twenty (G20) has turned on the pressure on hub economies, such as Singapore, Switzerland and Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has weathered Phase 1 of BEPS well through quick adjustments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But there is a Phase 2 coming along two dimensions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One, the EU and the United Kingdom want a cut of their own citizens' e-commerce revenue, even though existing rules dictate that tax revenue should largely reside in locations generating economic activities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The US currently stands in the way of this proposal, as they benefit from e-commerce.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But one cannot rule out a future compromise, to the detriment of hub economies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, some major developed economies are pushing for a minimal global tax so that they can tax their companies more, even if companies get a preferential tax rate elsewhere, regardless of the justification.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In troubled times like this, we can see the mettle of a country's governance system.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Yes, Singapore is undoubtedly the canary bird for globalisation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Pandemics, trade wars, terrorism, climate change, fake news can hit Singapore hard and fast.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, the world can expect Singapore, in the spirit of SG Together, to emerge stronger from every crisis because they know that the hallmark of Singapore is our ability to implement effectively and respond dynamically to short-term, medium-term and long-term challenges all at the same time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With that, I stand in support of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I rise to affirm my support for the recently delivered Singapore Budget Statement 2020 and to provide a response from the manufacturing and business community.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The general sentiment from the manufacturing and business community is that this is a Budget that recognises the current challenging local and global economic climate and which seeks to provide for a better short- to medium-term economic future for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, as one of the local TACs, and as one which represents an important contributor to Singapore's GDP, SMF wishes to state unequivocally that it will stand united and work with other TACs and Government agencies to drive our businesses through the current challenging times and forge better futures for enterprises.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: We stand ready to assist wherever we can and will do our utmost best to prepare our members to be in the best possible condition to take advantage of the opportunities that will come with the upturn of the economic cycle.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In relation to the relief measures for COVID-19 announced by Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat, the feedback is that many are glad that attention is given to both enterprises and to individual workers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This would aid businesses greatly by allowing them some degree of certainty in adjusting their budget amidst the current climate of uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Another aspect which is causing much anxiety and worry for the manufacturing and business community is that of the disruption of the worldwide supply chain.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As manufacturers, the worry is two-fold: one, the difficulty of attaining raw materials; and, secondly, even if products can be manufactured, how would goods reach the customers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This would, in turn, affect the manufacturing service providers downstream.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In a recent dialogue session with members from the SMF family, there are many who voiced real and genuine concerns over the current economic conditions.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In relation to preparing our businesses and economy for the future, SMF is extremely heartened that feedback from our members has been acknowledged by Deputy Prime Minister Heng in the Budget speech.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: SMF has always prided itself on being a collaborative TAC, working with the Government as well as commercial entities to broaden and open new opportunities for our members.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is pertinent to note that Deputy Prime Minister Heng mentioned in his speech the hope that Singapore companies digitalise and internationalise.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: SMF strongly believes in exploring new frontiers, which refers not just to new physical geographical locations, but also to the very much evolving digital realm.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I have always communicated to our business leaders whom I have the privilege of meeting, that digitalisation is important for both society and businesses to advance further than what Singapore is today.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is ever important that as the cyber world progresses, Singapore cannot be left behind as a third world nation or even as a developing nation because the speed of progression is simply too rapid.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I am happy to share with this House that SMF has already embarked on several programmes, working alongside the Government, to encourage our members to transform, innovate their business models towards Industry 4.0 and explore new frontiers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: These corporate transformational programmes include conducting hands-on knowledge and capability-building courses at our Centre for Corporate Learning, leading business missions to both local and overseas markets, organising Free Trade Agreement talks and seminars and being the first TAC to administer the SMEs-Go Digital – Digital Project Management Service.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: We also seek to attract young talent into the manufacturing community by being on board the Global Ready Talent Programme.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This is what I like to say is an example of how individuals coming together, which is aligned with the SG Together movement driven by a common aim, can indeed make a difference.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is my sincere hope that other TACs will also join in and work together in a concerted effort to drive our economy onwards and upwards.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The wise leaders of generations past of this country have practised financial prudence which has allowed for such a generous and decisive Budget today.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I humbly urge my fellow Singaporeans to not take this for granted.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In such uncertain economic times, the ability of the Government still to seek to deepen capabilities at every stage of growth and provide for every segment of society is, indeed, laudable.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident that, working together in unity as a united country, our Singapore flag will rise above all the uncertainties as a stronger, more resilient nation that will continue to thrive and succeed on the global stage.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With this, Sir, I affirm my support for Budget 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Employees who signed up for the MAD scheme received generous payouts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unexpectedly, less than a year later, business picked up again.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some of his former employees – the same ones who had received payouts under the MAD scheme – were rehired at their previous salaries and went on to work many more years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Now, we may laugh at the unfortunate name of the scheme and the apparent short-sightedness of the employer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But when business is down and the bottom nowhere in sight, it must cross the minds of bosses to cut jobs and save costs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, despite the uncertain outlook, retrenchments were maintained at 2018 levels.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, with the COVID-19 outbreak casting a pall, concerns have heightened.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The recent announcements by Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat, therefore, provide welcome relief.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This means that an SME with 10 local employees earning median salaries would get about $8,000 in Jobs Support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With the greater sense of uncertainty, employers may hold back or even reverse wage increases.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Through the enhanced Wage Credit Scheme, the Government will co-pay 20% of qualifying wage increases in 2019 and 15% of increases in 2020 if this higher wage is sustained.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Effectively, more than four months of the wage increase is borne by the Government over two years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Why so much emphasis on jobs and wages?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Neighbourhood stores have already noticed a sharp drop in revenues as shoppers cut back on spending.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When livelihoods are at stake or incomes stagnate, even necessary spending on essentials like healthcare and education may be delayed.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Individuals will also have limited capacity to upgrade their skills and stay relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Moreover, employers would need time to mobilise and train manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When the upturn comes, businesses could easily find themselves shorthanded and unable to respond to opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will result in the drag on our business community persisting longer than necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Understandably, besides jobs and wage support, businesses that hire foreign workers had hoped for levies to be waived.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members of Parliament like Mr Seah Kian Peng and Mr Arasu Duraisamy asked about it, too.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are waiving levies for employers whose foreign workers are required to serve quarantine, Leave of Absence or Stay-Home Notices when they have a travel history to China.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we have not done so for foreign workers in general because it will not benefit the many employers who only have local employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, we have not raised levies either.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, levies have remained the same since 2017 for the construction sector and 2016 or earlier for other sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are two other important reasons for not waiving levies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, in supporting businesses, our priority was also to preserve local employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, as much as we want to help businesses, measures to deal with the short-term fallout should not negate longer-term efforts for companies to become less reliant on foreign manpower for growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Levy waivers or reductions would have run counter to both objectives.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some commentators are troubled by the difficulty of attracting locals to these sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Others believe these moves are painful but necessary; they say it is "tough love".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I should point out that, unlike for the services sector, the quota cuts for the construction, marine and process sectors are at the S Pass level and not at the Work Permit level.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: S Pass jobs are skilled jobs which polytechnic graduates and even ITE upgraders are able to perform.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and several Members of Parliament asked that flexibility be provided to employers who find it difficult to attract Singaporeans to certain jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, employers can already enjoy short-term flexibility in meeting foreign workforce criteria under the CTP and the Lean Enterprise Development Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At a structural level, too, we recognise the differing appeal of sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the construction sector, out of 100 employees, up to 87 can be foreigners, of which 15 can be S Pass holders, even after the changes kick in by 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A company in the services sector of the same size can have up to 35 foreign employees, of which 10 can be S Pass holders starting from January 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Which subsector or occupation will accept having more restrictions compared to others that have less?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Looking at it from a different lens, which local employees would feel it is fair that their employers need not worry or try as hard to improve job quality to retain them because of more access to foreigners?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Can we be so sure that foreigners will always accept the work conditions our own people find unappealing or that will they not find better jobs back home in time to come?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Kenneth Loo, former President of the Singapore Contractors Association and Executive Director of Straits Construction, acknowledged this point and talked about the need to "…try to make jobs more meaningful and attractive through digitalisation, so that processes can change and the environment will be more palatable to workers".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If I may suggest to Mr Douglas Foo, employers in the manufacturing sector should plan ahead, too.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We would not have seen how industries can rise to the occasion.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One lunar new year about a decade ago, when I was still serving as a Labour Member of Parliament, Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong visited a leading hotel to thank the workers for sacrificing time with family to give tourists a great guest experience.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Sensing an opportunity not to be missed, the hotel's general manager literally ambushed the Prime Minister and gave an extended presentation on the hotel's manpower woes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I am not sure whether the Prime Minister remembers it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As in many sectors, he cited the unappealing nature of work and asked for "flexibility".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In contrast, my visit to Copthorne King's Singapore Hotel last Friday was a breath of fresh air.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our main purpose had been to understand how the hotel was coping with the sharp fall in occupancy due to the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: General Manager Kung Teong Wah, however, took delight to also outline the many ways in which work had been redesigned to raise productivity, easier and more satisfying for his employees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The mobile app is linked to an in-room control unit which also turns off electrical power when guests have left the room and alerts facilities managers when light bulbs or other amenities need fixing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Cross-training of staff to handle expanded job roles have led to manpower savings, better wages and increased job satisfaction.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even the cleaner I met, 58-year-old Pari, is happy that the washroom renovations and upgrading of cleaning solutions will help him to work more years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As a matter of fact, in the last few years, I have witnessed the resolve and creativity of hoteliers to overcome their manpower constraints.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Yotel at Orchard Road allows guests to check in themselves easily and get items delivered by a friendly robot.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Andaz Hotel no longer has a team of confectioners in its kitchen.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Instead, it keeps customers happy with supplies from Tiong Bahru Bakery and cleverly brands this as part of the heritage experience for guests.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Lyf at Funan replaced the usual laundry services with a hipster corner where guests can chill out while the washing machine does its job.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But they also show how important it is for us to stay the course and not give up too easily.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Productivity has improved greatly in some sectors, but not fully caught up with the best in the world.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Likewise, for other sectors, we should try our best to position ourselves for the future even when the chips are down.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is exactly why we have focused on Jobs Support and Wage Credits, so that businesses and their people can continue with operations and press on with restructuring with help from the Enterprise Transformation Package.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At this juncture, allow me to commend the tremendous efforts of NTUC in support of these aims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Starting with Secretary-General Ng Chee Meng, Labour Members of Parliament have outlined specific initiatives like CTCs and the Jobs Security Council.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOM, MOE and MTI and all the lead agencies for the relevant sectors will certainly work closely with unions in the spirit of SG Together to make it a success for businesses in terms of their transformation for the benefit of all workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked whether these efforts will be enough and whether unemployment insurance will be needed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, we had discussed this in Parliament extensively in May 2017.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Countries with unemployment insurance typically have persistently high unemployment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In contrast, Singapore has consistently had full employment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Willingness to pay for unemployment insurance is not the same as most people do not expect to need it and also have other buffers, for example, a working spouse or child.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While we keep an open mind on unemployment insurance, we should also be aware of its serious downsides, such as reducing employers' willingness to pay retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Studies have also found that unemployment benefits can have the unintended consequence of reducing motivation to find work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our current approach of focusing on employment support has shown encouraging results and is likely to be more sustainable.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Mr Lim Swee Say has pointed out, Singapore's way of managing the opportunities and challenges of globalisation has produced not just economic growth but, more importantly, employment and wage growth.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As long as jobs are still being created, our focus on employment support helps both individuals and businesses.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will continue to provide short-term financial relief to the needy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Programmes like Adapt and Grow and SkillsFuture help workers reskill and seize better opportunities in the longer term.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This approach has the full support of the unions and employers which other countries find harder to do.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As to the question of using CPF monies to fund reskilling, the key question is whether the lack of training funds is the main barrier to career transitions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government directly subsidises a very wide range of training programmes, up to 90% in some instances.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To fund the unsubsidised portion of reskilling or self-improvement courses, Singaporeans have access to workplace sponsorships and schemes, such as SkillsFuture, Mid-Career Enhanced Subsidy and Workfare Training Support.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At present, it does not appear that the lack of funds is a significant barrier.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Ms Sylvia Lim herself has also acknowledged, we are redoubling support to both employers and individuals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I suggest that we focus on these initiatives instead of putting at risk the Retirement Savings of our people.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time, focus on issues that matter to mid-career persons, which Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Jessica Tan and several Labour Members of Parliament talked about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It demonstrates the Government’s resolve to help businesses and workers ride out the challenges amidst economic uncertainties.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Focusing on helping Singaporeans retain their jobs and providing Wage Credit so that businesses can maintain the momentum of transformation will have a profound impact on our economy when it recovers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Amidst economic uncertainties, some businesses that employ foreign workers might ask, why does MOM not reduce or even waive foreign worker levies?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, as the saying goes, those who do not plan for the future will find trouble on their doorstep.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Although we want to help companies ride out the current economic uncertainties smoothly, we also hope that companies will sustain their transformation efforts and thereby reduce reliance on foreign workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, we must, first and foremost, ensure that all Singaporeans can keep their jobs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Hence, from the long-term point of view, companies must quicken the pace of transformation, improve productivity and create more jobs to attract Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As a whole, our measures must take into account two sets of considerations: reducing business costs in the short term, and keeping up with transformation efforts over the longer term.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am heartened to see that many companies are planning to use this lull period to send their employees for training.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think these companies have an eye on the future, because once the economy picks up, they will be in the forefront of the starting line and raring to go, and they would be able to take their businesses to greater heights.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, in the meantime, even with all the help provided, I acknowledge that some businesses may still have to manage excess manpower.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Is there a right way of doing it?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Yes, but let me tell Members of one wrong way.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: An employer claimed she was recently told by MOM to lay off employees much against her own wishes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Well, it turns out the employer did not tell the full story.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, she had decided to shut operations temporarily and told her workers to go on no-pay leave until further notice.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is unfortunate if she has to close even with Jobs Support and Wage Credits.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But asking the workers to bear the uncertainty of waiting for her business to restart makes matters worse.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For those workers without savings, they will need other jobs to pay their bills.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is one thing to ask if her employees would like to volunteer for no-pay leave; it is quite another to force it upon them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As the employer had stopped paying salaries, it would also not have been fair to expect her foreign workers to stay in Singapore with limited means of supporting themselves.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Instead of seeking levy waivers, MOM advised her that it would be more appropriate to repatriate the foreign workers responsibly and to reapply for Work Permits in future when business picks up.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower and Responsible Retrenchment recommends other options besides no-pay leave and layoffs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This could include redeployment to other work areas, shorter work weeks, job sharing or adjustments to certain wage components.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These options would at least maintain most, if not all of the workers' past incomes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will help employers whose Chinese workers have not gotten approval to return to Singapore and also cannot hire new Chinese workers because we have suspended approvals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am heartened to see that businesses are paying attention.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In their own ways, they are responding to these challenging times in the spirit of SG together.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some are asking their workers to clear their annual leave or time-off.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Others are exploring shorter work-weeks while sending their workers for skills upgrading.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: NTUC Health Co-operative shared with me that this virus situation has sparked a viral interest amongst its workers in leveraging technology for alternative work arrangements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Almost overnight, even if they are mature workers who were struggling to pick up digital tools, had found ways to hang out and engage in discussions virtually with their younger colleagues.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Kudos to the companies that are proactively considering such sensible measures not just to cut costs, but to save jobs as well.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is our commitment to Singaporeans in their 40s and 50s – that they, too, can have an extended runway; and that everyone, at every stage of life, will get the fair chance they deserve to grow and progress at work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Deputy Speaker, I have two clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First, it is regarding my suggestion on the use of CPF.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have actually filed a cut for the MOM Committee of Supply (COS), so please let me elaborate more at the time, and I will be interested to hear the Minister's response then.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second clarification is that I am glad to note the Minister saying the Government still keeps an open mind on solutions, including insurance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, how confident is the Government moving forward that you will be able to handle and find solutions for everyone who applies under those schemes?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I understand their anxieties and they matter very much to me.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We looked at it, at the level of all local PMETs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We looked at it also at the level of all citizen PMETs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, it is quite a comprehensive report and it is publicly available.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It was also quite well reported in the media.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We do not take the improved employment outcomes of our citizens for granted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have to work very hard for it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, in the last Parliament Sitting – actually, I think it was the same Parliament Sitting that Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat delivered the Budget Statement – Mr Pritam Singh had filed a question specifically on how we are helping these PMETs enter into areas of job growth, enter into occupations that they may have been unfamiliar with.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The results that we have so far are quite encouraging.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our approach in handling this challenge is to go at it from different angles.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the engine for job creation goes flat, all bets are off.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Which is why, in terms of how we think for enterprise growth, enterprise transformation, because ultimately it is businesses that create jobs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are very mindful to help make sure that they can upkeep a certain momentum.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, the first thing to do is that we must always keep creating jobs and not just any jobs, but good jobs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What that means is that you need to keep ensuring that the business environment is pro-business.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Lim Swee Say earlier talked about the importance of AI.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think it is AI plus many other domains where we want to make sure that our businesses will be able to develop a competitive edge in.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that is the most important foundation for ensuring good employment outcomes – PMETs and non PMETs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For this, I find the attitudes of Singaporeans very commendable.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most people are very aware of it and they are personally invested in it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, I think that is the reason why there have been so many calls consistently, "Please top up our SkillsFuture Credits" and so on.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think that is also another very important part of the effort.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, you have the three things that are necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Then, at the same time, we also need to ensure that there is continued Government support for reskilling and job creation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Those pieces, you need to have in place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Will there be individuals who still find difficulty?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, earlier in his opening speech to kick off the debate, highlighted how difficult it is to go through transition, the sense of insecurity, perhaps a sense of not being able to navigate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In Workforce Singapore as well as e2i, quite apart from doing job matching, we are very mindful that sometimes just getting jobseekers to a place where they are receptive to the different opportunities, that is also a very important part of the work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One significant barrier – I think much more so than the lack of funds for training – is that there is a concern about moving into new occupations or sectors that individuals are unfamiliar with.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, how can we provide the scaffolding and the handholding to help people to make those transitions?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is very much a part of the effort.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is the MOM COS debate coming up next week and we can speak more about that.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This Budget aims to provide Singaporeans with new job opportunities as well as care and support for those in need of financial and social assistance.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Just as important, I admire the foresightedness and proactiveness in safeguarding our future against the potential harm brought about by climate changes.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The decisive move of providing financial assistance to help businesses, especially those heavily impacted by COVID-19, is also critical and timely.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that a one-time funding of $500 may not be sufficient in paying for a fully effective, upskilling course as lifelong learning requires continuous, ongoing support.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, not everyone has the desire for upskilling and should there be much of these funds left unused, there will be misallocation and underutilisation of resources.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: While I understand that these courses are already highly subsidised, I am wondering if it would be more effective to further subsidise it, but add a limit to the number of courses each individual can take up per year, instead of mass distribution of these funds.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This would allow interested citizens to reap the full benefits of the subsidy while we continue to encourage those who have not signed up.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would like to declare my interest as the President of the Pharmaceutical Society of Singapore and the Head of Pharmacy at KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As a healthcare professional working in public over the past 20 years, I foresee potential loopholes.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: How can we tell if each claim is within reasonable limits and not excessive?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: And f there are excess claims, how are these rechannelled to help other needy patients and not inappropriately disposed of?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: There is a need to tighten how these funds are used to ensure that the taxpayers' money is spent appropriately.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Without central audits and controls in place, there is a potential for misuse.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat and Minister Josephine Teo spoke about foreign worker policy and the need to further restrict S Pass holders for the identified industries.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: While we agree that we should always put Singaporeans first and give them the best possible opportunities, but we know that there are jobs out there that are really challenging to find locals to take on.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: An example of healthcare-related jobs are pharmacy technicians, whose service is required 24/7, including public holidays and weekends.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Although we have polytechnics that specialise in training and educating diploma holders to support this pipeline of pharmacy technicians, most of our youngsters aspire to take on higher qualifications after their graduation, leaving a constant vacuum in the system.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned that if this persists, pharmaceutical care for our patients will be significantly impacted.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: To overcome this long drought, pharmacists are actually standing in to take on pharmacy technicians' duties.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This is extremely cost-inefficient, especially in view of rising healthcare cost, as we are not fully utilising their advanced skills and knowledge to serve our patients.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that service industries in other fields are also facing similar problems.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: While the Government may advocate for automation to improve productivity, there are situations where automation, for various reasons, is not feasible.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In healthcare, a lot of frontline patient care activities require healthcare professionals to display empathy and compassion to each individual patient.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Such duty of care simply cannot just be easily replaced by machines, and I think similar sentiments can apply to many service industries.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that if we want to reserve jobs for Singaporeans, we should reserve jobs that they prefer – jobs with good career upside and work-life balance.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: And if the intent is to avoid over-reliance on foreign workers, then there is a need to ensure that the solutions provided to solve current problems are feasible, for example, if there is good headway with mid-career transition programmes, before we further cut S Pass quotas.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Not all of them have to do with automation at all.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even in some areas where automation can play a part, it does not mean that we are asking companies in the services sector to automate human interaction or automate the customer experience.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In manufacturing, I visited a company making noodles.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Because at peak hours, when the customers start arriving in the restaurant in droves, you have no more time to do portioning.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You must be able to cook very quickly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Hokkien noodles are produced using the extrusion method.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You extrude the noodles, then you cook it in a big pot of water and then you —

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister Josephine Teo, are you giving another speech or are you providing a very extended clarification?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I apologise, but very quickly, let me just summarise.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Actually, there are many of these things that are backroom.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are so many more things that we can do.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And credit to the businesses – they are much more creative.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I just want to share that with the Member.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hope that, as the leader of your professional association, you can consider trying out these ideas, too.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Sir, the theme for this year's Budget is a Unity Budget, or in our national language "Bajet Perpaduan".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I welcome the efforts to provide more support to Singaporeans during a time when the people are facing the challenge of the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such financial assistance and support are essential because it will make those affected feel that their needs and their future are looked after and not neglected, and this will eventually preserve and strengthen social unity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is seen in many studies where social class divide has an impact on social unity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because those who lead a disadvantaged life will feel dissatisfied, because while they have to go through a difficult life and there is no one looking after them, there are others who live a life of luxury.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Building and maintaining psychological resilience is no easy task, as it requires patience and sustained efforts.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Building psychological resilience can only be achieved by inculcating positive thinking and values within society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We can all agree that any society that possesses strong psychological resilience will not easily crumble when going through challenging times like the one right now.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: When any crisis happens to a nation, society, family and individual, it has always been good practice or good culture if some introspection or self-reflection was done on its causes and the lessons that can be gleaned from it.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My experience as a family counsellor has taught me that we can choose whether we want to go through a crisis positively or negatively.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If we choose to see the crisis from a positive aspect, we will be able to learn many lessons behind each episode.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Conversely, if we choose to see it negatively, then there will be a lot of grievances, sadness, anger and even depression.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This situation is best described through an analogy called "The Eyes of a Fly" and "The Eyes of a Bee".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, when a bee flies into a place full of trash and other kinds of filth, it will still try to find a fragrant flower to land on.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This analogy, to me, is the best example that can be used to guide us whenever we face an undesirable situation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We can choose whether we wish to view a situation using "The Eyes of a Fly" or "The Eyes of a Bee".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: When looking for answers, finger-pointing and accusations often take place.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Finger-pointing is one of the negative traits that can exist in a person.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is human nature to have such negative feelings, and while it is not wrong to have such feelings, it is definitely wrong when we express those feelings through remarks, words and actions that hurt the feelings of others and make them angry.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Leaders in politics, community and organisations, including heads of households, have a duty to set a good example so that those under them will follow their lead.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As the bearer of this responsibility, a leader must be big hearted and view certain incidents with a sincere and compassionate heart.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In doing so, a leader will be able to make a positive and objective assessment whenever an adverse incident takes place, and thus will be able to think about and work on ways to improve the situation as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is no mean feat, but it is the duty of any leader to continue trying and developing the values that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Praises and words of encouragement have flooded social media channels and the mainstream media, directed towards fellow Singaporeans who are in the frontline in the fight against the COVID-19 virus outbreak.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It was amazing and heart-warming to hear about some F&B establishment owners coming forward to provide free food and drinks as a token of appreciation and support to those working in the frontline.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We also witnessed wonderful efforts from Singaporeans who wish to contribute positively to promote community spirit by distributing free masks and hand sanitisers to the public.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is something that we can be proud of and it is touching.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The unity on display in the situations I mentioned earlier is something positive that can ignite a community spirit that makes them stand united in the face of challenges.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Unfortunately, Sir, there had also been some incidents that were less pleasant and could erode this spirit of unity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Some members of the public also shared that they received sharp stares when they coughed or sneezed in public places.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many also gave their take on the reasons behind this situation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As a society, we must try to practise the following pearl of wisdom, that is, “It is Better to Stay Silent if One Does Not Have Anything Good To Say”.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We should all take a constructive and positive approach.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Employment and employability support measures are needed as jobs become more challenging to be created or retained.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, any form of support for both employers and employees to continue to hire and be hired, is very much welcomed.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For my speech on the Budget, I wish to speak on employment-related matters and will focus on three aspects: one, support for older workers to continue working; two, support for persons with disabilities or special needs to be employed and be financially independent; and three, flexi-work provisions and support.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, on support for older workers to continue working.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Singaporeans live longer and the proportion of older Singaporeans increase relative to younger residents, we have to make provisions and review our policies to ensure that older Singaporeans can continue to stay actively employed and engaged in our society.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Both initiatives will help older Singaporeans remain employable and provide opportunities for them to continue to learn and upskill.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At this juncture, Mr Deputy Speaker, please allow me to speak in Malay.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   A part of this year's Budget is for the allocation and assistance to Singaporean senior workers as well as mature workers in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I welcome such allocation and support for workers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I hope that our senior workers and mature workers will seize the opportunity to enhance their skills and continue training in their respective jobs and careers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Certainly, the journey and the effort towards upskilling and continuous training are not easy.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It takes time, it requires determination and hard work, it requires more expenditure and it also involves personal sacrifice.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, this sacrifice will result in a wealth of benefits and opportunities that will be enjoyed in the future – the chance for job promotion, job opportunities or higher pay, as well as growing our self-worth.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the saying goes, "You have to undergo hardship and difficulties before you can enjoy the fruits of your labour".

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And let us not give up too easily if things get tough when undergoing upskilling and continuous training.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the saying goes, “In for a penny, in for a pound”.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, we must also acknowledge that the times are changing rapidly and we cannot ignore the impact of disruptive technologies, as well as economic transformations that have and will change the way we work or do business.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, we must be ready to ride through this inevitable change.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to the details of these two initiatives during MOM's Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While numerous provisions, schemes, grants and initiatives have been introduced, implemented and led by the Government and Government agencies, employers need to also do their part to facilitate the training, continued employment and contributions of older workers in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For a start, the jobs that older workers do have to be meaningful and cannot simply be menial work that younger Singaporeans shun.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Taking on the role of mentors, trainers, coaches or supervisors would be more meaningful for older workers who have a wealth of experience to draw from and impart to younger workers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Employers need to explore ways to redesign jobs for older workers so that they can continue to contribute and draw from their experience, skills and knowledge meaningfully.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Persons with disabilities or special needs have always found it more challenging than most of us to be gainfully employed, stay employed and have opportunities for career progression.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For some of them, finding employment is a seemingly insurmountable hurdle.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Employer contribution and support are still substantially required and not many employers are willing to go that extra mile to invest in persons with disabilities or special needs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other than employer support, persons with disabilities or special needs seem to earn relatively lower salaries than typical hires.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While there is insuﬃcient data to confirm this, the anecdotal evidence is already quite disturbing.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do we expect persons with disabilities or special needs to be able to fend for themselves with much less disposable income?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do we expect them to be dependent on others for the rest of their lives?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can we not accord them greater recognition, as well as remuneration, for their abilities and talents out of the goodness of our hearts as fellow human beings and not just depend on numbers reflecting positive returns on investments?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will speak more on providing the necessary employment support for persons with disabilities or special needs in the MOM COS debate.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The current COVID-19 public health situation has been a very challenging one.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our daily work routines are drastically changed and remote interactions and communication have replaced physical interactions or face-to-face communication.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, with every challenge comes an opportunity for us to learn and initiate and embrace change.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We find that even with some initial inconveniences, we are able to work remotely, flexibly and still fulfil our daily work or meet our daily business targets, with some creative provisions and solutions, to ensure business and work continuity.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Flexi-work is not too diﬃcult to implement after all.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Necessity is truly the mother of all inventions.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that once we are able to ride out the current COVID-19 public health situation, we will remember the lessons we have learnt during this period and we will continue to implement flexi-work with the support of employers and companies.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just as we trust our workers and staﬀ to work remotely or on a flexible work arrangement during this period, we must continue to trust them to give the same amount of commitment and eﬀort when the worst is over.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To conclude, Mr Deputy Speaker, I reiterate my support for the various provisions, as well as the employment and employability assistance measures provided for in this year's Budget.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While there are still areas in which the necessary provisions and assistance can be even further enhanced, the Government is cognisant of the various needs of the diﬀerent segments of our society and has done much to ensure there is some help for everyone.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond the dollars and cents the Government will be spending on helping the diﬀerent segments of our society, including for employers, we have to continue to work together to make our society, communities and workplaces better, stronger and more inclusive.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us continue to build our "democracy of deeds".

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is what SG Together is all about.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If I may end with a quote by Winston Churchill: "We make a living by what we get; We make a life by what we give." Notwithstanding the suggestions I have for future provisions and assistance by the Government, I support this year's Budget.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, I asked for mental health to be a whole-of-Government priority.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It was unintentionally prescient then to see this in action now with the multi-Ministry task force set up to tackle the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The psychology of our people became more than a priority for the Government to understand so as to manage the panic buying, hoarding and shunning of healthcare workers, all coping mechanisms to deal with underlying fear and anxiety.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Research studies have found that these deficiencies of community resilience can be caused by poor mental health, leading affected communities to be less cohesive, adaptive and more vulnerable to shocks and disruption.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The near-term uncertainties and long-term structural shifts that the Deputy Prime Minister highlighted should, therefore, alarm us to the need to prioritise mental health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I was very encouraged in the recent month by Prime Minister Lee, the Deputy Prime Minister and several Ministers rallying Singaporeans around the need to strengthen social and psychological resilience, both critical pillars of our Total Defence strategy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, Mr Deputy Speaker, you will understand why I was disappointed that mental health was not mentioned at all by the Deputy Prime Minister during his speech, despite mentioning "resilience" four times.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The ability to adapt to significant and adverse changes we call resilience is not happenstance; it is enabled by good mental health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To put into perspective, which I also did last year to limited success apparently, the prevalence for diabetes in Singapore was 8.6% in 1992, peaked at 11.3% in 2010 and has seen remarkable improvements since the "war on diabetes", decreasing to 8.8% today.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As one doctor shared with me, "Until the Government starts taking the stand that mental health is as important as diabetes, there is a limit to what individual organisations can accomplish".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In comparison, many other developed countries, such as New Zealand, Scotland, Iceland, Finland, Canada, Norway and Australia, have identified mental health as a budget priority with significant resources dedicated to support mental well-being in their societies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But let me assure Members that I am not, although that would be clearly so much easier for this part-time Nominated Member of Parliament with no institutional support!

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, I shared the mental health struggles of those near and dear to me, including my own close shave with depression more than a decade ago.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, these sharings did not seem substantive or representative enough to persuade our policymakers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, earlier this year, my amazing team of volunteers and I decided to launch the first-ever public consultation on mental health in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Rudimentary it may be, given less-than-limited resources, we were surprised and heartened by the more than 400 responses received from Singaporeans, 70% with lived experiences whilst the rest from caregivers and mental healthcare professionals!

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
