text: Many of these personal stories are heart wrenching.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We even ended up doing "case work" with some!

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But since personal stories did not seem to move policymakers last year, I decided I will focus this year’s speech on where we are falling short in the specific areas of affordability, accessibility and quality in mental healthcare and concrete urgent actions that I hope the Deputy Prime Minister and relevant Ministers will take.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It broke my heart when I read one respondent "having to starve to afford therapy".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: At least 10 respondents shared they stopped seeking help because of financial struggles.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: How is it that our world-class healthcare system has denied so many people the mental healthcare that they need?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A respondent shared, I quote, "I paid over $10,000 total   for inpatient care after deduction of MediSave and MediShield Life for the past two years", even after "opt  for class B2 and C wards to save costs".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is time to remove this entrenched stigma by bringing these limits to parity for both mental and physical health conditions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Seventy-one respondents also shared that lack of relevant and trusted information was a prohibitive factor against seeking help.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I was, however, encouraged by the 23 respondents who commended the Community Health Assessment Team (CHAT), a public healthcare initiative by the Institute of Mental Health (IMH) located within the community.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, CHAT currently only serves the youth segment but I hope this model could be adapted and expanded to support all ages.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, let me commend our mental healthcare professionals for their hard work, many of whom I know personally.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, many respondents indicated that the poor quality could be attributed to the excessive workload which strains both professionals and the system.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As one respondent puts it, "While the Government is ostensibly pushing campaigns that aim to reduce the stigma of seeking help for mental health issues, there is a lack of parallel funding for actual mental health services, such as the hiring of more counsellors and mental health professionals".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Twenty-six respondents cited the importance of feedback on treatment to improve their health outcomes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One respondent lamented, I quote, "They never asked me for feedback.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I would like them to ask for feedback." Continuous improvements happen when we empower clients and patients by recognising that they are part of their care process, too.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the same vein, strategic plans, such as the Community Mental Health Masterplan, must involve extensive public consultation, especially those with lived experiences and their caregivers, while ensuring that aggregated public health data continues to be shared transparently.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This helps to improve local research on mental health issues and better coordinate efforts in supporting mental well-being of our communities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The recent launch of a multi-agency consultation effort on youth mental well-being is a wonderful start.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Incidentally, in the spirit of SG Together, my team of volunteers created a simple website called SGMentalHealth.com, so that we can also share what we found from the public consultation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We also received responses on other policies, ranging from confidentiality, support in schools and workplaces to issues surrounding mental healthcare for marginalised or vulnerable communities like the differently-abled, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer (LGBTQ+) and migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I will highlight these issues separately with the relevant Ministries during the COS debates.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These fundamental issues in affordability, accessibility and quality of our mental healthcare must be addressed by the Government with a fierce urgency or we risk another decade of increasing prevalence in mental illness, despite the well-meaning awareness and anti-stigma efforts.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The structural and policy issues discussed earlier aim to close the treatment gap.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But what if we could reduce the number of people getting ill in the first place?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: What if we paradigm-shift mental health as a public health issue?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: What would our policies for mental health promotion and illness prevention look like?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And the spike in the number of teenage suicides in 2018?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Might we not insist on conducting mental health screening for our students every year, like physical health and dental checks?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Will we begin to study the role of social justice, family and schools in mental health so that we can address the underlying social determinants?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Will we also start to understand the impact of public policies on the psychological capital of our people and endeavour to create a psychological safety climate for innovation and well-being to flourish that truly binds Singapore Together?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Another paradigm shift we urgently need to make, Sir, is the long overdue recognition that mental health is a critical part of total well-being.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is not "I'm mentally sick, or I'm not".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It’s not "I'm over it, or I'm still in it".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It's not "I got it, I will never get it".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We may think that mental health challenges only affect certain people, or some segments of our society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But if we just pause and have an honest conversation with ourselves, we will realise that we are navigating along this continuum at any point in time through our life.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Who has not had a major life transition?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Who has not felt overwhelmed with responsibility for another?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Who has not been marginalised in some way?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Who has not been made to feel like a failure?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: None of us in this House can pretend that we have not struggled with a dearth of mental health at some point in our lives.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Changing this paradigm of thought will help us think about how we can strengthen the support available within our communities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When asked what helped them most in their mental health journey, many respondents shared the importance of community support.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When we translate these paradigm shifts into strategies across the system, we may then see why it makes sense to expand physical health education to total health education in schools to include mental health; why workplace health and safety must be beyond physical health and safety, which I am very happy to note that the Tripartite Oversight Committee on Workplace Health and Safety – of which I declare I am a member of – has started doing good work in this area with employers and employees; why there is merit in making it explicitly clear to employers that the Sick Leave entitlement for each worker can also be used for mental health treatment and recovery and that mental health insurance is not a luxury but a necessity for employers to support their employees' total health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Strong mental health support at schools and workplaces directly impacts how we show up for our roles in our family and community – which contributes to how we support our children as parents, our elderly parents as caregivers and how we build strong ties and connections with our friends, colleagues and neighbours.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This returns us to the importance of resilience as individuals and communities, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The mental well-being of our people – man or woman, young or old, rich or poor, working or jobless, straight or gay – forms the bedrock of our psychological resilience and social cohesion, which may be the only sure way to secure our future in Advancing as One Singapore against the headwinds ahead.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Do we need to see more parents lose their children to suicide or more young people in distress for mental health to be a public health priority?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is surely the loudest anti-stigma signal to send!

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I also urge all Members of Parliament in this House to support the mental health needs of their constituents so as to create resilient communities as part of this SG Together effort.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To Singaporeans, I invite you to remember that wherever you are on the mental health continuum is not solely a matter of personal agency but also largely determined by your social support structures, or lack of.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, if you are struggling right now, I hope you know it is not a personal failing.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We are all responsible for one another's mental well-being, including the Government and institutions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: You have, in fact, shown us what true resilience is by fiercely living each day with less-than-adequate state support in mental healthcare whilst constantly dealing with structural stigma and discriminative behaviours.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They have bravely come forward to share their struggles.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Their generosity and courage keep me going on this crusade for change.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I share the same hope as this respondent who said, “I hope that the day comes soon where no one has to feel alone in their mental health journey.”

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The US-China trade war was still not settled and technology continued to disrupt businesses and threaten jobs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: At the same time, it allows us to focus on the longer term to transform our economy and reskill our workers for our long-term sustainability and success.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is a good reminder that the reason why we have been able to put together such a package is because of the surplus generated and Reserves accumulated over the years by our previous generations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Successive generations of Government and Singaporeans have worked hand in hand to get to where we are today.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our Pioneers led the way and the Merdeka Generation worked hard and transformed our country.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One of the values that have got us this far is resilience, as a nation and as individuals.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This year's Tampines East Edusave Merits Bursary (EMB) ceremonies coincided with Total Defence Day.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I took the opportunity to remind the audience that Total Defence is more than just military deterrence.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Home team agencies and institutions, such as our hospitals, play a critical role, too.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The COVID-19 crisis has shown us once again that defending Singapore against threats often requires a whole-of-Government approach.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It involves coordination among multiple Ministries and agencies, with an eye always on the bigger picture.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our response to the COVID-19 emergency has been admired by many.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This entire response and operations that the taskforce has mounted are not something we should take for granted.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: On behalf of my residents, may I say "thank you" to all involved in dealing with the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What is heartening is that during my house visits, I met several residents who told me “we have to play our part against the virus”.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some of them, I learnt, sanitised the lifts daily on their own accord and their neighbours were not aware.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They also realised that the cleaners were busy cleaning common touchpoints and so swept their own corridors.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: At EMB ceremonies, I noticed some of the children were having stage fright.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I encouraged parents to share with their children their own fears and insecurities.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Let our children know that everyone has fears and we must try and overcome them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I told the audience I do not like public speaking.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But I am really glad I did not let that stop me from doing my work now.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Likewise, parents can share meaningful lessons in their lives so that their children get to understand difficult situations and decisions.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They can learn to think through some of the challenges and build resilience.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In Tampines, we have a free bowling programme during the school holidays.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We deliberately mix students of different races and schools during the game.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One of the girls went home crying because she was afraid and uncomfortable mixing with students she did not know.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Her mum took leave to bring her for the next session and shared with her that she will not be able to choose her own secondary school classmates or work colleagues in future.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She told her to try and adapt and she will be there to support her.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We watched the girl as she finally enjoyed the company of her lane mates and even forgot about our presence.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We love and protect our children, give them the very best we can, put them first.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But the most important value we can teach is to instill strength, the tenacity to try things, be adventurous in thoughts if not actions.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Striving is a fulfilling process but it is not an easy one.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am heartened that this Budget signals that the Government is standing with all Singaporeans in their determination to build a better future for themselves and their children.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And coupled with resilience, we will all emerge stronger and better together.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Resilience is only one face of the Singapore Spirit.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The other equally important face embodies the graciousness and kindness that many Singaporeans are displaying every day.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I witnessed that firsthand in Tampines earlier this month.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Not only did more volunteers turn up to help, we also saw more residents, including new faces, approaching us to donate food items.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some thoughtfully added bottles of hand soap in their donations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: During the same period, I visited a family in Tampines which has a member who was infected.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The rest of the family members were quarantined at home.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We delivered some daily necessities to the family.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I also took the opportunity to visit the other residents in the block.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: My heart swelled with pride as I witnessed our residents putting aside their concerns to step forward to help fellow residents in need.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: So, let us persist and continue to strive together for our people and our country.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: I dedicate my speech today to two important issues close to my heart, caregiving and ending sexual violence.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: It is my hope in 2020 that we dedicate more attention to addressing these critical issues and make greater strides towards a more inclusive society and a safer society for all.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: They lead active lives, but 10 years down the road, their lives could possibly be very different as they enter their golden years.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: As a child to my ageing parents, the prospect of assuming some caregiving responsibilities sometime in the near future weighs on my mind.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Around me, peers of my age share similar concerns.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: The old age dependency ratio in Singapore has been declining over the decades.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: As our loved ones grow older, there are fewer of us to share the labour and responsibilities of caregiving with.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: How will we continue to lead the lives we have when we potentially also have to be caregivers?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Would our work schedules allow us to juggle work and care?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Would we be able to afford hiring professional help?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: What other options are there for our parents to age with dignity?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: For women, the pressures are felt even more acutely as societal norms continue to promote caregiving as women's responsibility.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: The female caregivers are also usually wives or adult daughters of the care recipient.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: The pressure on women to be caregivers has a great impact on their ability to engage in paid work.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: In comparison, just over 15,000 men cited the same reason for being outside the labour force.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: The compromises that women make to their work lives negatively impacts their financial security.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: According to Central Provident Fund (CPF) statistics, about four in 10 active CPF members who turned 55 in 2017 did not meet the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) of $83,000 in their Retirement Accounts.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Among them, women have more difficulty meeting the BRS.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Ask any caregiver around you and you will know that it demands a great deal of energy, time, resources and attention.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: You could find yourself waking up several times throughout the night to attend to your loved ones' needs, or having to spend hours persuading them to take their medication, or even straining your back trying to physically move them.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: For the hundreds of thousands of caregivers out there, stress, burnout and feelings of resentment may not be uncommon.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Not only do they have to contend with the physical stress of caregiving, they are also struggling to balance the demands of paid work and dealing with care-related expenses which they are also now responsible for.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: When you become a caregiver, it very often becomes the central identity and the focal point of your life, and you find that the other aspects of your life: your job, friends, hobbies, leisure time have to accommodate caregiving, not the other way around.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: How can we better redistribute caregiving responsibilities between men and women, but also between the family, community and state?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: How can we, as a society, ensure that caregivers are not compromising on their own health and financial security as they carry out this often invisible and thankless work?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Over the years, the Government has introduced numerous policies to support family caregivers, including most recently the Caregiver Support Action Plan.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these initiatives, such as the subsidies for long-term care services and foreign domestic worker levy, have no doubt been of tremendous help to those who benefited from them.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: However, I believe that our efforts can still be strengthened and would call for even bolder moves.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: To start, we need up-to-date and more robust data on caregivers in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: The last national survey on informal caregiving was conducted almost a decade ago.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: There should be regular systematic tracking of the number of caregivers in order to understand the scale of challenges they are facing.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I highlight two workplace policy suggestions that have been raised by various experts and civil society organisations like the Singapore Alliance of Women in Ageing.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Workplaces need to accommodate care, not the other way around when we recognise and accept the fact that all workers, including those who are employers, will likely find themselves with caregiving responsibilities at some point in their lives.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Can we consider legislating the right for employees to request for flexible work arrangements (FWA)?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Such legislation has already been successfully introduced in the United Kingdom (UK), New Zealand, Canada and Australia.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Research shows that current utilisation of FWAs is low due to bias by middle management and requirements for "facetime" at the office for performance appraisal, bias against part-timers and reluctance to change the status quo.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Without equal mandated access, those most in need, like caregivers, are likely to be denied access to FWA and will have no choice but to exit the workforce.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Second, childcare leave should be converted to family care leave so that all workers have the option to utilise it for their dependants.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Those with children and other older dependants should be given a longer quantum of leave.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Unpaid caregiving leave is not sufficient for caregivers as they must use up their own personal and medical leave, leading to caregiver burnout and health problems.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, family leave that allows for caregiving of relatives is voluntary, unlike childcare leave that is mandated at six days paid per parent for Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: We need to make these options affordable for families.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: The figures are 24% to 63% for upper middle-income households.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Government can review the subsidy system to ensure that the cost of these services are not prohibitively high to families, including middle-income ones.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: On to the next topic, having just graduated from Singapore Management University (SMU) in the recent years, I am particularly concerned about the recent spate in campus sexual violence cases as well as how the use of technology has enabled new forms of sexual violence to be committed.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: This next part of my speech would focus on how we can better address these two forms of violence.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: But first, I would stress the importance that sex education plays in ending violence against women.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Efforts to address sexual violence are usually focused on legislation, punishment and remedying the effects for survivors.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is a crucial need to address social norms and attitudes which enable sexual violence.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: The prevalence of sexual violence, committed overwhelmingly by men against women, reveals an ugly truth about the way society views women: that women are not human.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Sexual violence is fundamentally rooted in the idea that women are objects, devoid of agency, rights and feelings, that women exist for men's pleasure, that women are not equal to men.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Education on consent, sexual violence, gender equality, is, therefore, absolutely necessary to transform society's understanding and views for the better.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: In this vein, I believe that the sexuality education children and young persons receive in schools is a powerful tool to catalyse change from young.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Is the current sexuality education curriculum reflective of and relatable to young people's experiences with sex, sexuality and gender-based violence today?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Are students themselves consulted to find what they need and want to learn from sexuality education?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: What needs and gaps in knowledge do they have that are not being met by the curriculum?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: According to the United Nations, comprehensive sexuality education, apart from providing scientifically accurate information about sexual and reproductive health, also importantly includes discussion about gender roles, human rights, gender equality and threats, such as discrimination and sexual violence.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Our sexuality education syllabus should be inclusive and explicitly address these topics.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: I now turn my attention to campus sexual violence.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: News headlines have recently been dominated by sexual offences committed within education institutions.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Given the stigma around sexual violence, it is reasonable to assume that many more of such cases go unreported.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Students have a right to feel safe in schools.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: In 2016, it was asked if the Ministry of Education (MOE) would formulate guidelines and provide anti-harassment training to staff in tertiary institutions in Singapore based on the recommendations of the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Workplace Harassment.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Then, they responded that institution-specific codes of conduct were already in place to prevent harassment on campuses across the nation.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: However, in the wake of Monica Baey's brave sharing last year, it has become apparent that relying on individual institutions to develop their own policies and protocols is often inadequate.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: There is an uneven level of protection across institutions, with differing definitions of what constitutes harassment, and varying complaint, investigation and disciplinary processes.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: This means that whether students get their case investigated, how it will be investigated and what the outcome may be, and what support they receive as victims would differ, depending on where they go to school.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: This code should set out the duties of the schools to ensure zero tolerance of sexual harassment, provide adequate victim-care support and set out standards and principles for investigating and managing complaints.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Another worrying trend is the rise of sexual violence involving the use of technology, such as social media, spy cameras and mobile recording devices.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Having one’s privacy being invaded and intimate images of themselves shared publicly without consent render a distressing sense of helplessness.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Even with the successful conviction of the perpetrator, the traumatic effects of having one’s intimate images and recordings still circulating in the public domain will still be felt by survivors.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that survivors of such offences can be better protected.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: In Australia, complaints about one’s intimate recording being shared non-consensually can be made to the eSafety Commissioner online.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat and the team behind the Budget will take these suggestions into consideration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: "Daddy, why don't I take the school bus so that you do not need to rush anymore?" Those words by my daughter Ella cut through my heart like a knife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My six-year-old daughter taught me an important lesson that morning when I was sending her to school last year, a very painful lesson.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She made me realise that it was time to slow down and not rush all the time, especially in front of her, how my actions had made her feel bad and a reminder about how precious time is. "Spend time with those you love, one of these days you will either say I wish I had or I'm glad I did".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I used this quote in this House a few years ago and I am sharing it again not just because it is a beautiful quote to live by but also as a timely reminder to myself and to all of us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I love singing all the Disney songs with her on the way to school, I love listening to her talk about her dreams, how she was at the ice palace and enchanted forest and met Elsa.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I love listening to all the gossips and playground politics in her school and, my goodness, there is so much politics.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But, most of all, I love just spending time with her, precious Daddy-Ella time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But if there is one thing we did not give out, it is time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Time, which is priceless and time which our Government can give out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need more precious time with our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need more time with our children who desperately need us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We already know that the vast majority of childcare centres have six days of annual closure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that, for most parents, the entire six days of childcare leave could be used just for these annual closures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us not forget about the additional three half-day closures on the eve of any of the five stipulated public holidays.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What happens when your child falls sick or for any other times when childcare leave is needed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Applications for such leave must be supported by a medical certificate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is much needed as parents should be there to look after their children when they are sick.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Out of all the illnesses, including chicken pox, influenza, stomach flu and the list goes on, let me focus on the Hand Foot and Mouth Disease (HFMD) as an example of why we need more childcare leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is something almost all parents face and we should help them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is extremely difficult for parents to find help to look after their children as the infection can last for up to two weeks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also hard to find someone to look after your child as the caregiver has a good chance of being infected.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was infected by my children when they had HFMD.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: From the employers' standpoint, do they really want their employee who may also be infected to come to the office and possibly spread the disease or any other illness to other employees, resulting in everyone going on medical leave?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Also, do we honestly think that the employee can concentrate at work and be productive?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would they not be worrying about their child who is sick?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our current childcare leave does not make sense.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Surely, we can all agree here that if you need six days of childcare leave for one child, you cannot also only need six days of childcare leave for two, three or four children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It may make sense if you can make sure all your children fall sick at the same time, which is not quite possible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, officers with two children, one of whom is below age seven is eligible for four days of childcare leave per year with a medical certificate (MC).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An officer with three or more children, has nine days of childcare leave per year with MC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is on top of the six days of childcare leave per year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government clearly feels that childcare leave is important for people who work for the Government, why then would it not be important for the people we serve?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There may be an argument that giving more childcare leave can inadvertently affect the employment prospects of parents with more children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this is not the case for the Public Service and, surely, this cannot be a reason for us to not do what is right for our people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Surely, the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices can be used to address this concern.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we want Singaporeans to have kids and have more kids, then we need to give them more time to look after and be with their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not just about making preschool more affordable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reply to my suggestions might be that we rather focus on FWAs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can work on providing more FWAs for our people but also legislate more childcare leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I used to help out at his Meet-the-People Session (MPS) and he always made sure I go home as early as possible once MPS ended.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He said to me, "Louis, make sure you don’t go home one day and your daughter calls you uncle!".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That advice is not just for me but for everyone and a timely reminder that while we work hard, we should also spend quality time with our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And it is not just about spending time with our children but also with our parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has stated, "With a rapidly ageing population and smaller family units, officers with elderly parents will need time to take care of them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new parent-care leave reflects our position as a family-friendly employer." It is encouraging that an increasing number of private companies are providing this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But 20% is still really a small percentage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our parents are the reason we are here today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They worked hard to bring us up and looked after us when we were young.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should be there for them when they are ageing and now need us to look after them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On 11 May 2015, I was getting ready to go to work and I told my wife I was going to inform the Animal Concerns Research and Education Society (ACRES) team that I needed to take some time off to spend with my Dad who was in hospital.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was already visiting him every day but I decided I should spend more time with him.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I was about to leave my house, my sister called and told me that Daddy had lost consciousness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I really wish I can turn back time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I made a mistake and I regret it till today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I wish I had spent more time with Daddy and I miss him dearly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, through sharing this with everyone, this wound might finally heal and, through sharing, I hope that others will not make the same mistake I made.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government's statement: "With a rapidly ageing population and smaller family units, officers with elderly parents will need time to take care of them", holds true for all of us and not just civil servants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the Government feels that it is important for civil servants to have parent-care leave, then why not others?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will address the feedback we have received and, if we want to, we can take it a step further and offer parent-care leave in blocks of hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is, ultimately, a personal choice to take leave to spend time with those you love but this Government can help make things easier for employees and I hope we do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We will always do our best to help you and your children progress with Singapore and have a better life".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us also stand with our workers when it comes to childcare leave and parent-care leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope this Budget is not just about the economy but also about giving our people precious time to rest and to spend with their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Vivian Balakrishnan once said, "Life is a one-way ticket.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A baby will only remain a baby for a very short time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They will grow up before we even realise it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The thing about life is we cannot rewind time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, my advice to young parents here is, your children need you, they need you desperately and they need you only for a very very transient time in their lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we miss it, we can never get it back." Sir, I thought I should end by saying that I am still sending my daughter to school and picking her up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A few months ago, she made a card in school for me and gave it to me when I picked her up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This time, she melted my heart with her words.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She said, "I love you, Daddy, because you always take me to school".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am now a part-time school bus driver as I now have to send our twins, Katie and Poppy, to school as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They, too, melt my heart with their words.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I picked Poppy up the other day and she gave me a big hug and said, "Daddy, I really missed you".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to more previous Daddy-Ella, Daddy-Katie and Daddy-Poppy time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to more hugs, more laughs and much more sweet words from them that give me that warm fuzzy feeling.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This year, I would like to devote my time to speak on environmental resiliency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The world today is at a crossroads facing down the existential threat of human-induced climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over 11,000 scientists worldwide now warn that the world "clearly and unequivocally faces a climate emergency".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore's vulnerability to climate change is also evident.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One in 10 people on the planet now live in a place that has declared a climate emergency and have effectively used it as a jumping point for real action.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Inspired by young Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, youths across the world are rising up and demanding immediate action to address the climate emergency we are facing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore's recent SG Climate Rally is a cry for action from our youths, one that the leaders of today ought to heed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleagues and I in the Workers' Party have heard it loud and clear.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We agree with them and have sought actively to raise concerns about climate change and the policies that can be taken by the Government.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are glad that some policies have been looked into and taken up.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, it would be prudent to recognise that there is a long way to go in building environmental resiliency in view of the lessons the world has learnt and is continuing to learn about our relationship with our environment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the certainty of climate change, we, as a nation should be daring and set a bold Green Agenda to guide Singapore's trajectory of development.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Please allow me to put forth some ideas to this House.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need a holistic view on climate emergency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need a holistic response to all issues of climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, the success of efforts to combat climate change must not solely be measured by the effectiveness of any one policy narrowly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must also invest in and track efforts to address the wide-ranging impacts of climate change and our policies on society at large, whether be it on urban drainage systems, food security, water security, waste management, urban liveability or public health, to cite but a few impact areas.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An example of this is coastal adaptation and flood protection.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the Government commits to investing more in coastal adaptation and flood protection though, where will this money be spent on?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the money be invested in the best science so that better projections of sea level rise can be made for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will investments be made in the best social science, so that the prioritisation of coastal land uses can be better assessed?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will soft-engineering, nature-based approaches, such as the restoration of intertidal ecosystems, which have the potential to protect our coastlines, be considered for use under this fund, or will only hard-engineering approaches, such as polders and land reclamation, be chosen?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would be useful if the Government could give a sense of its spending priorities in this regard.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Preparing to adapt to climate change alone would be unwise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There must also be a move to mitigate climate change while we still can.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even as we have committed to the 36% cut on emissions intensity by 2030 in our first pledge, how have our efforts been to date?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Workers' Party also welcomes both the announcement by Minister Masagos Zulkifli at the Madrid Climate Conference last December that Singapore will submit its long-term Low Emissions Development Strategy soon, and the announcement by the Deputy Prime Minister that Singapore's commitment to the Paris Agreement will be updated this year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We look forward to the Government's updates, and to understand how they represent progress beyond our current commitments and strategies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Climate change has also accelerated the need to calibrate Singapore's infrastructural development to meet environmental challenges.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Transport is a major sector which requires such calibration.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, many practical electric vehicle (EV) issues are to be hammered out in the interim and I would like to ask what actions the Government will take on them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The biggest elephant in the room is on rebuilding an infrastructure currently tailored for ICE engines.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The power grid, in particular, will be taxed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While Singapore is in a power glut now, electricity demand will only go up as Singapore moves on in its Smart Nation ambitions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One looks to Sweden with a ban on ICE vehicles slated for 2030, where demand for electricity is currently outgrowing capacity in local grids, forcing EV charging networks to compete with other infrastructure projects for electricity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not to mention that Singapore currently generates upward to 95% of its energy via natural gas.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While it is the least-polluting fossil fuel and has higher efficiency compared to ICE vehicles, there will continue to be a carbon footprint generated.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Should we even be contented with this ratio?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides intelligent charging solutions, should the Government also consider the alternative of battery swap stations which have the advantage of speed, ensuring load on our power grid can be managed well, as well as providing a ready infrastructure for battery recycling?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has been tested in China and should be a key consideration here.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How soon can we electrify our public bus and private hire infrastructure to EVs will also be important as many Singaporeans rely on such services.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Ministry of Transport give a timeline on this happening separately from the 2040 overall target?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) internal combustion engine cooperation is also needed if we are to successfully electrify our transport system.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A key consideration here is Malaysia, where people and trade currently travel via the Causeway and the Tuas Second Link on ICE vehicles currently.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we do phase out ICE vehicles here, are we also implementing a ban on foreign ICE vehicles from entering Singapore?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If there is no infrastructure in place in Malaysia to support commercial EVs, would that also impact our businesses with a top partner in trade?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is important to get right as, on one hand, foreign ICE vehicles and how we handle the issue, may have a significant impact on our EV plans and, on the other hand, we should not be seen to export our green problems away with unilateral bans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, we can work with Malaysia's state and federal authorities to build a sustainable and inclusive ecosystem for EVs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To go one step further, we can propose an ASEAN Autonomous Vehicle and Electric Vehicle project that holistically looks at all the challenges of EVs that my colleague Mr Leon Perera had previously mooted in this House.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will help to focus minds towards a target and benefit interconnectivity across the region.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The effective solving of these issues I have highlighted in the adoption of EVs can turn us into the bellwether state in ASEAN for EV adoption, just as Norway is for both the Nordic region and the world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Housing is another area where calibration is required.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If urban planning is right, we can reduce the Urban Heat Island effect, increase energy efficiency and promote better waste management in our towns.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We, therefore, welcome the Housing and Development Board (HDB) Green Towns Programme as it encourages sustainable living.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, will the benefits afforded by this concept be accessible only to new towns, or will our current HDB estates in places, such as Hougang and Aljunied, be retroactively upgraded to enjoy these benefits?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should also not forget about private properties and improving green efforts there.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, improved greening efforts there can help net bigger gains.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Government consider expanding the Estate Upgrading Programme to include greening items for private estates?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This may include solar-friendly installations in common areas and greening up shelters or building community gardens that act as carbon sinks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, could there be further incentives to push for solar installations across private households that allow excess power to be sold back to the power grid?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, payment is made by way of a credit adjustment based on the prevailing nodal prices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, there does not seem to be incentives beyond that for private households.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If private property owners can buy into such plans, this can help us reach the two gigawatts-peak (GWp) capacity target sooner and give further sustainability and robustness to our power grid.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us next talk about Protecting our Green Areas and Redefining Development.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition to gearing up our economy and infrastructure to prepare for the climate emergency, it is worthwhile to ask ourselves whether we are doing our best to reap the benefits of environmental sustainability for our society.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government often lauds its green accomplishments under the City in a Garden paradigm – on increasing accessibility to parks, on the upkeep of community gardens, and on projects like Gardens by the Bay, for example.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each of these efforts bear their own positive outcomes for environmental education, community involvement, ecotourism and liveability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But amidst the continual urban greening of Singapore, are we prepared to risk undermining the benefits provided by the relatively more natural and more sensitive green ecosystems in our country?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These ecosystems benefit us in a plethora of ways, from helping us store carbon and cool Singapore, thus aiding our response to climate change, to acting as havens for biodiversity with educational value.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition to their potential as sites for low-impact, sustainable ecotourism, they provide Singaporeans with recreational value and with relief from our stressful urban environment, a benefit that is much harder to quantify but is nonetheless important.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The latter two of these have been styled as a "forest town" project and a "nature destination", respectively.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will speak more on this in the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources' (MEWR's) Committee of Supply (COS) debate next week.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Beyond good policy, Singaporeans also need to come together in buying in to this Green Agenda.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mindsets must shift in the way we consume, to only use what we need to use.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just to cite a common example: single-use plastic bags.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we take or use what we really need?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we pack more things into each plastic bag?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do we really need to double bag all our groceries at the checkouts?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we only need to use, say, one or two plastic bags for refuse disposal a day, do we need to take 20 bags from the supermarket a week?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can also reduce the number of single use plastic bags we need to take for our refuse by concurrently using good quality reusable shopping bags.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We may end up using fewer single-use plastic bags and may still have enough bags for our refuse.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To encourage Singaporeans, we should ramp up our public education to reach out to Singaporeans of all ages and educational levels and in different languages.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should even encourage easy accessibility to the latest research on climate change by the average citizen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Translating this research into readable, digestible commentaries for Singaporeans gives further buy-in and builds awareness.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should spare no effort to lead the region and the world in this effort, not only as an honest broker but also as an innovator in the space.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We owe it to our future generations to do so.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Whether it is the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) scores of our 15-year-olds, our economic competitiveness, our healthcare outcomes, our CPF system or our public housing, the world looks to us as a model of a highly-functioning and thriving country.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: To be sure, we are still a young nation and we, too, look to other nations for examples of how to do better here.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This is more than a 50-fold increase in a short span of 54 years.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Put it another way, we have achieved a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of about 8%, on average, each and every year over the last 54 years.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I believe the preconditions of success are, firstly, the peace and stability afforded us by an effective Ministry of Foreign Affairs, our Singapore Armed Forces and our Home Team.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Beyond that, an effective and honest Government, which is sometimes quite rare, and working hand-in-hand with our employers and workers.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I can think of two key principles that have served us well and have brought us here.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Achieving fiscal prudence starts with having a balanced Budget during every term of Government.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Unlike in many other countries, Singapore has been building up its Reserves, instead of running deficits.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: How we achieve this is to ensure that recurrent revenue – those that are built into our system and are not one-off in nature – equals to or exceeds recurrent expenditures – those that we expect to incur year after year after year and not one-off in nature.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: So, recurrent revenue must equal or exceed recurrent expenses.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: That is a formula for a balanced Budget and that is very important for fiscal prudence.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: As pointed out in this House, Singapore is facing rising healthcare costs for two reasons – advances in medical technology and, specific to Singapore, a very rapidly ageing population.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: And also because we did so well in healthcare, our life expectancy is getting longer and that also means that medical costs will go up.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This figure is expected to further increase over the next decade for the reasons I cited.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Now, the need for more recurring revenue becomes even clearer if we also consider two other risks to our fiscal revenues.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: First, our Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) and, secondly, the OECD's proposed Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) regime.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: First, let me talk about the risk of a lower NIRC.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Today, the NIRC from our Reserves is the biggest component of our revenue.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Going forward, it will be increasingly challenging to achieve a similarly high NIRC due to the very low interest rate environment all around the world.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: In fact, last night's 10-year treasury is about 1.35%.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: In some other countries like Germany, Switzerland, Japan and so forth, they are even experiencing negative interest rates.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The Government of Singapore Investment Corporation's (GIC's) mission is to beat inflation by investing in non-Singapore dollar assets and one of the instruments that they would use would be bonds.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: And if interest rates remain low, the risk of achieving high NIRC over the next decade or so may become more challenging.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: What it means is that the OECD seeks to change the current corporate tax system from one which is based on the "residency of the company".

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: So, if you are a company incorporated in Singapore, you pay taxes here.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: If this company has a subsidiary in the UK, it pays taxes in the UK.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The proposal here is to change that concept of "residency of the company" to one where the "consumer is based".

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: So, even if you are a company based in Singapore but if you sell digital services or other products or services to another country, say, in the United States (US), which has a large consumer base, then the US will be the country collecting the taxes.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Singapore is a small hub economy with a lower consumer base compared to larger economies with higher consumption.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Should the OECD's BEPS proposal be adopted, we could end up with lower corporate tax revenues.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: So, the two risks are our NIRC facing challenges to generate high returns and, secondly, if the OECD's BEPS is adopted, then our corporate tax revenue will be negatively affected.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: It is understandable that raising GST is very unpopular.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: But as an honest Government, we need to level with our people and we need to continue to abide by the principle of fiscal prudence, having recurring revenue matching or exceeding recurring expenses.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: And this is the formula which has secured Singapore's success so far and we should not throw that away.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Of course, this Government can ignore it because I do not think we will run into deep problems any time soon.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: But this is like kicking the can down the road and letting future generations deal with the problems.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I do not think this is the right way forward.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: However, I hope that the Finance Minister, when raising GST, would design the Assurance Package in such a way that makes GST progressive.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: So, while we raise recurrent revenue, we also try to reduce the income inequality here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: But some have argued to forget about raising GST.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: So, why not dip into it to fund our expenditure?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Again, our Reserves are finite and, if we have recurring expenses, we need to think about recurring revenue in the system and not dip into a finite savings pool.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: But more important than that, we should not forget that Singapore is a country without natural resources.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: We have no oil, no natural gas, no minerals, no gold, no silver, the list goes on.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: If we deplete it, Singapore has no fallback.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: We have no backstop facility to draw upon.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: We have no European Union equivalent to bail us out.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: And if we have to resort to the International Monetary Fund, as past examples have shown, we would have to go "hat-in-hand", and such rescue package will come with many, many onerous conditions that will bog us down for many, many years to come.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This is not where we want to be.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: It is, indeed, the fiduciary duty of the Government, as stewards, to ensure the fiscal sustainability and not to squander away the Reserves, which, strictly speaking, we did not earn in totality but our forefathers and past governments have earned it for us.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Therefore, squandering it would be leaving future generations ill-equipped and vulnerable to deal with future crises and to continue to bring Singapore forward.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The second important principle other than fiscal prudence, is long-term planning.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: In fact, we should not look at Budget 2020 in isolation.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: But we should look at all such Government Budgets across the years, and you will see a theme emerging.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This Government has, over many years, built up our infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This is a problem that would probably only happen maybe in 100 years, maybe in 50 years, but this Government now, today, is dealing with this, and this is what long-term planning is about.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The other sterling example is Marina Bay where we had to reclaim land, let it settle for 25 years, and then solving a water problem and also creating a beautiful skyline at the same time.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: And that would not have happened had we not adopted long-term planning.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: But beyond physical infrastructure, we also invested in digitalisation, which is a very important aspect of transforming our economy.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Most importantly, for many years now, the second largest expenditure item in our Budget, after defence, has been education.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This is testament to our commitment to develop Human Capital.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: In fact, many economists have said that investing in human capital is perhaps the best way forward.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Because the more you invest in infrastructure, the more maintenance cost you will incur, and the risk of obsolescence is high.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: So, I am glad that we have put education right up there as the second biggest budget item in many, many Budgets of the past.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Equipping the Singaporean worker with the ability to be more productive and employable will enable them to earn higher wages.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This is the best way to becoming a more equal society.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: It gives hope and it allows our citizens to have a higher quality of living.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: And I applaud the Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister for looking into this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The magnitude of global events has increased and the impact of these events is far-reaching.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, just as the world saw a potential improvement in the global economic landscape last year with the inking of Phase 1 of the trade agreement between the US and China, along came the COVID-19 virus to make an unforgettable impact on the international stage.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The true impact of COVID-19 on countries and economies is hard to estimate, and it is likely that the long-tail impact of the outbreak could be significant.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am thus heartened to know that the Singapore Government has put forth an expansionary Budget to cushion the impact of COVID-19 and help Singapore-based companies and our citizens emerge stronger from this episode.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Based on current medical knowledge, COVID-19 is more infectious than the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) and current epidemiology models seem to predict that the outbreak is likely to last longer than SARS.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But even when the worst is over, it will take many more months before it is "business as usual".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government cater more funds to support businesses and Singaporeans if the downturn period turns out to last longer than expected?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, will the Government consider extending help to other industries, besides the five already mentioned in the Budget, if the economic fallout spreads to other industries?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Moving on to the topic of supporting families, Mr Speaker, Sir, building on the momentum of the past few Budgets, the current Budget continues the trend of investing in our children and youths by enhancing the level of support for the preschool and early childhood sector.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Part of this investment will be used to enhance grants to ensure that quality preschool remains accessible and affordable for young parents and that every young Singaporean child will be able to have a good headstart in education to maximise their potential and human capital gains regardless of their family's socioeconomic situation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is part of the overall effort to transform the social services sector so that the SSAs can better meet the complex needs of our evolving society, especially when Singapore is experiencing a rapidly ageing population.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that this is a step in the right direction towards building a more caring society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also need to constantly encourage and incentivise our companies to employ people who are differently-abled.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An example of one such company is Foreword Coffee that employs people with special needs as their baristas and cashiers or fast-food restaurants that hire differently-abled individuals as wait staff and service staff.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can we further incentivise companies to employ differently-abled individuals by providing more direct incentives to these companies, perhaps in the form of tax rebates?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe these direct incentives will provide a strong impetus for companies to offer fair and equal employment opportunities to everyone.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, the COVID-19 situation, though challenging, has brought out and continues to bring out some of the best behaviour from Singaporeans from all walks of life as Singaporeans and local communities have come forward to support their fellow citizens.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some have left masks and sanitisers at lift landings for their fellow residents.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Others have come forward to organise food delivery and even social programmes for those who are under quarantine or those who have to stay at home.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many Singaporeans have also extended similar courtesies not only to their fellow countrymen, but also to the foreigners in our midst.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Non-government organisations have come forward to distribute masks and sanitisers to migrant workers, to educate them on proper hygiene to prevent the spread of COVID-19 among the migrant communities, and some have even raised funds for those who need it.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are examples of the indomitable spirit and resilience of our people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, instead of sharing pictures of empty shelves at supermarkets or showing videos of residential storerooms that are stacked with hoarded goods, let us showcase more positive examples of how Singaporeans and Singaporean residents have rallied together to weather through this storm as one people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am thus confident that this Budget is well-designed for such extraordinary times and end my speech in support of the Budget.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It has to be visionary to prepare our economy and people for the future, but yet also address immediate needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: To me, the Budget is also an opportunity to nudge behaviours and shape norms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government's schemes and policies send an important signal on key issues and should encourage efforts that make Singapore better as a nation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For example, the support given to firms to train and redesign jobs for workers would hopefully translate to businesses and a workforce that is more productive and future-ready.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Incentives for energy-efficient appliances or cleaner energy products should encourage better adoption of such products and, in the long run, create a greener Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Support for employers to hire Singaporean persons with disabilities (PwDs) should encourage more to be inclusive and allow more space for PwDs to participate and contribute to the economy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In recent years, I have had the great privilege of engaging with family members and caregivers of people with different abilities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is a whole range of disabilities, including intellectual and physical disabilities, and PwDs come from a broad spectrum of age groups, from infants to the elderly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In my speech in 2018 on the Motion in support of inclusive education, I shared some of the challenges faced by parents of children with disabilities and called for more support for these families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Last year, as part of the People's Action Party Women's Wing paper on supporting parenthood and families, my colleagues and I engaged many parents to hear their views on the support needed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Dr Intan Azura, Miss Cheryl Chan and I had carried out an online survey to get a sensing of the needs of these families and we also held a dialogue to hear their stories.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We had to summarise much of the information we received to fit the paper, but we shared our insights with the relevant Ministries after the paper was finalised.
