speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some families, for example, may have more than one child with special needs and may need more support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, the infrastructure and services available need to be more pervasive and accessible to families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Facilities, like playgrounds, should ideally be equipped for children with different abilities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We may have a few of such inclusive playgrounds but only in certain parts of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We also have a hub at Enabling Village in Bukit Merah where parents and caregivers could get assistance with some services.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is also a Caregivers' Pod in the village meant for caregivers' use.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, those living in the east or north of Singapore may find it to be too far from them and are not able to benefit from the support and facilities available.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Much have been done in the sector, through the Enabling Masterplans, various policies and schemes as well as through the formation of workgroups to review the support to address different aspects of disabilities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, there is still some way to go in closing the gaps to better support PwDs and their families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Parents, especially, worry about the world they would be leaving their differently-abled children in when they pass away.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Could their children be meaningfully integrated within the community and be given opportunities like others?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Will the society be kind, patient and understanding of their child's needs?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is, therefore, a fervent hope that the Government continues to make effort to create awareness, build infrastructure and implement policies that would normalise inclusiveness and allow for people with different needs and abilities to be truly embraced as part of the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This may sound like a lofty ideal to some, but not one which we should shy away from.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to constantly and relentlessly participate in such efforts and seek partners from amongst the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In seeking partners for causes that matter to humanity, I have found hope in the youths.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I feel that the youths of today are very accepting of differences and have a strong sense of social fairness.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Over the years, I have continued to be involved in the youth sector efforts, especially through my engagements under M3, the collaboration among the People's Association Malay Activity Executive Committees Council (MESRA), the Council for the Education of Muslim Children (MENDAKI) and the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS), and as a council member of the National Youth Council.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In my dialogues and discussions with young people, many of them have shown much desire for a more inclusive, more compassionate society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am very heartened by their passion and I feel that it is so important to continue to engage them and seek their views as we build this nation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, I laud the Government's efforts through the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) and the National Youth Council (NYC) to meaningfully engage our young people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am hoping that many youths from different backgrounds can take up this opportunity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   It is very important for us to continue engaging and supporting our youths because they are the next generation who will inherit our nation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We must empower them and help them achieve their aspirations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I oversee the third workgroup under M3 related to youth matters, and one of the focus areas in our current projects is the development of a culture of mentoring within our community, so that our young can receive guidance and knowledge from those who are more experienced.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This will hopefully help our youths grow their confidence and seize any available opportunity so that they can continue to progress.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At the same time, we also encourage our youths to get involved and give back to society, regardless of race, religion or background.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope that our community will continue supporting this effort and we can achieve our objective to develop youths who are highly competent, competitive, confident and show concern towards the people around them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Indeed, the efforts to empower, mentor and engage youths should continue.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that if we work together, we can harness our diverse strengths and bring Singapore to greater heights.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is akin to what we see here in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Budget season is one of the more exciting periods for the House.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The House is abuzz with anecdotes, findings and information about a myriad of issues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Members of this House pour our hearts and souls to the issues we champion because they matter to us, to the people we represent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have seen the views that we raise in Parliament make their way to the formation of policies and I trust this will continue to be how the Singapore Government improves and builds on its framework for the future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This Budget is aptly named Our Unity Budget as we stand together, united by our desire to make Singapore stronger and better for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The past year has been a challenging year for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many businessmen whom I had spoken to lament about the slowdown in their business due to the ongoing trade war between China and the US.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They worry whether their business will be able to sustain in the long term.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When the COVID-19 virus outbreak hit Singapore, it was an even greater blow to these businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The drop in tourist figures, the fact that more Singaporeans are staying at home have affected the confidence of many.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, the expansionary Budget announced by the Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister last week is a real confidence booster.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As stated by many in the media, the Budget was generous and provided for several measures to help affected Singaporeans and businesses cope with the economic slowdown.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There were also many long-term measures to help affected Singaporeans prepare for the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This will help alleviate the cost of living pressures for the residents.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I support the principle that those who are in the lower-income group should receive more.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am also glad that the cash component of the Care and Support scheme is pegged to their income and not tied to the property type of the Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Last year, I had called on the Government to do away with distribution of Budget benefits based on home type alone.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I believe this will benefit many retirees or seniors who are living in private properties but without any income.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, my appeal to the Government is to consider extending other benefits like the U-save vouchers and GST vouchers to retirees or seniors without income but staying in private properties.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Again, here I wish to stress to the Minister that these retirees would not have income.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The fact that they stay in private property does not in any way mean that they are rich or are able to sustain themselves.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What they are looking for is also whether the Government can do more to recognise them for their contribution to nation-building when they were younger.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For many Singaporeans whom I meet, their main concern is whether they can get a good job which pays them commensurate with their skills and experience.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The majority of such stall licensees are small businesses and the rental waiver for them would go a long way to helping them sustain their small businesses during such trying times when the food centres are quieter and business has dropped drastically for them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, in the long term, what is important is not just cash handouts to affected Singaporeans or tax rebates to help businesses tide over difficult times.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These payments cannot be permanent and moneys will eventually run out some day.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, I support the Government's emphasis on helping business to transform and grow; to help our workers to upgrade and learn new skills; to help our students venture overseas so as to be better equipped to face challenges in the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is akin to the old Chinese saying that if "you give a man one fish, you feed him for a day.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If you teach him how to fish, you feed him for a lifetime." We must not ease our efforts in pushing our local enterprises to change and grow into efficient and competitive businesses that can make Singapore proud.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I long for the day when Singapore can boast of our own large corporations like Alibaba, Samsung, Apple and Google.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I support the provision of Enhanced Housing Grant (EHG) to first-time flat buyers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The purpose of EHG is to allow Singaporeans to own their own home and this is important for nation-building.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, the quantum of EHG given is currently based on the monthly income of the flat buyer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If the applicant’s income is higher, the EHG will be lower.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This means there is less incentive to buy a resale flat because you will get a lower EHG if your income is higher.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This may result in Singaporeans with higher income always applying for a Build-To-Order flat where the subsidy will not change based on their income level.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I urge the Government to review the tagging of the amount of EHG based on the income of the applicant.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also urge the Government to consider providing the EHG based on per capita basis and not just based on gross income.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Otherwise, a Singaporean who may have a higher income will get less EHG even though he may have more expenses and need to provide for more children or retired parents.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Are the unutilised figures within the expectation of the Government?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Will the Government consider targeted useful courses that would help nudge Singaporeans to apply to use these funds to improve themselves to upgrade their skills?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And it used to be Education when the Minister for Finance was Minister for Education.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I acknowledge that healthcare costs have gone up and the recent COVID-19 outbreak has caused Singaporeans to be more aware of the need to ensure that our healthcare system works.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This crisis has shown the importance and relevance of our Government's tradition of prudence.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should be prepared for a protracted outbreak as the situation is still evolving with growing cases reported globally.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The solution does not lie in just successful containment in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a global effort by all countries to find a solution, as indicated by the World Health Organization (WHO).

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Should the COVID-19 outbreak become more prolonged and have an even greater impact on households and companies than what is currently experienced, we believe that the Government would draw upon the surplus funds to finance further measures to help.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would first like to touch on support measures.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The combination of cash, rebates and grocery vouchers will help households to manage their living expenses for a period of time.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For Singaporeans living in 1-room and 2-room HDB flats, the $100 Groceries Vouchers provided to assist them are limited for use at participating supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will also be a way of supporting small businesses in our housing estates.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I welcome the widening of qualifying criteria for the $100 cash support to citizens who earned more than $100,000 in 2019 or who live in private properties.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This recognises that the COVID-19 situation is a challenge that all Singaporeans are facing and may be affected in one way or another regardless of their income level.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would be good if the Ministry would share how it arrived at the various financial assistance figures.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will help to illustrate the intended impact of the financial assistance and also the timeliness of the payouts.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat has said that the Government "…will be prepared to do more when the situation warrants it".

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Has the Ministry also set for itself some indicators internally to decide on when further assistance would be rendered should the outbreak crisis deepen?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In such a scenario, the cost of certain essential goods may increase, as disruptions in supply chains may create shortages in supply.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singaporeans may then suffer the double whammy of lower or even loss of income, and a higher cost of living.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What about businesses that started operating this year which are also affected by COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Government consider helping them as well?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, may I request for the grants to be given out earlier, especially for smaller businesses which operate on tight cash flows and are already severely impacted?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the decline in sales, operators will immediately look at cost-cutting.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Operating hours will be shortened, the number of part-timers hired will be reduced, full-time staff will be placed on part-time shifts and asked to clear their leave or take no-pay leave.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the event of a prolonged crisis, what can be done to support businesses so that job losses are kept to a minimum?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is good for the Government to elaborate on the working assumption of the timeframe for these rebates.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the rebates are meant to cover serious business earnings loss for February to April, one or half-month rental rebates put in this context does seem reasonable.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, businesses seek the assurance that more help would be available if the situation prolongs or deteriorates further.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would also like to request for more support to be given to companies embarking or expanding their sales via e-channels.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This crisis provides the impetus to push small and medium enterprises (SMEs) which have been reluctant to consider this sales avenue.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the current cost structure and labour situation, it is inevitable that e-commerce would become the norm and form an essential part of any business.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, I would like to touch on positioning for the longer term.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Budget, like previous Budgets, have schemes to support the transformation of our local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of these incentives have a preset time period, for example, three years, or are subject to renewals or extensions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Companies change and transform at different paces, depending on the maturity of the industry and support available, especially for smaller ones.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To encourage companies to plan ahead and remain continuously invested in the future, would the Government consider setting longer-term horizons for selected incentives?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, when Pioneer Tax Incentives were first introduced, longer durations, up to 15 years, were given.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we continue on the digital transformation of our economy, more support would be needed to help smaller companies adopt new technology, not only with respect to the technical aspects but also with the costs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The trust among our people, our businesses and the Government is strong and that is the main reason for my belief.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Responsive because it addresses an immediate crisis, responsible because it remains fiscally sound, and remarkable because it took all of a few weeks to prepare.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That we are facing potential global financial instability is moot.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What we face is not just an invisible enemy but also the real visible damage it causes to the economy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Last Sunday, I stopped by Marina Square at about 1.20 pm between my events.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I wanted to pick up some things from a maternity shop.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I was somewhat apprehensive because I knew how crowded Marina Square can be on weekends.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, I entered a car park that was sparse.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From the car park to the shop, I consciously counted a total of only 38 shoppers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At one of the empty children's playgrounds in the shopping centre, I saw the counter staff staring blankly into space because there was never one shadow of a child within the space.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At Jewel, outlets famous for their long queues were momentarily famous for non-existent queues.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Although the crowds and confidence have returned in the last week, the damage has been done.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Heartland malls have fared a little bit better but still report lower numbers than usual.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Food and grocery delivery services perhaps have benefited most from this crisis.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But tourism and service sectors hit directly will take time to recover.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is also no longer a regional problem.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A responsive expansionary Budget is a needed assurance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is not just for business but for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are not many governments that can do this and do this quickly, and be so detailed in its response to a crisis.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And this is just on fear of COVID-19 impacting the American economy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need, therefore, to buffer ourselves against a potential recession.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The two packages are significant, but how much will the needle move?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How much does the Government expect the worst downside to be?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Are we able and prepared to do more?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can we still be as responsive as we are currently?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They have taken to heart what this Budget has provided.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But it may take more than care, support and stabilisation to shore up, if this drags on.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the Ministerial Statement on COVID-19, I asked if more can be done quicker.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am heartened by the Budget announcements but urge more haste and more heart for those who are affected.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And I hope the Deputy Prime Minister can provide further reassurance on this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is about 2.1% of our gross domestic product (GDP).

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, our fiscal prudence means we will not be drawing on Past Reserves.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a hallmark of stability and a responsible Government.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are not many governments that can do this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We only need to look around us and observe how things can go wrong.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Looking north in the last few days, we are lucky to be spared the intrigue and drama in our system.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Perhaps we should be thankful to the late Tengku Abdul Rahman that we are no longer party to this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We wish our northern neighbour well but we also wish that such distractions may never plague us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, despite the major interruption posed by COVID-19, we have not allowed ourselves to be distracted.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While responding to the crisis decisively, this Government has also not shifted focus.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With an eye on the future, SkillsFuture prepares us as a people for future challenges, gives us both the resources and also encourages personal responsibility.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, we also need to be mindful of how we implement the schemes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I heard feedback from SkillsFuture Workforce Skills Qualifications (WSQ) course providers of the challenges they face in claims, especially when participants do not complete or fail their course.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many end up not being able to pay and providers cannot claim.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some providers have also been told that if a trainee does not complete, they should factor the trainees as part of attrition or bad debts to be written off.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Honest course providers commit resources to develop and maintain these courses and hope to be reimbursed in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hope that while we care for our workers and help them upgrade, that course providers, being mostly SMEs, are also aptly protected for playing their part and not to be left without recourse or assistance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Beyond the short to mid term, the Budget also looks far ahead to an existential threat brought about by global warming.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The problem is not immediate, but committing an initial $5 billion to Coastal Protection does show our commitment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yesterday, it was said in this House that, "If you have nothing good to say, then best to keep quiet." That, Mr Speaker, is the easy thing to do.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is easy to only say nice things.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is easy not to have to make hard decisions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is easy to be popular and likeable.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But being a good and effective leader is not easy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The difficult task is to tell it like it is.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The difficult task is sacrificing personal standing to say the needful.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And the difficult task is calling out bad behaviour when required.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This Government knows that hard truths hurt but does not shy away from it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Without these hard truths and hard decisions, Singapore would not be where it is today.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That, to me, is the mark of true leadership and wisdom.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When someone takes his or her duty seriously to make hard decisions, that is true responsibility.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This Budget would have been a long process.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But to turn it around in face of a crisis takes mettle.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A government that can respond to trouble and not fall to the temptation of being populist in the process, all this is because we also have a remarkable people and a remarkable country.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our common response to COVID-19 is mirrored in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When DORSCON Orange was declared, many banded together to do something for the community.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have heard many examples over the course of the many speeches in this House.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My own volunteers in my constituency asked what we could do to encourage our frontline heroes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In three days, we managed to pull together a programme which we called "Cookies for SG Heroes".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We started off wanting to bake cookies and progressed to preparing care packs for the staff of Tan Tock Seng Hospital and Ng Teng Fong General Hospital.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Within hours of putting the word out, the Girl Guides responded, donating their famous biscuit tins, Hock Hua Tonic responded offering their herbal tea at cost, the Singapore Kindness Movement responded providing encouragement decals, Gain City came on board offering the use of their show kitchens, residents, Singaporeans responded.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By the morning, we had so much that we needed bigger bags to pack the care bags.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One of our baking coordinators, Pey Yng, was interviewed for a video.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She had moved out of our constituency a few years earlier but responded immediately when we asked for help.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When asked why she wanted to help and stepped forward, she said, almost tearing, "Instead of discriminating, we should be encouraging them." Mr Speaker, these frontline heroes include our medical staff, allied healthcare workers, cleaners, conservancy workers, security personnel, back office staff and many, many others.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are our fellow Singaporeans, our brothers and sisters.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are battling a stealthy enemy that does not discriminate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yesterday, a former colleague of mine shared his wife’s experience.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She works in the frontline and she was helping with contact tracing and temperature taking.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, someone felt that, even amidst the heightened alert, that he was entitled to take it out on her and her colleagues, throwing the pen at her and shouting at her colleagues.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Actually, there is no need for a because.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another resident confided in me, sending me a Facebook message.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I asked for her permission to share this with everyone.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She wrote: "Sir, I do not know why people treat us like this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Why is my uniform, which I aspired to and was inspired by others to don, now deemed as a mark of shame?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Why do people stand away from me even when I am on the way to work, and not the other way around?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Why do people look at me with a glint of horror?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I will keep doing what I love.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I will keep on saving lives because many Singaporeans are not like them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And when those who shun us arrive in my hospital, I will care for them just the same as the others.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I, therefore, add my voice in support of this Budget.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is like a very much needed vaccine to support our economy, especially the badly affected sectors, and also to protect jobs for our people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Having said that, I would like to raise a few pointers for the Minister to consider.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Currently, many people are concerned about the impact on the economy brought about by COVID-19.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Employers are worried that they are unable to carry on with their businesses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, will the Government reduce the rental until the DORSCON level returns to Green?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: JTC or HDB, for example, can take the lead to reduce rentals of their commercial tenants and office spaces.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe this will be able to reduce the impact brought about by the outbreak.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Besides tourism-related sectors, many other industries, such as manufacturing, maritime and construction, are also affected severely due to various extra expenditures and the fact that China's manufacturing industry has come to a standstill.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They asked if the foreign workers' levy could be temporarily waived.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why is everybody looking to the Government for help in times like these?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The outbreak has no mercy, but there is warmth in the world.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Have faith in our Government, which is a caring Government.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to urge taxi companies to consider reducing the taxi rental rates until the DORSCON level returns to Green.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many taxi drivers have shared with me that their income has dipped by 50%.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A reduction of the monthly taxi rental rate by 50% will help them get through this difficult period.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, I will now move on to climate change.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are we exploring our full potential for photovoltaic (PV) systems?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A PV system employs solar modules, each comprising a number of solar cells, which generate electrical power.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are we ready to allow Town Councils to install PV panels on roofs and vertical areas, such as lift shafts?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A case in point is MPC@Khatib, our covered multi-purpose court that can accommodate four basketball courts.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: During its design, we enquired if PV panels could be installed to harvest the solar energy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As usual, I always explore ways to make Nee Soon South cleaner and greener.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, the answer from HDB then was no.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Maybe at that time, they were not ready.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, I would like to urge them to review this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many residents welcome the SkillsFuture top-up which is very useful.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I urge the Government to monitor if course providers raise their prices as a response.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I note there is a reduction in S Pass sub-dependency ratio ceilings (DRCs) for the Construction, Shipyard and Process sectors.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is good that the Government has a long-term view to reduce Singapore’s reliance on foreign labour.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But if we do not have a pipeline of Singaporean labour for construction and shipyards, then cutting the DRCs might be an additional burden on companies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This could leave the companies no choice but to relocate out of Singapore, especially the shipyards.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In facing the COVID-19 difficulties, it is important to have the entire industry, that is, developers, contractors, consultants, subcontractors, suppliers and all stakeholders, tackle the challenges cohesively as a whole.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the same way as how the relief measures are rolled out for the hospitality and retail sectors, the same should be done for the Property and Construction sector.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This sector also holds a lot of jobs and should not be neglected.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many local contractors also told me that they feel discriminated in the recent few contract awards.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Another example, LTA awarded contract N112 tender to a foreign contractor though our local contractor submitted the lowest tender.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The lowest tenderer is an established homegrown contractor.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I know there is such thing as PQM (Price Quality Method) scoring.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But if there is a gap in the capabilities of our local contractors, then we should handhold them and nurture them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need our homegrown contractors to grow, to build up their experience, their portfolio, so that they can venture overseas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If we do not even support our own contractors, who will support them?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we consistently apply the policy of Buy Singapore First?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: New Budget measures aimed at boosting the retirement incomes and employability of seniors are a step in the right direction, but I feel we need to understand residents' needs better and get the priority right.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I had seen cases where residents do not have enough money to service their mortgage loan or no roof over their heads, but they have money in the retirement accounts.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To many residents, having a roof is more immediate and a more important need than providing for retirement.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And I feel financial incentives alone may not be enough to encourage businesses to hire and retain older workers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I move on to issues that residents are facing.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Noise pollution from vehicle engines is a common occurrence faced by Nee Soon South residents and I am sure in many other parts of Singapore, too.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, the implication is that besides the noise nuisance, they also create health issues and a cost to society.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are also intelligent speed bumps that flatten when you are driving within speed limit.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is Singapore exploring some of these new technologies?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And will there be more stringent action against car workshops which do illegal modification to the motorcycles and cars?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Town Councils are essential in improving the environment of HDB residents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But often, Town Councils are hampered by regulations.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, Nee Soon Town Council has been flying drones for its estate inspection.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But due to the regulations, our drone inspection could only be carried out during weekends.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, the Government is on the Government Electronic Business System (GeBIZ), but Town Councils are not allowed to make use of GeBIZ for procurement.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are e-procurement platforms that we could adopt.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But HDB has not come back to us on our request.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Also, can I ask the Ministry of National Development to consider providing additional grants to Town Councils for older flats or flats built for the silver generation for the maintenance of silver-friendly facilities, such as the Alarm Alert System?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Such systems and others are expensive to maintain.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On this note, I would like to request for those flats in Nee Soon South which were built in 1987 to be among the first few batches.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: My residents have been waiting for the programme for a long, long time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I fully appreciate the Deputy Prime Minister's thoughtfulness and insightfulness to swiftly get into the thick of things, given that this COVID-19 only came to attention in January.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He was able to adroitly dribble his way and roll out so many measures across so many fronts.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He was able to assess the impact on our economy and the ramifications globally, and work out the packages, without forgetting the packages for our seniors and for families.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And while doing all these, the coronavirus was still evolving.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: No one knows how severe it would pan out.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even as we gather here today to debate, the virus is rearing its ugly head in many places worldwide.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think it is very fitting that we assure the Deputy Prime Minister that we stand behind him and he is not alone.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, my thoughts would be best expressed by quoting the lyrics from the Liverpool Football Club song: "When you are walking through a storm, hold your head up high.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Don't be afraid of the dark because, at the end of the storm, there's a golden sky." Mr Speaker, I would not sing, I cannot and I do not want!

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I was about to say that the HIP II flats should come to Kembangan-Chai Chee first, before Nee Soon.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But because you quoted that song, I will let you go first.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Speaker, Sir, the arts have always played an important role in defining our nation's cultural identity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: For the arts to remain sustainable and accessible for all in Singapore, giving plays a vital role to allow arts to live strong, develop and grow.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Amid the evolving coronavirus COVID-19 outbreak, the arts community brings people together, spreads love and positivity.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: My colleague in the Singapore Symphony Orchestra (SSO), the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of SSO, Chng Hak-Peng, shared "three reasons why the arts in general, and classical music concerts in particular, are essential even during times of crisis for a modern and complex society like Singapore", in The Straits Times on 25 February 2020.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The arts is an essential part of life.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: As shared by Hak-Peng, firstly, it is important to maintain an environment of normalcy as life goes on.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: And it re-energises and allows audiences to breathe.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, the arts help us to cope with uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to quote him in his article, "For me, this is like building our psychological resilience.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The arts help you to surrender yourself to the unknown, and the beauty of a piece of art or music reinvigorates your belief that, as human beings, we have the ability to transcend today’s problems and attain greatness." The current measures to limit the spread of COVID-19 have led to a number of shows and performances being cancelled or postponed.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This has spurred arts groups to consider creative alternatives, such as digital performances, to bring some comfort during this trying time.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Ding Yi Music Company held a very first digital concert Together We Stand with local artistes, and our Minister for Community, Youth and Sports Grace Fu sang in the finale piece.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: It was a touching and inspiring piece to battle COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Prime Minister Lee also shared a special music video of "Home", performed by the Singapore Chinese Orchestra (SCO) in tribute to our healthcare and frontline workers, on both his Facebook page and Instagram.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In his post, he mentioned that he was glad the arts community is doing its part to rally Singaporeans during the outbreak, including the National Arts Council.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They produced a very interesting and inspiring video called "#StayStrong and #DontKancheong" video, which involved many local artists and they shared what they have been up to and what they have to say to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Other than tapping on online platforms and social media, some arts groups and individuals continue to perform and bring the audiences some encouragement and positivity.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: When a group of people see others appear calm and able to appreciate the arts, it reinforces a sense of peace and chill in the community.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This is more positive and encouraging than seeing one another rushing to buy daily necessities like rice and toilet paper and develop a sense of panic.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Just over the weekend, SSO organised two full-house concerts at The Esplanade.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Just last evening, two young gentlemen – Wong Qin Kai and Goh Shunta – held a recital, "The Erhu Works" which I had the honour of attending; I was there at the performance.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: And it was almost full house, even during this trying period.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I hope such examples will inspire more to come forward to build a more caring, cohesive and confident society, together.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Giving to the arts and culture has been significant in the past few years.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened by the news and I thank the Government for putting aside this sum of money to boost community partnership and efforts, to bring forth more opportunities for all and to empower the arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This Fund continues to help create access and opportunities to arts of different forms and engage Singaporeans of all ages.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The arts build a more cohesive society and I wonder how this Fund can be further extended to help arts and culture companies and enterprises to bring more Singaporeans together, groom and grow attendance and participation for the arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The COVID-19 outbreak has also an impact on the worldwide economy.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Economists believe that the growth of the economy has slowed down and, in the case of a downturn, it would have an impact on arts giving and sponsorship.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that a more targeted and well-defined Cultural Matching Fund (CMF) policy can help small, medium arts groups in Singapore to enjoy the benefits.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: To battle the economic downturn, I propose to review and reconsider CMF.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This could be a long-term measure, instead of a short-term or mid-term measure.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This would help many of the smaller-scale arts groups with less fundraising power to be able to tap on the matching fund.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I will share more during the COS debate.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Arts have always played an important role in defining Singaporeans' cultural identity.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: With the increasing number of artists and people involved in arts groups in Singapore and a vibrant arts sector, every Singaporean is able to enjoy the arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The COVID-19 outbreak has sparked worldwide concern and impacted public life.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: With the DORSCON outbreak alert level raised to Orange, many Singaporeans inevitably felt anxious.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Quite a number of arts performances were also cancelled or postponed.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In an attempt to uplift public spirit amidst the outbreak, local chamber music group Ding Yi Music Company held a digital concert on Valentine's Day to spread positivity to frontline healthcare workers and members of the public who are feeling uneasy.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, online platforms have become a channel for many arts groups which seek to be heard.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The National Arts Council also launched a video with the theme "Stay Strong, Don't Kancheong" on 20 February, with many local artists joining in the video to boost the morale of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, SCO produced a heartwarming music video in a tribute to healthcare workers battling the COVID-19 virus at the frontlines.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The music video, featuring one of Singapore’s national songs "Home", was brimming with emotions.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Although everybody is feeling anxious amidst the outbreak, healthcare workers braving the storm deserve special support and care from the community.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The music video by SCO received a "like" from Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong who said he was glad the arts community is doing its part to rally Singaporeans to fight the outbreak and is able to continue performing for the public by going online.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The value of arts in the daily lives of Singaporeans has also been recognised.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: During this extraordinary period, arts groups have sought to encourage and unite the nation, as well as pay tribute to healthcare workers, through arts and music.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In times of crisis, arts and culture can uplift spirits.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: For example, last weekend, SSO performed two sold-out concerts; two young Erhu musicians Wang Qin Kai and Wu Fu Jun also performed to a full-house audience last night.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I personally attended this concert and am heartened to see the huge turnout.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The music does not stop, and life must go on!

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This is to encourage Singaporeans from a wider range of domains to initiate and launch more meaningful community projects.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Arts knows no boundaries in terms of age and background, everyone can enjoy the arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Arts help to build confidence, enhance one’s image and attractiveness.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Looking ahead, I hope that culture and the arts will continue to bring diverse communities together and contribute to a more cohesive society.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): I am in support of Budget 2020.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A government has many competing needs for expenditure and it is always a difficult exercise to allocate scarce resources to these competing needs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, this Budget does an excellent job of both addressing our short-term needs in relation to cushioning the economic impact of COVID-19 while continuing to invest in our people and meeting our country's long-term structural needs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I will focus on the implications of COVID-19 for us in this speech, as I believe it is an important area in which the Government can send the right signals and messages, but ultimately, the entire population needs to come together with the right mindset to weather the storm.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The situation in relation to COVID-19 is rapidly evolving.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has dealt with pandemics before in recent memory.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These include the SARS outbreak in 2002 and the Hemagglutinin 1 and Neuraminidase 1 (H1N1) outbreak in 2009.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: COVID-19 appears to be less deadly than SARS but more infectious, but less infectious than H1N1.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And while it has killed many people in Wuhan and China, the overall death rate appears to go down as more cases are diagnosed and we have evidence of more people making recoveries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore had taken very firm measures to try and contain this, led by the Fourth-Generation (4G) team of leaders, and its efforts have won praise from many quarters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We had to develop a strategy for dealing with the virus in very short order, including developing protocols for confining those at risk, treating those who were diagnosed and, at the same time, trying to keep the economy going.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Businesses were encouraged to test out Business Continuity Plans and many businesses are now experimenting with teams working remotely, and these include banks, financial institutions, law firms, including mine, and even the Courts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have to admit I was a little sceptical at first about the need for trying out such plans, but having tried working from home, I have actually found it is quite workable and, in some respects, even more productive as you have less distractions and do not have to spend so much time travelling to and from the office.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: All in all, I think we can come out stronger.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, this does not detract from the very real harm that COVID-19 has done to many sectors of the economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Air travel and tourism, in particular, have been very badly hit.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Changi Airport, one of the busiest airports in the world, has been relatively quiet, including the Jewel, where I understand you can now get an A&W meal without much queuing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: F&B places are not getting their usual crowds, particularly those in town, and employers and workers in these sectors are clearly worried.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this respect, the Government's measures to assist businesses are timely and send the right message.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am also heartened that many of the bigger landlords have also taken the cue and have confirmed they will be passing on these rebates to their tenants.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, I hope we can come through this episode building stronger relationships with one another, whether it is with landlord, employee or customer and do not just see these relationships as transactional ones.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Budget sends the right signal, but we need everyone to work together to make it work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   COVID-19 has created slowdowns throughout the economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: F&B, retail, transport and events-related businesses are all suffering.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Budget plays an important role in helping businesses and workers tide through this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is important though for us to look out for one another during this time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For property owners getting tax rebates, please pass this down to your tenants.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For businesses that get rental rebates and wage support, please keep your workers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If business is down, this will be a good time to go for training.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For older workers, please use the additional SkillsFuture grants wisely, and go for training that may help you pick up the skills that will be helpful at work or to transition to new work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Government can create opportunities, but you need to come forward and use them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is my hope that we will come out of this adverse time stronger than before, like we had done during our previous challenges in 2008 during the Global Financial Crisis and in 2002 with SARS.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In English): In Singapore, we have had some good news over the last week.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While in the early days, we were getting more and more news of people infected and some in critical condition, now we get more news of people being discharged.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: According to a Channel NewsAsia report yesterday, we now have 58 cases of people who have made full recovery.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, COVID-19 is now spreading rapidly outside our borders.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Cases are now emerging all around the world, including in Europe, South America, the Middle East and the US.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If other countries start closing borders or restricting business activities in response, there could be serious economic repercussions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this respect, it will be important for our companies to be braced and prepared for the implications of significant disruptions in global trade and supply chains.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the short term, for companies that need to pay wages, bills and rentals on a monthly basis, it may appear existential, but in the long term, most analysts believe this will be a bump on the road.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe if we ride the storm together, we can come out stronger.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And this Budget is a big help in that process.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In the preceding years, many Singaporeans have expressed concerns over the size of this surplus.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: They have always wondered whether we could invest more in our people.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: First, our ability to quickly respond to crises; second, creating a future-ready city; and third, continued investments in our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: As Members are aware, COVID-19 spread like a wildfire.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Without doubt, COVID-19 is one of the biggest crises Singapore has faced in over a decade.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: As the impact of COVID-19 continues to unfold, Budget 2020 addresses several of our immediate macro-economic concerns and, with such a forward-looking Budget, I am confident that, together, we will overcome this crisis and emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: However, Mr Speaker, in my conversations with our fellow Singaporeans, many have expressed the views that the crisis management aspect of the Budget will only last a few months.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Those of us who experienced SARS keenly remember its impact.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Given the uncertainty behind the long-term progression of COVID-19, I wish to ask the hon Minister what further measures can we expect in a Supplementary Budget.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In the event that the war against the virus becomes protracted, how will this House respond?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: I am sure that a positive response will allay the anxieties of many.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Next, I wish to speak about the individuals fighting on the frontlines.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: As we continue to manage the outbreak, we are witnessing many companies tightening their belt.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Reports of companies freezing staff salaries, implementing pay and bonus cuts are increasingly surfacing in the media.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: To my understanding, our healthcare system is not immune to these financial pressures.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Our hospitals have understandably been forced to shelve their revenue-generating cases to deal with this outbreak.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: It is understood that this decrease in revenue will have an impact on the bonuses that our healthcare workers will receive.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In this regard, I echo the suggestions made by Member Murali Pillai yesterday.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Additionally, would the Minister consider increasing GST in stages, from 7% to 8% and, eventually, from 8% to 9%?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In view of the economic crunch that we are facing, I wonder if the Government would consider granting a similar tax rebate for Personal Income Tax to help Singaporeans with their cash flow.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: The rationale behind our Budget surplus has always been twofold.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: First, to ensure that Singapore has room to manoeuvre in times of crisis; second, to ensure that future generations can have a share in the fruits of our growth.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: We are facing a clear and present crisis with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: It is imperative that we do not lose sight of the big picture, avoid knee-jerk reactions, and respond swiftly for the well-being of fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Next, I turn to speak about creating a future-ready Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: As the COVID-19 crisis shows us, Mr Speaker, our nation's success is not something which occurred in a vacuum.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: We are successful because we have continually planned ahead.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Given our time constraints, I will focus on our national efforts in preparing for climate change.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Today, I aim to spark a deeper conversation about whether Singapore has the infrastructure to survive.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: I begin by speaking about our nation’s food resilience.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In particular, I will speak on our investments in future technologies.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: The rising temperatures and concurrent decline in global fish stocks are an existential threat to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: I remind this House that over 90% of the food consumed in Singapore is imported.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In this vein, Singapore must ensure that we are food-resilient.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: As the recent panic buying episode reminds us, we have the capacity to withstand sudden shocks in our supply chain.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: However, what happens if we face a long-term disruption?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: First, what success did previous programmes aiming to encourage the production of local produce have?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: If those successes were limited, what changes are we making to ensure that our "Grow Local" strategy will be successful?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Second, do we have a local pool of agri-tech startups which will benefit from the increasing funding set aside for them?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Third, does the Government intend to support and encourage deeper integration of research and development (R&D) processes between business and our tertiary education institutions in this regard?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: If so, what funds are being allocated to this in order to catalyse the process?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: As we continue to invest in creating a food-resilient Singapore, simply setting money aside is insufficient.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: We must create an innovative ecosystem with positive feedback loops.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: It is my vision for future generations of Singaporeans to be able to consume local produce daily.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Looking closer to our immediate future, Sir, I speak about our transition to electric vehicles (EVs).

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: First, I state for the record my support for our efforts in encouraging cleaner modes of transport.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: After years of investment, the electric future is almost upon us.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: However, I have some concerns about the overall impact of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: I raise them in the form of questions for the Minister to address.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Are there any proportionate investments being made in transforming our energy mix?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Second, it is not disputed that public transport is more efficient and less polluting, compared to personal vehicles.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: A perennial problem preventing greater utilisation of public transport is "first-mile and last-mile" connectivity issues.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In this regard, does the Government intend to accelerate our investment in our park connector networks to ensure greater access to public transport hubs and to encourage alternative modes of transport via cycling?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Lastly, as we even transition toward EVs, how can we ensure that even less pollutive technologies, such as hydrogen fuel cells, are not locked out of the market?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Ultimately, I submit that simply transitioning to EVs is not enough.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: If we want to have a significant impact, we must be prepared to think boldly.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: We must take the lead in moving towards a fossil fuel-free future in our region.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Thus, over the next few years, I hope that this House will seriously consider adopting alternative power sources, including nuclear energy, given the advances in technology and to look beyond EVs.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In this final segment, I will focus on how we can continue to invest in our fellow citizens.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In this segment, I will first address our SkillsFuture programme.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Following that, I will speak about how we can further invest in our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In order to succeed, our people must be adaptable to changes.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: They should be able to ride the structural waves that are disrupting the world.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Our aims of becoming a global node of innovation and enterprise will materialise when we can ensure that our Singaporeans who are locally trained are globally framed.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: On to SkillsFuture, Mr Speaker, I welcome the Government’s proposal to top up the individual SkillsFuture funds.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: This sends a strong signal about our priorities.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: However, beyond topping up our SkillsFuture funds, I raise the following questions for the Minister to consider.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In this regard, Sir, I have two potential solutions which this House can consider moving forward.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: The first involves tapping on the existing expertise of our local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: The second will require us to leverage existing technologies.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In this programme, students will undergo apprenticeships which will eventually culminate in a full bachelor's degree or industry recognised standards or qualifications.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: All these while earning a real wage and being trained in the skills employers want.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: We currently have the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) Traineeship programme.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: This is an apprenticeship programme that benefits both employers and employees where students can work towards their ITE qualification while gaining practical experience.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: In the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS) and SMU, part-time degree programmes are also available to individuals who wish to work and study.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: I am confident that our SkillsFuture programmes will see higher participation rates if we are able to provide practical pathways to success.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: More than a specific programme, Sir, I suggest that we leverage existing technologies to enhance our SkillsFuture experience.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Currently, our SkillsFuture programmes exclude workers with little control over their schedule, such as shift workers.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Singapore is poorer for the fact that a segment of our population cannot upskill themselves adequately.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Over the last two years, our IHLs have seamlessly transitioned to e-learning following the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Thus far, many lessons and tutorials have gone online.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: For instance, in our local universities, even group work and presentations are being held virtually.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: This move clearly shows that the required infrastructure, platforms and systems are well in place.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Indeed, there are many models available for the Public Service to consider.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Such a synergy has the potential to lay the foundation for a public, open university that offers alternative structured higher education pathways for those seeking to upgrade themselves for their career progression.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: At the end of the day, Sir, I hope that SkillsFuture will be made more accessible for our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: We should enable them to upskill, no matter the circumstance.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: My last point on investing in our fellow Singaporeans, Mr Speaker, can be summarised with this phrase "Locally Trained and Globally Framed".

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Since our separation from Malaysia, we have always recognised that Singapore cannot be insular in our economic approach.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: We have invested heavily in ensuring that we are an attractive place to do business.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: However, as the current crisis demonstrates, it is not enough that we create jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: They must possess an international outlook and must hold their own in this ever-changing world.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Budget 2020 is a clear and unambiguous reflection of the latter.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: On this note, Mr Speaker, I state my support for Budget 2020.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, instead of giving in to the temptation to vaingloriously bask in such rankings, we looked critically at the report on real shortcomings so that we can reflect on them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The WEF report highlighted room for improvement in respect of promoting entrepreneurship and improving the skills base, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before I begin, I declare my interest as the CEO of a research consultancy that undertakes work in a variety of business arenas, including industry 4.0 spaces.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Decades ago, Singapore's GDP growth was consistently among the highest in the region and the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, it has been more modest but still better than or the same as other developed countries in this region.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's forecast for 2020 is roughly the same rate of growth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, our SMEs and, particularly micro businesses, will face headwinds, not only from the coronavirus, but also the more general China slowdown.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fourth, while the GDP share of R&D is decent, it is not as high as in some developed countries, and there is some evidence that R&D GDP share is linked to Total Factor Productivity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More importantly, beyond the MNC sector, it is not at all clear if R&D is being taken up and commercialised successfully on a substantial scale by our local companies, notwithstanding some take-up of licences from the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) by local enterprises, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fifth, we continue to be successful in attracting foreign direct investment (FDI).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we have all come to acknowledge that future FDI inflows may be under threat from anti-globalisation trends that my party Chairman Ms Sylvia Lim spoke about yesterday, in particular, the deliberate efforts some countries may take to pull back supply chains to their domestic economies in light of things like the coronavirus and US-China geopolitical tensions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To insulate against this risk, we face the challenge of raising the game of our local firms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sixth, with the rise of uniquely disruptive technologies like artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous vehicles, the Internet of Things and drones, whole categories of employment may be wiped out practically overnight.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The advent of autonomous vehicles may put at risk the jobs of drivers in the taxi and private car hire industry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many jobs in backend operations and frontend services are also at risk from AI, robots and chatbots.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, one additional challenge is to ensure that our people can keep their heads above tomorrow's rising waters of employability amidst the sea of economic disruption not seen in generations, not only in respect of skillsets like deep tech and coding but also soft skills like creativity, leadership, entrepreneurial acumen and resilience.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, the authors of the WEF report cited room for improvement for Singapore in skills like critical thinking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The next broad point I will speak on is livability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A blind chase for vibrancy of an economy is no full guarantee of the well-being of its citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Putting effort into livability, therefore, is one of the most crucial challenges facing Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What else can be done to breed confidence that our system will manage livability in the future?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our total fertility rate has been one of the lowest in the world for years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I suspect that getting livability right would make a difference on these fronts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The approach to managing the cost of living is a case in point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why not develop an approach to policymaking that commits the state to adjust for future conditions by building the adjustment mechanism into policy design, rather than leaving it to future acts of Executive discretion, which may or may not happen?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, this is done in some cases, like permanent GST Vouchers, but not in others.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Parliament can still vote against inflation-based increases should fiscal resources be insufficient.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the mechanism can still contain an element of evaluation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the fact that the design of the policy has a built-in mechanism to recommend changes and adjust based on inflation at certain defined time intervals creates some assurance that, yes, society will not leave me stranded in the future one day.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not just a benefit for today leaving me uncertain about tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a very specific example to make the general point that if more well thought through social protections and stabilisers are built into policy design, it may assure Singaporeans that the society has their back.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
