text: And this may reduce risk adversity and the focus on short-term income rather than long-term income.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This, in turn, may promote a culture of being more willing to take risks to reskill, start a business and, possibly, even to have children, because one is more confident about the future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some research suggests that our economic outlook and our sense of economic security does impact these behaviours.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if we fail to address the challenge of livability like parts of the US and England, our people may turn against globalisation which would damage prospects for vibrancy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a call for building into policy design mechanisms that self-correct and have built-in adjustment processes rather than leaving it purely to future Executive discretion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Executive and Parliament can still decide not to go ahead if the money is not there.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, Sir, I want to talk about sustainability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Vibrancy and livability are already difficult challenges in themselves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we must ensure that policies aimed to address these challenges are sustainable and are responsible.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many countries do not have this and have high levels of fiscal debt relative to GDP.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But are there not also dangers in going to the other extreme and being too prudent as it were?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could that also lead to a failure to seize opportunities to develop the capacities of our people for the future?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clearly, we have to find the Goldilocks zone between these two extremes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An analogy from the business world might be the two extremes of spending too much and running into a cash crunch on the one hand and not investing enough in the company to develop the capabilities of the employees, new business strategies and intellectual property (IP) on the other.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not suggesting drawing down on the Reserves at this point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But in the longer term, is there more scope to slow the rate of Reserves growth, so as to release more funds to invest in our people and address the challenges we face in terms of livability, employability, innovation and so on that I spoke about in the first part of my speech?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Should our Reserves always go up and up at the same rate?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we not have reasonable conversations about how to vary the slope of Reserves growth while agreeing that the principal should only be drawn down in an emergency?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And how, in doing that, we can invest in our people and companies so as to help them become the most creative, resilient, innovative and entrepreneurial that they can possibly be so that they can deal with any challenges the world can throw at us with confidence?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we do use more fiscal resources to do that, we should also recognise that if our efforts are successful, we may be able to save social safety net spending further downstream and we may also raise GDP and, hence, tax revenue which are good fiscal outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My analogy here would be spending more to make vaccines free or close to free, a subject that I have raised a few times in this House, which may have the effect of reducing state spending on hospital subsidies, MediFund and so on further downstream.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, as formidable as the challenges are, they are not insurmountable if we tackle them earnestly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, I would like to conclude with just a few directional suggestions on how we might address these future challenges from where we are at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was how the Japanese built up their world-beating giant firms – the Japanese and Koreans I should say.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For those local firms which can consistently deliver financial and economic growth while safeguarding or growing domestic jobs to those firms that significantly enhance our economic vibrancy, more support could be provided beyond the caps and limits associated with current economic schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I had an exchange on the subject in this House with the then Minister for Trade and Industry, Mr Iswaran in 2017.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand his counter argument that we do not want to go too far down the path of picking winners.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But some of our existing efforts like state-backed co-investment, for example, could be seen as picking winners anyway.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Conversely, support to local firms that do not demonstrate ambition and performance can be disciplined and focused on competitiveness improvement, job safeguarding and business succession planning.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not a call to give away state monies to local firms irrespective of outcomes, and I trust that it will not be referred to as the latter.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we not do more to tap on our fiscal resources to channel substantial R&D investment into creating IP that is then seeded to local companies in a very substantial and systematic way, but with the IP owned by the state and licensed to the firm's so that the state can nudge these firms to grow in ways that benefit the domestic economy and locals?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The area's earmarked for R&D investment in this way could be targeted so as to fill gaps in the global IP landscape in future-ready fields like AI so as to ensure maximum "commercialisability", so to speak.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I know that there are limits to how much we can do under WTO rules and other treaty obligations, but surely there are ways to navigate these obstacles to some degree.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And, as I referred to earlier, A*STAR has licensed IP to SMES, but the question I am raising here is how to upscale this to enhance the commercial impact and provide enablers to ambitious local firms to become world-beating.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, many of our talented youths go into the Civil Service.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a programme could help them develop skillsets relating to fundraising, employee recruitment and retention, marketing and so on, not so much training but coaching and pointing them in the right direction as well as connecting them with funding sources, including state-backed ones.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, we do not only want locals to get the $7,000 jobs and the $10,000 jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also want some locals to create such jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having a pool of workers with such training could also help attract both foreign and domestic investments in these high-growth sectors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, any such move has to be done in tandem with the growth of investments in these sectors to ensure the jobs and career paths are available to those who join such industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Beyond just hard skills and cognitive intelligence, it is these capacities that we need to nurture in the long term.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is these capacities that will be our surest defence against whatever economic and technological evolutions bring; and tracking them in the SPOR report is a nod to the fact that our policies do play some role, not the main role, or the only role to be sure, but some role, in nurturing these capabilities and capacities among our people.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are dealing with huge geopolitical shifts, massive economic disruption, changing demographics, the existential threat of climate change and the possibility of Black Swan events like disease pandemics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But uncertainty is never a reason not to make projections and not to make plans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Times of change and crisis are also moments for the agile, the resilient and the creative to find new opportunities, anticipating and adapting to those moments in history like our own that see non-linear change can bring immense benefits not only in economic terms.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It also addresses short-term inadequacies while setting out plans for our strategic long term.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I am thus encouraged by this Budget and glad the Government has prioritised assistance for different groups of citizens across our society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Over the years, we have seen significant financial packages announced to address long-term healthcare needs for our ageing population, GST offsets for the lower-income groups, housing support, education subsidies to level the playing field for improved social equality and much more.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: These packages seek to enhance social mobility, provide care for those more in need and promote greater wealth distribution across society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Without doubt, these packages, which have a long tail, will have a hefty price tag as they cater for increasingly larger groups of Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In this regard, I wholeheartedly agree that the responsibility of the Government is to provide for those who have less resources and are less able to sustain their daily needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But the cost of living has been a perennial concern amongst Singaporeans, and even more so as we age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How can we better address this in the current uncertain times?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Are the financial packages that we see now an indicator of the Government on what is to come in future?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Are we moving towards more of a welfare state?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And to what extent can the society safety net provide if self-sufficiency from family and personal means remain as the first line of support in our country?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is a topic that we should begin to consider – retirement adequacy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some Singaporeans also had misconceptions about when to start planning for their finances.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Whether the number of survey respondents were in the thousands or less, this is reflective of a worrying trend and the existing mindset of the young working class.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is totally understandable that our current Pioneers and some Merdekas will need all the support that can be given as they earn lower wages in their lifetime and thus limited savings, much less a decent CPF savings to depend upon.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But this cannot be the case for the younger generation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Today, most seniors rely on their CPF, housing, personal savings and some income from work if they are still gainfully employed or if their children are willing or able to provide for them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, we need to recognise that this landscape is changing for the middle-aged individuals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Parents are naturally more indulgent in their expenditures for every child.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: From enrichment classes, tuition, gifts, holidays and more, it is impossible to imagine any parent will give less to their offspring even if they do not compare with others in society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Through growing affluence, changing lifestyles and personal aspirations, it is par for the course today that each family has more expenses outlay over time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While the general income level has risen and, theoretically, should be more for dual income families, it appears that meeting immediate financial needs are already a problem for some.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To plan for retirement which may be two to three decades down the road, may be a tall order for many of them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For some, the necessity to plan is just before they are about to enter retirement or have less certainty in being employed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The issue will be further exacerbated with fewer children in each family and for those whose children may be able to but are less willing to provide financially for their parents.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For their benefit, we encourage more to internationalise to learn and capture broader experiences and opportunities globally.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But with a rising percentage of such families living overseas, their retirement support pillars will inevitably change.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For those living and working overseas early in their career, they may not have invested in housing within Singapore, and the CPF contributions differ depending on their compensation package or the nature of their work.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: When they choose to return to Singapore in the later years, the cost of building their retirement nest will take a different starting point.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: By then, some may face different challenges in their ability to accumulate sufficiently for their retirement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On one hand, I support and feel it is necessary for the country to continue to provide for its citizens.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But on the other hand, I think it is time for us to consider if and how we can continue to afford these long term, larger support packages for every generation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As working and income patterns change, increased exposure of living or working in more than just the home country before retirement, and investments in the next generation burgeoning for each family, I cannot help but ask if our citizens should plan their financial and retirement needs more holistically and earlier.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This has consequences on how and when we provide subsidies for those who cannot afford or those who are more vulnerable.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How can we measure who qualifies or not for any scheme?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Simply means testing by per capita income for each household may see the need for a different yardstick, or how intrusive would it be for the state to assess deeper on their situation beyond funds availability or even immediate family support.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: These are areas worth pondering and better sooner than later.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On this issue of retirement adequacy, I would also like to draw attention to the group of special needs individuals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There is a large spectrum of people with varying needs and the type of support required.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As able-bodied persons, it is typical for us to have our own concerns about growing up, education, livelihood, family and occasional thoughts of what life might be like in our senior years.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But for individuals with special needs, these may not even be fleeting thoughts for some of them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some lack the ability to plan and fend for themselves, others could be limited for different reasons, thus, becoming an added worry for their parents who are ageing.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) has also continuously engaged different groups to understand and assist through provision of integrated support services aimed at promoting inclusion of persons with disabilities in the community and to enhance their quality of life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How are we ensuring opportunities for all via our social strategies in education, healthcare and housing?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If we must begin the process, it starts from helping and partnering them, allowing them to be a part of our community from young.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Indeed, this is a much-needed step to provide their parents, family and themselves a little more comfort that they can live, work and socialise as a part of the community while comfortably being themselves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There are a number of supports that we can provide for them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I will cover more of this in the COS debate on their living environment in public housing, their employment post-schooling age and how the community and businesses can partner them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One, rally the society to be inclusive from young.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As a start, we must recognise the presence of people with special needs and their ability as an individual.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Preschools and formal schools can do more to educate the children in embracing differences and welcoming them from within the school community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As individuals, all of us, too, can be more gracious, accepting and forgiving to families who have children of special needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They deserve a place in our community, from the neighbourhood playgrounds to public transport and common dining places.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There is no need for cold stares, harsh words or social media commentaries for any special needs individual.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They are individuals with their own rights and well-deserved to be treated with dignity like any other person.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We should have campaigns that counter such negativity and give more room for families with special needs to be out in our community to share our common spaces and feel at ease that they are one of us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For special needs individuals, some may have disabilities or are cognitively challenged to handle legal matters on their own when their legal guardians are no longer around with them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Be it a Will, having an acting Attorney-in-fact or managing other legal matters that involve their daily lives, they are more likely to need better access and support at affordable cost on a regular basis.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Having trusted parties who have a long-standing relationship with them and being able to defend their interests are crucial for those with special needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With the extensive assistance schemes available across the Ministries or specific to their special needs, it is not an easy task for them to navigate and know how to seek help.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is uncommon today for each special needs person to have been assigned to a social worker or being supported in network groups.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: When their legal guardians are no longer able to extend the help in organising their life needs, this will be an escalating concern and possibly more pressing for them apart from financial aids.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: My concerns, notwithstanding, Sir, I stand in support of the Budget.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Around the world, we observed how the deficit of trust in government and public institutions prevented or worsened efforts to contain and control the outbreak.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In one Asian economy, hundreds rallied for days to protest against plans to turn some buildings into quarantine centres.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In one European economy, hundreds in a town protested having their fellow countrymen who were COVID-19 evacuees from China from being quarantined in their town despite assurances by the government that none had symptoms of infections.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They put up roadblocks, burned tyres and hurled stones at buses, resulting in several injuries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Out of desperation, the health minister declared she would spend the next two weeks locked up in quarantine with the returnees.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In other places, government attempts to refute false rumours, although backed by medical experts, were ignored at best and stoked fear at worst.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: People hoarded critical supplies and deprived them from people in high-risk environments who needed them the most.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In a public health crisis, it is heartbreaking to see such anti-social behaviours.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Where has the “leave no one behind” belief gone to?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is a different scene in Singapore, thankfully.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In Singapore, we see some of the ugly behaviours, too, but there is a lot more of the good acts that we have observed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Where we saw frontline workers being discriminated or denied service by some individuals, we see an even stronger response from many Singaporeans who wrote messages and prepared gifts to express their support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We also see ground-up initiatives by groups of volunteers who engaged seniors and the more vulnerable within our communities to give out practical items, such as hand sanitisers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, another example is when the silent majority seemingly came to life during the recent "Twitter Parliament", suggesting that hoarding and, therefore, depriving others of essentials, should not be encouraged.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With decisive leadership and strong public institutions, we have so far kept the situation under control.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our leaders regularly inform the public of the latest developments in Singapore, and the Government responds to queries with clarity and transparency.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Civil servants worked tirelessly every day since before Chinese New Year to ensure "no stone is left unturned".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Medical frontliners bravely stepped up to care for patients, and cleaners worked extra hours to ensure a clean and safe environment for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In fact, our efforts to combat the COVID-19 virus has been widely recognised.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Kudos to my fellow Singaporeans who demonstrated calm, reason and compassion in the face of uncertainties that allowed us to control the outbreak quickly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These would not have been possible if not for the trust between our Government and the people, as well as the strong social cohesion forged over time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must cherish this and never be complacent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Speaker, Sir, I see Budget 2020 as one that preserves jobs and social cohesion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the midst of our battle against the coronavirus, we have this Budget Debate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am glad that in his Budget, the Deputy Prime Minister addressed the impact of COVID-19 on our economy as well as the long-term needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Budget 2020 is a responsive Budget that prepares Singaporeans for the challenges ahead.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Against uncertainties arising from global headwinds, it is essential to ensure that Singaporean workers remain supported and adaptive, with measures to encourage them to be more productive and innovative.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Jobs are important to Singaporeans' livelihood, important to keeping families financially buoyant and important to social cohesion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Various studies, including one by the World Bank in 2013, have shown that job access has a direct impact on a society's trust and civic engagement.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The same 2013 World Bank report also stated that jobs and the types of jobs influence people's aspirations, social beliefs and their sense of belonging to the country.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I, therefore, applaud the decisive move to set aside a whopping $4 billion to help Singapore companies and Singaporeans in this time of difficulty.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To ensure that the Government's intent of providing our citizens with strong and reliable support is achieved, I have two suggestions, based on feedback from my residents and grassroots leaders.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, ensure the goodwill that comes from these Budget measures ultimately flows through to the micro and small enterprises.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For instance, passing on cost savings from commercial landlords to tenants and ensuring access to the Enterprise Financing Scheme by micro enterprises.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Banks may be less motivated to serve individual micro enterprises, even with a greater risk-share by the Government, but these enterprises can band together if facilitated by the respective merchant associations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, it is not just the Government that can help the smaller enterprises.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I note the recent launch of an “SME Help Fund” that aims to help SMEs whose businesses are struck by the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When I spoke with one of the fund's founders, JL Family Office CEO Andy Lim, he said they wanted to help SMEs and that this is one practical way of how Singaporeans help Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is an example of how different groups in the society can take the initiative to help fellow Singaporeans in times of need.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Their efforts complement the Government's and, collectively, these efforts help to strengthen our social cohesion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, provide more recognition and support for freelancers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Freelancers are especially vulnerable to changes in the economic conditions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many events and work assignments are cancelled or deferred as a result of the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A number of them have taken their own initiative to band together online to support one another as they are hit by the outbreak.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I trust that the unions are actively reaching out to them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Freelancers are especially vulnerable to changes in the economic conditions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many events and work assignments are cancelled or deferred as a result of the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They have little savings or "fats" to see them through this period of work drought.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Worse, if they have a family to support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many of the financing options available now are not readily accessible to them as they are not registered companies and have no GST registrations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we address the immediate impact of the COVID-19 outbreak, we should also not lose sight of investing for the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am glad that the Government continues to have a firm grip on this, evident in the other components in the Budget.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Still, I would like to reiterate the importance of investing in our people to ensure a high concentration of high-quality talents in Singapore, for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During this period of economic uncertainty, it is a precious opportunity for us to reskill and upskill our workforce, catalyse the transformation and get ready for the future economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore is clear about our future economy direction.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Technological disruptions have resulted in jobs becoming obsolete.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But with technological advancements, many more new jobs will be created.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to provide good and meaningful jobs, where workers are empowered and have agency.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But to take on these future jobs, Singaporeans need to be equipped with the right skills and possess international perspectives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I support the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) and welcome the next bound of SkillsFuture initiatives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singaporeans should be encouraged to work with employers to determine what courses to attend to ensure job relevance and be guided along as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, I wonder if these measures are enough.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Also, to attract top enterprises to Singapore to create good jobs, we need a high concentration of skilled workers with a critical mass of world-class talents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore excels in the biotech sector now after 20 years of investments.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A critical success factor is the large pool of high-quality talents that we built up over the years, enabling Singapore to lead in this sector ahead of competition.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Looking ahead, Singapore needs to offer an abundance of talents who not only meet existing demands but also attract future unicorns to Singapore from the region and beyond.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As talents beget talents, there is a virtuous cycle to this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, global competition for skilled workers is stiff.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Respondents expect market and technology trends to play a big part in these shifts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: More dramatically, the WEF describes the world as facing a "reskilling emergency".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Companies and countries are motivated to close the skills gap fast.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore needs to be even faster – one to two years' window of opportunity, according to some prominent business leaders I encountered from within and outside of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government has been investing and introducing targeted programmes to build up our talent pool.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the Chinese saying goes, "百年树人", talent cultivation takes time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Topping up with foreign talents may be part of the solution, but strengthening our Singaporean Core is, of course, the core solution.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, to reinforce the momentum, may I suggest the following.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, we need a stronger push for Singaporeans to reskill and upskill, and right-skill from young.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is a good step, but I hope the Government can consider taking an even bolder step and recognise it as part of formal curriculum.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Furthermore, some would argue that computer language is increasingly akin to English or mother tongue languages that we learn in school.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the digital future is inevitable, why not take that step further and recognise coding as our third language?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We also need stronger incentives to encourage adults to take on future economy-oriented courses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The additional SkillsFuture credits in this year’s Budget are a welcome addition, but to help Singaporeans pick up essential skills that allow them to compete globally over the long term, there should be stronger guidance and more targeted initiatives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, we must continue to encourage international exposures for students and younger working adults.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is essential for young adults to be given full internship opportunities as well in countries like the US, China, Israel and other emerging economies with a vibrant tech scene, such as Indonesia and Vietnam, for them to gain a global perspective and foster meaningful networks that will benefit them and their professional community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to work on availing more of such overseas opportunities for our young, so that we can cultivate a critical mass of young Singapore talents with a world view.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, we need to deepen our relationships with global top talents and facilitate value transfer to our own local talents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could we consider a mentorship programme that attracts top talents and company founders from around the world to mentor our youths and startups?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore is a hub for many top technology and professional talents, and we should make use of this opportunity to groom our younger generation and benefit from their mentors' expertise, experience and networks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This initiative will also increase Singapore's mindshare among these top talents and foster our youths' image as motivated, hardworking and bright young individuals who are globally competitive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, through this COVID-19 crisis, we can see the composure and decisiveness of Singapore leaders, the efficiency and meticulousness of organisations within the Government, the bravery and kindness of our frontline workers, as well as the generosity and mutual concern that Singaporeans have for one another.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It has shown what Singapore is capable of, and how beautiful this country is.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In comparison, we have seen how citizens from other countries have lost faith in their government, discriminated against their fellow countrymen, prevented disease control measures from being implemented, resulting in the spread of the disease.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, the deep trust between our people and the Government is especially valuable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This was built over the years, with Government policies that have always put the long-term interests of Singapore and Singaporeans at the core, allowing Singaporeans to enjoy a good quality of life and stable jobs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There should be no let-up in efforts to build this trust.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In difficult times, the ability of governments to figure out the root cause of problems and implement targeted solutions to minimise impact on the people is very important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I am very happy that the Deputy Prime Minister has introduced a Budget to deal with the situation during this critical period.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Besides ensuring adequate supplies for frontline workers, funds have also been set aside to reduce the impact on companies' cash flow, so as to protect jobs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Although it is important to deal with the current situation, it is equally important to plan for the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore has experienced many rounds of economic transformation and ventured into new emerging industries at different junctures, maintaining its lead successfully.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The key to our success is the high concentration of good quality talent here who can meet the skills demand of new industries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With Singapore moving towards the future economy, there will definitely be a strong demand for talents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But more importantly, we need to ensure that Singaporeans upgrade their skills and that we nurture our young to equip them with future skills and global mindsets.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Although talent development schemes have been included in both last year’s and this year’s Budgets, I hope that the Government can consider the suggestions below.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, continue to encourage students and young working adults to intern in countries where technology development is more rapid.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Aside from gaining experience, these internships will also broaden their horizon and their networks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fourth, set up mentorship programmes where top-notch talent and entrepreneurs can be matched with young local talents and startups with potential, to build capabilities, share experiences and network.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): As we enter more uncertain times, with pressure on our community from the COVID-19 epidemic and global financial turmoils, I am heartened to learn that this year’s Budget is comprehensive and inclusive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is a Budget for our people and our future.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I wish to speak on 3Ms pertaining to the Budget.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: You might think, given the generosity of the Budget that my 3Ms stand for Massively More Money.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: But no, the 3Ms I will speak on today are mobility, maturity and mentality.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Social mobility is the holy grail of governance.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we have made persistent efforts to boost social mobility with significant injections of social spending, especially within the past decade.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot underestimate the impact of such subsidies.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I recall that when I volunteered at the charity Food from the Heart, children from poor families who received monthly food goodie bags saw improved grades.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Once their parents stopped bickering over where the next meal would come from, and there was money left over for transport, the children started to attend school more regularly and this translated tangibly into improved academic performance.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond these financial measures, however, what more can we do to ensure that our society is not overly stricken by the proverbial Great Gatsby Curve?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This curve describes how family resources and social networks influence a child's future earning potential.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: When this curve is too pronounced, the advantages conferred by family wealth and connections get entrenched over time, leading to social stratification.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As the World Bank's Fair Progress report argued, low mobility, both real and perceived, can dampen an individual’s aspirations for the future.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As the saying goes, "you cannot be what you cannot see".

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We, therefore, need to invest more strategically in more after-school programmes where students from lower-income families are offered targeted academic support and career guidance in order to bridge the privilege gap.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As our economy matures and digitalises ever more intensively, we are at a critical crossroads to consider future growth directions.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Clearly, in our well-connected society where we are bound together by the Internet of people and also the Internet of Things, a promising path for us to explore is the one illuminated by big data.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The application of data analytics in virtually all aspects of life, including finance, business, urban planning, healthcare and education, can generate powerful insights for enhancing resource optimisation, service delivery and efficiency gains.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: With data to fuel AI and Machine Learning, we can forge a culture of data-driven innovation that aims to raise our quality of life.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: But that begs the question as to who should own the data and be allowed to profit from it.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The social compact between people and corporations which are collecting data about us is riddled with inequity.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, the "compact" is one of distinct asymmetry between the big technology companies and consumers.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Hitherto, technology companies, such as Facebook, Amazon and Alibaba, have selfishly hoarded their data, from which they distill critical insights to create market dominating products and services.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: If we continue to let these Goliaths have exclusive rights to exploit the data that they harvest essentially for free from all their users, what chance is there for the scrappy startups of the world to innovate for the greater good?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We must leave the door wide open for startups to compete against the incumbents.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In the same vein, the European Commission recently issued a document titled “European strategy for data” which outlined potential steps it may introduce to require companies to share and pool data.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This will have the twin benefits of levelling the playing field between first movers and startups and fostering a vibrant pro-innovation environment.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, too, academics should not be left out of the data game.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: At this point, let me declare my interest as a professor at the Singapore University of Technology and Design and a member of the Social Science Research Council.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The best and brightest talents in our world-leading universities have much to offer by way of problem solving, as the multifaceted COVID-19 crisis has highlighted.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: With more concerted regulation around data sharing, we can ensure that universities are well-equipped with robust data to conduct research for societal benefit.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such data can help to facilitate productive and evidence-based policy analysis by academics and researchers in our universities and research institutes.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Concerns around data security can be addressed through the generation of synthetic data that realistically represents authentic data but that protects privacy and confidentiality.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad that plans are apparently underway for such data sharing and I welcome further details as soon as they are available.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward, we should also consider studying the experience of countries, such as New Zealand and the UK, that have advanced data sharing infrastructures and procedures, to identify best practices that we can seek to emulate.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Data sharing by the Government is a strategic shift we must undertake to fully realise our Smart Nation ambitions.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: However, this infusion of funds will be for nought if attitudes to upskilling do not shift.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Our collective mentality around upskilling must change from "nice to have", to "must do".

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: And this mentality has to be shared by workers, employers and educators.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: During a recent conference, I had the benefit of exchanging insights with practitioners and researchers in the adult learning ecosystem.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We all converged around several sobering points, that while our workers need to constantly upskill, they do not find the necessary motivation to do so.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This arises from a combination of work-life pressures, inertia and resistance to change, and a sense of defeatism that the new skills they acquire will not translate into concrete improvements in their salaries or job prospects.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Separately, when employers are dismissive of their employees’ needs or interest to upskill, their motivation is further undermined.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such negative mentalities around upskilling must be addressed, be it through nudges, support programmes or public education efforts.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, too, we cannot expect Singaporeans to develop an inherent drive to learn unless they associate schools and other learning environments with positive experiences.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As I mentioned in my Adjournment Motion in Parliament last month on the fear of failure, the overwhelming achievement orientation in our education system does not imbue an intrinsic love for learning.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, students become Machiavellian and grade-oriented, while instructors then teach to the test to meet key performance indicators.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: To become a nation of lifelong learners, we need to accelerate our transition away from a focus on grades towards broader and more enduring learning outcomes.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Students should not just be learning but learning how to learn.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: With greater attention to these three "Ms" of mobility, maturity and mentality, I am confident that we can overcome the challenges ahead, both distant and immediate.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to, therefore, conclude by underlining my strong endorsement of the subsidies announced in response to the current COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Given the concerns over COVID-19, I am proud that Budget 2020 is the result of quick response, built on a deep understanding of what Singaporeans are feeling and going through.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Budget is one which will help us all to ride through this period of global panic in a calm manner.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At this juncture, I would like to thank the frontline staff, especially the healthcare heroes, the Ministry of Health's (MOH’s) team and all involved in fighting the COVID-19 for their sacrifices, dedication and determination.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I am also heartened that in preparing Budget 2020, Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat and his team had spoken to more than 1,000 people, including corporate chiefs, to collect feedback.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As someone who is active in both the public and private sectors, the issue of balancing regulations to take care of the interest of the regulators and the companies being regulated, is one which continues to be of concern to many.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Following my speech during the 2019 Budget Debate about cutting red tape, I was heartened that there were anecdotal improvements.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But apart from extraordinary situations, it is important for the policymakers to consult the stakeholders regularly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Such consultation is a continuous process and a never-ending journey.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: One area that catches my attention is the Singapore Exchange's (SGX's) competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is a good move to reduce compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, SGX seems to be losing its shine.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I understand that many local companies are listing on other stock exchanges in New York, London and, especially Hong Kong, over SGX.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is a 25% increase from 2018, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Computer gaming accessories company Razer chose to list not in Singapore but in Hong Kong in November 2017.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Some of these firms listed overseas are apparently drawn to better liquidity and higher valuations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I have personally spoken to the head of two companies that listed their companies in Hong Kong last year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Worse, according to Euromoney.com, delistings over the last five years have outnumbered listings.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: From the reply to my Parliamentary Question in January 2020, I understand that SGX is not tracking the number of local companies that choose to list in other countries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It may be wise for SGX to connect with some of these companies to find out why they choose to list their companies overseas.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This would also have implications on Singapore’s ambitions to become a prime financial hub.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, I would like to touch on the issue of sustainable transport.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As a person intimately involved in the management of a large fleet of more than 10,000 taxis, sustainable transport is an issue which I am most concerned with.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: On a yearly basis, ComfortDelGro Taxi replaces more than 1,000 vehicles on average and we are keen to replace them with cleaner vehicles that emit less carbon dioxide.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Currently, we are trying to speed up the replacement of diesel taxis with petrol-electric hybrid taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Meanwhile, we also have four full electric taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When we do a calculation based on the more popular Korean full electric passenger car, the EEAI scheme does not appear to be attractive.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In fact, the current Carbon Emission-Based Vehicle Scheme (CEVS) which offers a rebate of up to $30,000 off the ARF is more attractive than the EEAI scheme of only $20,000.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The additional road tax makes EEAI even less attractive.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In addition, cabbies who drive EVs have to endure the inconvenience of taking 30 minutes to one hour to fully charge their electric taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The promise of halving the charging time and halving the cost of car battery every three years still remain a promise.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In fact, some in the car battery industry point out that "exaggerated claims are commonplace, and that not everyone is convinced” that planned car battery breakthroughs will become a reality.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I would like to clarify with MOF whether they really think that the EEAI will entice fleet owners like us to choose EVs over hybrid vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Do not get me wrong, I am supportive of having more "green" and "clean" vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is just that we do not want Singapore to bet on the wrong "green" car, like the experience we had with compressed natural gas (CNG) cars.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Rather than putting all eggs in one basket, I would like to suggest considering other alternatives to not replace, but supplement EVs, like fuel cell or hydrogen vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Can PMO or the Land Transport Authority (LTA) share their preliminary thoughts while waiting for the full report of the study?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This year's Budget, Mr Speaker, is the Unity Budget with an eye on COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   The COVID-19 outbreak has seriously impacted many Singaporeans, including taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When people talk about the smaller crowd in downtown areas, I lament the fall in businesses for taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: During the SARS outbreak, even though there was a drop in foreign tourists, locals still go to work as usual.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But today, many office workers take turns to work from home and this has worsened the situation for taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We thank the Government for launching a special relief package for taxi drivers on Valentine’s Day.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In total, taxi drivers will receive rental rebates of $20 per day.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In other words, taxi drivers will enjoy up to $36.50 in rental rebates per day.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Even though taxi companies will be running at a loss by doing so, for the sake of taxi drivers and the taxi industry, taxi companies still decided to go ahead with the rental rebates.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But still, many taxi drivers are unable to make a living.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We, therefore, hope that Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Heng Swee Keat will consider providing more assistance for taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In English): For taxi drivers, their loved ones are most impacted by the outbreak.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: All the taxi companies are providing additional help over and above the Government's Special Relief Fund (SRF) of $10 per day.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With these additional rebates, the taxi companies will go into the red over the next few months.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Even then, the cabbies are still suffering a significant drop in their net income.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I call on the Government to do more for cabbies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Perhaps the Government can consider matching what the taxi companies are doing for the cabbies by increasing the quantum of the SRF.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Singaporeans will remember the good deed by the Government.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Just a couple of days ago, one cabby by the name of Robert Chew wrote me a touching email.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These are, indeed, very hard times for us as our incomes have been severely hit and many drivers have given up.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Not to mention also the daily stress of fearing for our own health as we are frontline service providers who do not want to be a problem to our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This fight is far from over and may last several more months.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Let us work together in our fight against this epidemic as we look forward to coming out of this crisis stronger and better.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: May you and your loved ones stay safe and healthy." Robert summarises nicely the sentiment of many taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Other than point-to-point drivers, the livelihood of Singaporeans working in the private sectors have been badly affected by the negative impact of the economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Those working in the tourism industry are the worse hit.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Gig workers and freelance workers are also badly hit.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many freelance workers are engaged by Government departments.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For example, fitness instructors engaged by Active SG, orchestra music instructors engaged by MOE schools are having their earnings significantly reduced when organisations are cancelling activities involving more than 50 people.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While there is a cancellation clause which is included in the contracts of some legally savvy freelancers, many others do not.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Such help will go a long way in keeping them afloat.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Another vulnerable group are those in society who receive help from charities and non-profit groups.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As fundraising has almost come to a standstill, this is because many businesses are more concerned with survival than corporate philanthropy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, we must do what we can to help keep these charities and non-profit groups going and stretch their fundraising dollars.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It was supposed to end on 31 March this year in 2020.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But I strongly advocate that it be extended until the end of 2020 so that the beneficiaries whose lives depend on the money raised from well-wishers can continue to get help.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The greater challenge now is how we can pull together and help one another.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Those who can must help those who cannot to tide over the economic crisis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Budget has made a very good first step and the rest of the journey is for us to walk together and, together, we can overcome the odds.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.00 pm until 4.20 pm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Inequality would not rise to the same level until the 1700s.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The cause was not productivity improvements or upskilling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, the cause was the Black Death, also called the Plague, which killed, by some estimates, more than one-third of the population in Europe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The demand for labour went up and land was redistributed amongst the survivors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The bacterium is endemic to rodents and carried by the fleas that infest rats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Plague originated in China, was carried west along the Silk Road by traders and spread thence to Europe, most famously, by Italian traders fleeing the Mongol siege of Caffa by ship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Plague destroyed not only populations, but also the existing social and economic order throughout Europe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Governments of the day responded with novel and extreme measures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Governments also realised, perhaps belatedly, that inequality itself weakened society's ability to resist the Plague.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The poor could not afford treatment, but they could pose a risk to all if they contracted it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As a result, towns hired plague doctors to treat rich and poor alike without payment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I tell this story in the hope that history does not repeat itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But it is startling what the parallels are between the Plague and COVID-19.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The policy questions have changed little over the years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: COVID-19 is more than a public health risk: it is a threat to the present global political, economic and social order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: China's strong policy of containment has essentially decoupled China temporarily from the global economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But even if, as we hope, the impact of COVID-19 will be short-lived, it would be irrational to plan to return to the same apparently prosperous world that we inhabited just a few months ago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Countries and companies are assessing whether economies and supply chains should be so tightly coupled.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, for our part, we should take this opportunity to strengthen weaknesses in our economy and society that may yet affect the course of the outbreak and our resilience to future ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: International experts, Mr Deputy Speaker, have judged that Singapore's approach to COVID-19 is a model for public health systems worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should be proud of the hard work that our healthcare and Home Team institutions have put in to protect our society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We can afford the tremendous costs of containing COVID-19 because we have a highly successful market-based economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our efforts to contain COVID-19 now depend on many people in the frontline who have benefited much less from the market economy than others have.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our efforts also do not depend on the private healthcare sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They instead depend on the strength of our public healthcare institutions which are paid for outside the market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To understand this, we need to deconstruct the ideology or the myth of market forces.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In crude terms, the myth is the idea that the price and distribution of goods and services, determined by competitive market processes, must be efficient and socially appropriate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This model of market forces underlies our policy thinking about economic restructuring because, for the most part, it works well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is impossible to protect all jobs or industries in economic restructuring, because doing so would cripple the efficiency of the economy and harm ourselves in the long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, we should never assume that the market price is equivalent to social value.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Market prices may be efficient, but that says little about it being equitable or socially desirable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What comes to mind to illustrate this is how the frontlines of our war against COVID-19 have been increasingly manned by people whose market prices are low but social values immeasurable, especially during a public health crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Rosalind, one of the cleaners at my university, does more on a daily basis to protect our students and staff from COVID-19 than I possibly can.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: She and her colleagues go into our offices and classrooms and toilets daily to make sure that they are disinfected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: She bears the risks of cleaning up dirt and spills and worse things and she has more work now but the same pay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our Town Councils, likewise, largely depend on foreign workers and elderly local cleaners who do jobs that few of us would accept for the same pay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This disconnect between market prices and social value is not a problem confined to those of the lowest incomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Security officers put themselves at risk serving quarantine notices and screening for sick persons at our institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: One such officer did, in fact, contract COVID-19.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our emergency medical responders and nurses put themselves at risk every day as their work puts them in direct physical contact with the sick.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And our general practitioners (GPs) are working under very difficult circumstances to screen and treat the sick, to make the judgement call if a patient is a suspect COVID-19 case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the rewards for GPs have never been very high compared to that for specialists and surgeons, to say nothing of the pay for nurses and first responders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There may be market reasons why elective aesthetic surgery gives a doctor a much better living than primary care, but surely, there are few social reasons why this is so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A second reason for interrogating the myth of market forces is that there is no guarantee that market prices and allocations reflect efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In theory, prices in a competitive market track the marginal productivity of any resource closely.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This implies the market allocation of resources should be efficient at producing the greatest useful output for society at the least cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But this need not be true, especially once we consider the importance of resilience in maintaining social functioning in difficult times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Medical institutions worldwide do not keep significant reserve stocks because the supply chain is usually swift and reliable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In normal times, yes, the globalised system of production is superbly efficient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We would, in fact, question normally whether it is good value for money if MOH were to start subsidising the costly production of surgical masks in Singapore, or the creation of a stockpile that far exceeds that of projected clinical use.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Straits Times reported on 21 February, just last week, that private hospitals in Singapore have seen big drops in foreign patients.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Usually, they get about 40,000 medical tourists a month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Now, normally, it is a good thing to have a thriving private medical sector in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And yet, it is the market outcome, because there is market demand to pay for excess capacity in the private sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is none to pay for it in the public sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our public healthcare system is under pressure, as are healthcare systems worldwide, to be more efficient, to cut waste and slack.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To keep public healthcare prices low, we schedule appointments for subsidised healthcare as tightly as possible, to extract the most out of our manpower and equipment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This comes at a hidden cost to the resilience and morale of our healthcare workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In a crisis, these effects become more salient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Any lack of slack means that, in a crisis, we risk having insufficient spare capacity to deal with unexpected surges in demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We must then rely on our healthcare workers to work overtime to keep us safe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: China and now Korea’s experiences in managing the current crisis are important reminders of how vulnerable our public healthcare system could be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We are just one unlucky "super spreading" incident away from severely taxing our public hospitals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To be sure, the Government has done well in planning ahead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The National Centre for Infectious Diseases (NCID), which has been a mainstay of our fight against COVID-19, is proof that we have taken the lessons of SARS to heart.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we must guard against the short-sighted pursuit of efficiency at the expense of resilience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We may have to prepare for a new normal where increased globalisation and the disintegration of public health systems worldwide mean that we will face imported disease outbreaks more frequently than ever before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The COVID-19 outbreak is likely to hurt the livelihoods of those who already live precarious economic lives – the freelancers, the workers in SMEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The market forces myth explains inequality through the argument that pay is equal to productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This, in turn, forces us to emphasise improving our productivity in order to raise wages, which, in the long run, is more sustainable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But there are any number of market distortions which would explain why the productivity-to-pay relationship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While it may hold on average and in the long run, it does not always hold for the individual or even the sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, wages for low-income workers stagnated for much of the 2000s.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Were the prices right for low-wage labour in the mid-2000s?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we believe fully in price theory, the answer is yes and there is nothing that can be done about it beyond Government support and transfers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In 2012, the former Chairman of the National Wages Council, Prof Lim Chong Yah, called for "wage shock therapy" to raise the wages of the bottom income earners while freezing that at the top.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen a strong reversal of formerly stagnant wage growth for low-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Does this mean that productivity for low-wage workers has jumped by 30% over the last decade?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is difficult to take at face value without more study the price theory implication that cleaners have suddenly become hugely more productive, even with the benefit of training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I suspect it is more likely that wages were simply too low, possibly because of the easy access back then to low-wage foreign workers and our low-wage workers' lack of bargaining power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In any case, the solution to being a nurse is not for that nurse to become a doctor, and the solution for cleaners is not to hope that our children do not have to take up that job or to depend on an inexhaustible supply of low-cost foreign labour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Society needs both nurses and doctors, cleaners and lawyers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I applaud these moves to demonstrate solidarity with Singaporeans on the ground.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They are important not just for the morale of frontline staff, who may yet face cost-cutting, but also send a signal that the risks and costs of COVID-19 should be socially distributed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Today, we commend our cleaners, security guards, nurses and public health workers for being on the frontline of protecting us against COVID-19.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We acknowledge the work of our public transport workers, hawkers and shopkeepers in keeping our supply lines and life running as normal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: More fundamentally, COVID-19 and the demands of economic restructuring should have us question whether our social risk-sharing institutions for unemployment, housing and healthcare provide sufficient protection and resilience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There was a lively debate yesterday on unemployment insurance in the Chamber and the discussion should continue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot depend just on charity for filling in the gaps, especially since charitable activity may also be hurt by an economic or social crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, our resilience today to major shocks, such as COVID-19, depends very much on the Government of the day enacting strong and tailored measures, because we do not have many automatic risk-sharing measures in place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is both a strength and a weakness because resilience depends on the performance of the political leadership of the day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Events near to us show that this cannot be guaranteed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I started this speech by noting how the Black Death fundamentally reshaped economic and social institutions in Europe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The long-run history of economic inequality is that significant reductions have only occurred in the wake of huge disasters, such as the Black Death, the collapse of empires, the First and Second World Wars.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Left unspoken is whether inequality played a role in precipitating these collapses.
