speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: At the moment, it seems, if we are fortunate, COVID-19 will only be a shock, not a disaster, for the global economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we have to continue the work of strengthening and restructuring our economic and societal institutions to ensure that when the next test comes, Singapore will stand as resilient as it has today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: However, we take heart that since SARS, we have built up our defences and are better prepared to deal with this virus outbreak today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We are deeply thankful to our healthcare workers, Government agencies, cleaners and many frontline personnel who have put their duties first, to protect us.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Apart from these, we have a strong foundation of community help and network to respond to challenges that come our way.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Since its formation, the Community Development Councils (CDCs) have played a critical role in partnering the community to strengthen bonds and help vulnerable groups.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We have the “ABC" mission – A stands for Assist the Needy, B stands for Bond the People, C stands for Connect the Community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The mission is even more crucial than ever in a time like this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Each of the five CDCs – Central Singapore CDC led by Mayor Denise Phua; Northeast CDC led by Mayor Desmond Choo; Northwest CDC led by Mayor Teo Ho Pin; Southeast CDC led by Mayor Maliki Osman; and Southwest CDC helmed by myself – has its own set of local assistance schemes to meet local needs, as well as programmes to foster community development and ownership.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: A diverse range of partners from the community contribute to improving the welfare of the community and those in need.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To this end, the five CDCs have been working together to launch an island-wide initiative to provide meals in the heartlands for vulnerable families.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This effort not only complements the Care and Support package to help Singaporeans who need extra support with the cost of living, it will also bring business to many heartland food joints and coffee shops which are feeling the effects of the slowdown due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Yesterday, Member Mr Png Eng Huat had suggested that the grocery vouchers for low-income families be extended for use in small retail shops.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In the past few years, our local constituencies have been working with heartland retailers and businesses to meet the nutritional needs of low-income families.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The mayors and the CDCs welcome the timely $20 million injection of funds which will provide additional resources for us to scale up these efforts across the nation and reach out to more of those in need, as well as boost the support for local businesses and heartland enterprises.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The upcoming Free Meals and Drinks scheme will be redeemable at participating coffee shops, participating food courts and participating heartland enterprises.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Details are currently being worked out and will be released in due course.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Earlier, Prof Lim Sun Sun also talked about the importance of nutritional meals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: These are important for the kids to start the day right.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For example, the ability to have a simple breakfast of kaya toast and eggs – whether with Milo for the kids and Kopi-O for the parents – as a family can start the day right, and put parents and kids in a better mood to bond, talk and share.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: These kinds of moments can often be elusive for those preoccupied in making ends meet.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, it is even more important for them to receive greater help in this area.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Taking a ground-up approach, the CDCs will work closely with partners in the community, merchant associations, F&B outlets, self-help groups, Social Service Organisations, grassroots leaders and volunteers to form a cohesive network of support to shore up the nutritional, physical and psychological needs of this group of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This win-win solution not only provides businesses with additional revenue during uncertain times, it serves the families in need and brings the community closer together in mutual support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This type of collaboration benefits the community at large and the CDCs have often involved volunteers and organisations who reach out to those in need.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For instance, we have had the Central Singapore Milk fund for children; we have the NorthEast Community Vouchers; we have the NorthWest Food Aid Fund that provides food vouchers, cooked meals and food rations; we have the SouthEast Roxy Family Fund for daily expenses like diapers, food or medicine; and we have Food Connect@SouthWest and Meal Service@SouthWest.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In the coming months, we will see the CDCs widening our outreach and deepening our engagement with partners as we work together to beat the COVID-19 storm.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Since 2013, seven years ago, CDCs have partnered Enterprise Singapore, key trade associations and business chambers to each set up an SME Centre in each of the five CDCs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The SME Centres reach out to heartland enterprises and support them through capability workshops, Government schemes, advisory services and help them improve productivity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The CDCs will continue to do more for our SMEs as they face the need to constantly evolve to stay relevant in today’s disruptive climate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: From training and talent development to business advice and community partnerships, we will continue to deepen our efforts with heartland businesses to energise their growth and survival as SMEs provide the majority of jobs in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Apart from working alongside SMEs, the CDCs are dedicated to improving the future and prospects of Singaporean workers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The CDCs have since surpassed the initial outreach target of 80,000 individuals in three years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Building on this strong foundation, the five CDCs look forward to closer collaborations with SkillsFuture Singapore, Workforce Singapore and the National Trades Union Congress' Employment and Employability Institute to expand our SkillsFuture Advice outreach.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: All five CDCs will intensify our momentum to help Singaporeans, especially mid-career and also mature workers, to be better equipped and resourced to cope with the impact that COVID-19 may have on their careers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: (In Mandarin):   Neighbourhood shops and micro businesses in the heartlands are important members of our community and are important to the larger community as well.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Over time, many residents and shopkeepers have become friends, and the entire neighbourhood feels like a close-knit family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The merchants' associations are important organisations that represent merchants and they exist in many constituencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Grassroots organisations, CDCs and various merchant associations have always been in close communication, working together to organise various activities and events to inject vibrancy into the neighbourhoods, boosting pedestrian traffic to bring in more business.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In the Bukit Gombak constituency where I serve, a Chinese New Year (CNY) event that is similar to the River Hongbao is organised every year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Businesses in the neighbourhood would participate in the CNY bazaar, and there would be large lantern displays and Getai to attract residents to the town centre to shop, eat and enjoy Getai performances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Both residents and neighbourhood merchants benefit from this win-win event, and I know that many constituencies have similar CNY bazaars.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: From this example, we can see that maintaining the vibrancy of communities and neighbourhoods can help to ensure a sustainable business environment for heartland merchants.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This will allow CDCs to work with neighbourhood merchants to help low-income families through their individual platforms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: At the same time, this will help to boost residents’ spending at neighbourhood shops and coffee shops.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: More details will be revealed by the five CDCs soon.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The mission of the five CDCs is to build a caring and cohesive society, and many assistance schemes by the CDCs are people-centred.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To better assist our neighbourhood shops in achieving success, the CDCs, Enterprise Singapore, trade associations and merchant associations have banded together to set up SME centres to provide advisory services for heartland merchants.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Another 2,400 small and micro businesses have also participated in workshops to improve their operations, management and promotion strategies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Although large merchants have the advantage of providing new and diversified offerings, neighbourhood merchants have the advantage of providing personalised services, as well as friendships and mutual understanding with customers built over the years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: People say that there will be business for shops as long as the community is vibrant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: One crucial factor is taking proactive measures to drive customer traffic in the neighbourhood.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It is the shared responsibility of everyone to ensure that the community and neighbourhood remain vibrant, to build a pro-people, pro-business and friendly neighbourhood.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, although the months ahead may hold uncertainties, we can be sure that, on the ground, the five CDCs are fortifying the network of support across the heartlands and strengthening our local businesses, our vulnerable families and Singaporean workers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With concerted and specific measures as well as fresh resources, we are closing ranks with fellow Singaporeans and heartland enterprises as well as local businesses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As we fight back, as we steady our ship, as we hold our ground, we can get through this together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For no matter what the odds may be, we stand as one – SG United – overcomers, to emerge even stronger.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But Singaporeans can take heart that we are better placed than almost any other country to deal with this crisis and to mitigate its impact.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Government has gone all out to address the potential fallout from COVID-19, and my residents would like to express their thanks to the Government for this Budget and all the help that it has been offering.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My residents have also asked me to express thanks to our frontline workers whose bravery, commitment and calmness have inspired all of us to carry on.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, COVID-19 is a once-in-a-decade threat to the economy and the full effects are not even apparent yet.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even if it does not get worse, it has already blasted a hole in the world’s supply chain.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Chinese manufacturers have shut down for a month and many industries are hurt because of lower Chinese demand and because of the broken Chinese supply chain.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To cushion the impact on local businesses, the Government has introduced a comprehensive set of measures in this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Protecting businesses means protecting jobs and protecting families.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The first point relates to feedback from the SME community.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is a "sandwich" class of companies where it is too big for such small help to matter but too small to survive for long periods of negative cash flows.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a small drop in the ocean for such companies.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even a $600,000 loan guarantee by the Government may not be enough for a medium enterprise whose revenue may be up to the region of $50 million to $100 million a year.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The second question relates to the timing of the help.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What can the Government do to speed up cash flow assistance to these companies?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It has been almost six weeks since the virus started to impact travel and commerce.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many businesses are already running down on their reserves and they cannot depend on their suppliers to extend credit because their supplies are similarly impacted.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Cash flow is the lifeline of every business.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, I would like to ask the Government what more can we do to open the spigot to make sure that these companies do not go down because of the virus in the short term.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The third point relates to what we must do to prevent short-term pain becoming chronic, in the form of long-term unemployment among mature professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs).

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If companies go under because of COVID-19, many jobs will disappear and may never come back.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even if they come back, they might go to a different, younger crowd.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Employment for mature PMETs exhibits a ratchet effect.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is much easier for a mature PMET to lose a job than to be hired back into one.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, the emphasis on SkillsFuture 2, SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit and the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Support Package in this year’s Budget is, therefore, much welcomed.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am also gratified to learn from the Deputy Prime Minister's Budget speech that in the last three years, productivity has risen by 2.6% per year and real median income has risen by 3.6% per year.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are positive developments for the Singaporean worker.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I would also like to ask how we can get Singaporeans to do the relevant training, instead of spending their SkillsFuture money on new skills and interests that might not help them to stay employed.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I totally agree with the Deputy Prime Minister when he said that enterprises know best what are the skills needed for their businesses to transform.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But under the Enhanced Training Support for SMEs, the Government already pays for 90% of the course fees and 80% of workers' salary while employees are undergoing training.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Minister Josephine Teo also said in her speech that funding is not the constraint or the impediment that is preventing workers from getting training.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I know that SMEs are unwilling to send their workers because it is just too difficult for them to take their workers away from day-to-day work.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, the new SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit that is capped at $10,000 per year might see a very low take-up rate.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And this might even include having to pay the salary of such temporary replacements.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This would encourage them to upskill their workers while not compromising their day-to-day activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Residents have also given feedback that it is difficult to get placement into the Professional Conversion Programmes which operate on a "place and train" basis.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Place and train means that you have to get placed in a job first before you can undergo training.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But it creates a catch-22 situation for mature PMETs.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The fourth point is what do we do for the longer term, how do we increase the resilience of our economy and our workforce?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The speed and ability of the Government Technology Agency to swing into action and update from "gov.sg" or "maskgowhere" are testament that inhouse ability matters in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One way of doing so is to build up a local ecosystem of SMEs with the requisite local expertise to operate these industries to become our version of Mittelstand.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Germany has its famous Mittelstand – the heart of German industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The unifying mindset is a focus on social, intergenerational and community responsibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mittelstand companies contribute to the local economic and social welfare.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They also offer stability and loyalty to their staff by investing heavily in training and retaining staff in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This stands in contrast to the more common Western style of capitalism, with an exclusive focus on profits.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Their overriding obligation is to their shareholders, not to other stakeholders like workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This "winner takes all" mentality might have also contributed to the growing inequality problem that we see in the world today.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From a societal perspective, it is not always clear that unbridled capitalism will lead to the best outcome.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Perhaps it is time for us to explore how we can build a core of locally-anchored, stakeholder-conscious Singapore businesses that can help our economy in both good times and bad times.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore already has many of the ingredients to cultivate our own Mittelstand ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are uniquely placed to work together as a Government and as a society to achieve a bold vision.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Enterprise Singapore and the private sector can work together to identify the right industries.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Economic Development Board can bring these businesses to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Innovation can be driven by research and academic institutions, with funding from the National Research Foundation (NRF) and the Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE), and there can be tripartite collaboration with the unions to make sure that our workers have a voice.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Trade associations can also help to mobilise the workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our emphasis on lifelong learning will provide a skilled workforce of craftsmen and domain experts.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us show our pioneering spirit once again.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With the current COVID-19 outbreak fast spreading across the world, the outlook for 2020 is even bleaker and more uncertain.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat has provided much-needed assurance, by announcing a rock-solid Budget that inspires confidence to press ahead.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But I can think of many things money, in the right hands, can provide: peace of mind, opportunities to better one’s circumstances and hope for the future.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore’s economic foundations have been and continue to be strong.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Budget 2020 will provide "Stabilisation and Support" for the current COVID-19 outbreak, enable Singapore to seize opportunities to transform and grow, as well as to build and secure our future.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The money will come from diversified sources of tax, NIRC from our Reserves as well as accumulated surplus from previous years’ fiscal prudence and discipline.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is at times like this when we really appreciate having this reservoir of financial resources to keep Singapore on an even keel, come what may.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is at times like this when we should also reflect on the significant contributions made by NIRC.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, in five short years, it has gone from 13% to 22%.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am worried about calls from some quarters for the Government to take more from our Reserves, rather than to safeguard our strategic "asset".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Is it not unwise to kill the "goose that lays the golden egg”?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am even more worried about the growing dependency on NIRC.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As NIRC is subject to volatility from tough investment environments, I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister whether it might be prudent to consider setting a threshold on NIRC dependency, beyond which recurrent spending should only be funded through recurrent revenue.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst he has assured us that GST will not increase for at least another two years and has also provided support in the form of the GST Assurance Package, some Singaporeans are still wondering why would we need to raise GST at all, given the apparent Budget surpluses and additional capacity of $6 billion of GST offsets?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Increases in cost of living is foremost in the minds of many people, particularly retirees.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even though the wealthy are already contributing substantially to our taxes through a progressive Personal Income Tax, GST, property tax, Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD) and so on, I really believe there is still room to consider wealth tax and estate duties, all aimed at building an even fairer and more equal society.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Some may be concerned that a reintroduction of estate duties, previously abolished in 2008, may harm Singapore's status as a leading wealth management centre and incentivise wealth and business owners to engage in complex structures for tax avoidance.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As other forms of wealth taxation are now being considered by a number of other countries, the notion of wealth taxes generally do give rise to concerns about how taxpayers might react.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But income and wealth inequality are global issues and there are wide recognition amongst governments and wealth and business owners of the need to address them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As the world moves towards considering broader and fairer tax systems, Singapore should maintain its principles of keeping tax structures simple and tax rates low whilst meeting the interests of all stakeholders, particularly of those who are most in need.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, now we live in a new era of automatic information exchange under the Common Reporting Standard and other global requirements to disclose beneficial ownership across the world.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Transparency in ownership and value of assets is rapidly becoming a new norm.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: When tax is well structured at competitive and fair rates, together with tax treaties similar to those to which other jurisdictions are parties, an effective estate duty and perhaps accompanying wealth tax regime, may actually be an allure for assets to be maintained in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In a world of turbulence and uncertainty, Singapore's world-class infrastructure, rule of law, financial and political stability are priceless for peace of mind of the wealthy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is especially so when the environment in Hong Kong, Asia's other leading wealth management centre, has been marred by months of street protests and instability, and long-term uncertainties regarding its tax and legal systems.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst there is a really "feel good" sentiment on the ground, more needs to be done to help Singaporeans understand exactly how these measures will benefit them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And I am picking this up when I am on the ground trying to explain.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There are many different schemes to keep track of, from the new schemes, such as Care and Support Package, Matched Retirement Savings Scheme, GST Assurance Package, to enhancements to existing programmes, such as the Silver Support Scheme and SkillsFuture top-ups.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: On top of existing support programmes, they all have very different qualifying criteria, some based on housing type, individual income, household income, age criteria and, often, combinations of criteria.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And I do agree these multifaceted targeted schemes are more cost-effective than broad based ones.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But together, they can become too complex for the average person on the street to digest.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The coronavirus outbreak has hit the businesses hard.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Besides the dramatic impact on tourism, aviation and retail sectors, COVID-19 has significantly disrupted supply chains in manufacturing to even vegetables for the restaurants.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Locked-down Chinese cities are unable to supply the parts that have become integral components of the supply chains here.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many workers are stuck in China, unable to return.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Activation of Business Continuity Plans, extra cleaning, medical leave, leave of absence and so on have put additional pressure on costs and manpower.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It will be especially crucial, I agree with Member Ong Teng Koon, to provide relief for cash flows to tide them over this difficult period.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Would he also consider coordinating efforts with banks to restructure loans, so that SMEs and affected individuals can get a moratorium on repayments for, say, up to six months, just to ease their cash flow?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In the meantime, it is heartening to see large corporations and landlords rise to the occasion in support of the smaller ones, including rental rebates by Changi Airport Group to retailers, and the Hope fund, put together by the Young Business Leaders of the Singapore Business Federation (SBF), to support SMEs with immediate working capital.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is the time for the big boys to chip in and help their smaller brothers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The issue of manpower constraint continues to be a major struggle for businesses across the board, even as we are resolved to reducing our dependency on foreign workers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We need to urgently develop new ways to find, train and retain the talent necessary to sustain growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Learning from the Swiss, industry associations can play a pivotal role in galvanising players in the sector to join forces in curating and delivering impactful training for the industry.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I believe that Singaporeans will become more accepting of supplementary foreign labour if we actualise the systematic plan to train and develop them for attractive careers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister had set an ambitious goal to tackle climate change and has put aside a $5 billion Coastal and Flood Protection Fund.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The spark in Singapore's climate change journey has been lit in this Budget.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singaporeans can look forward to a sustainable future and participate in exciting new developments as we manage Singapore's transition to a low carbon, low emissions, clean economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It has provided Singaporeans with peace of mind, ample opportunities and a sustainable future.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The concerns over COVID-19 will eventually fade over time, but the efforts to transform Singapore as a Global-Asia Node of Technology, Innovation and Enterprise will ensure Singapore remains exceptional.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I cannot agree more with Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat when he says that the Singapore Spirit is strong and growing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On Wednesday, I found out that I was speaker number 48 out of 48.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What can you say after a list of 47 esteemed speakers?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The past two days' speeches – many made passionately – reminded me of a British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) documentary which I had listened to last month while I was on the way to work.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It was not a guide about how to better disagreements.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather, it was a guide about how to resolve disagreements better.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because the documentary touched on the negative repercussions on societies when they are polarised.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The danger the BCC documentary sought to point out is the very danger so many of us in this House seek to battle.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In short, in Singapore, we do things quite differently.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Why is this important, especially at this time?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because the crisis can bring out the best or the worst in society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These will relate to fiscal measures, social policy and issues of societal values.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But how we resolve these differences, and come out of a large crisis or mini crisis, is key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The willingness to listen, to be open with one another, to share and risk empathy, and then to decide.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are all essential for an efficient decision-making body and have been so aptly displayed by so many of the 47 speakers before me.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, many of us in the Chamber regard the unity of Singapore and the united response to the crisis as the priority.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ms Jessica Tan gave real-life examples from her constituency as to why providing opportunities in education is key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ms Denise Phua shared how these opportunities should be extended to SMEs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Desmond Choo talked about giving working mothers and mothers on maternity leave the best shot in their careers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And you see characteristics of each in Budget 2020 – the umbrella of opportunities for reskilling, retraining and advancement for the Singaporean workforce.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: You see the undercurrent of unity in so many of the speeches.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: You see that in Mr Png Eng Huat's speech where he talked about the need to unite rather than point fingers and stigmatise, how we should not ostracise China, and that it was good that we sent them a second humanitarian shipment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, the BBC documentary sought to point to the danger of disunity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yet, in this House, through the 47 speeches before me, you see an overarching priority to unite, and that is quite novel in the world today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And it is, in fact, inspiring and encouraging.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we look at the globe, there is sectarianism, I versus you, hardly any effort to build the common ground or common paths forward.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yet, so many of the speeches in this debate here have had as their foundation the topic of unity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is also the need for transparency, honesty, as Mr Cedric Foo emphasised, and being open with difficult facts, too.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And I see how that framework is being deployed in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It makes for the politics of trust and honesty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, as with Budget 2020, as with the debate of the 47 speakers before me, as with the manner in which the Ministerial task force in COVID-19 is addressing the difficulties facing our country today, facts discussed candidly and openly, and a sharing of ideas and suggestions and then, importantly, decisions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is what we are doing in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is like a steady ship in the ocean.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have gone through storms together before and we can go through them again.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my view, such stratification is not the way it should be.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This was also a point raised by Prof Yaacob Ibrahim and Mr Alex Yam, and I agree with them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order to stem the spread of the COVID-19 virus, office buildings carry out temperature-taking.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Those manning the temperature booths, often security guards, are important as they provide a first line of defence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the guards are putting themselves at risk.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Other measures that have been taken are the increased cleaning and disinfecting of places, such as playgrounds and high touchpoints, such as lifts and hotel rooms.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our housekeeping staff, uncles and aunties in the hotel industries, frontline staff, cleaners – they all play such an important role in the prevention of the spread of the virus.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many have had to work overtime due to the crisis to meet the increased rate of cleaning common areas.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And yes, these diligent and determined workers also put themselves at risk.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In a Straits Times' interview entitled, "Coronavirus: It’s a dirty job, but if I don’t do it, who will?", one of the cleaning companies has had their teams work seven days a week these few weeks, all hands on deck, including the manager Mdm Tay.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I quote from the article, "Few Singaporeans are interested in working in the cleaning industry, but Madam Tay hopes that through the work they do, especially during this outbreak, people will learn to respect the job.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are helping to prevent the spread of the virus in Singapore", says Mdm Tay.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, are the enforcement operations managers of MOM.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The nurses and those working at the service counters at hospitals and healthcare institutions play a crucial and important role.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: All workers on the frontline should be appreciated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: None of us asked for this to happen.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But since it has happened, we need all hands on deck.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There should be an appreciation that everyone, even those who play less visible roles, is important to our society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should be less focused on hierarchy and more focused on appreciating each member of our society, especially as we battle COVID-19 in a singular and united determination.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And I hope that we will also retain this experience, that everyone in our society is important, even after we overcome this crisis, as we forge our collective future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially important to the hotel, tourism and F&B industry.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, for those on private property, it is the landlords of those retailers on private properties who are given property tax rebates and encouraged to pass on to the retailers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead of relying on the goodwill of landlords to pass on savings to their lessees, is there no other more direct way we can alleviate the challenges that those in the F&B industry are facing?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, will the Ministry consider requiring landlords to declare whether they have passed on the rebate to their lessees?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And if so, how much has been passed down in dollar terms?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Already, it has been reported by the Restaurant Association Singapore that 200,000 employees have been affected since the outbreak.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As Business Continuity Plans already need to be in place, it may also be a good opportunity for businesses to test and hopefully prove that flexible working arrangements work.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If it works, more firms may be ready and confident to try adopting it as an available standard practice to support our working parents with	young children	and working caregivers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For	some	of the enterprises which want to take this opportunity to change the way they work, this Enterprise SkillsFuture Credit may come in useful.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, in relation to using this crisis as a place to plan for the future, there is one particular area that we have announced our intention to look for new sources of	supply	and look into the capabilities	for	local manufacturing, that, is, masks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It would be especially useful since epidemics will spread among countries more quickly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the issue of masks	also points to a larger priority, namely, the diversification of our supply sources.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, the coronavirus or COVID-19 is affecting the world	trade of	goods	and supplies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In light of this, we need to take stock of what other items, besides masks, we potentially need to manufacture on our own in the future, and if we do manufacture them, whether our supply sources for the materials are sufficiently diverse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Budget 2020 also has its eye on the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Businesses have	been	given	incentive	measures	to	take	this opportunity to reskill and retrain workers to increase future productivity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We also need, however, to instil measures that make learning something that is embedded in the way things are done in Singapore long term.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is crucial as we are facing an economy characterised by disruptive technology.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just like COVID-19 presented itself to us as a disruption, or another phrase by Deputy Prime Minister Heng, as "a spur and a test" that COVID-19 has presented to us, we cannot run away from such a change, disruption, spur or test.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to change the way we think about learning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Year after year, we cite the Chinese saying "live until old, learn until old", that is, lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Do we see learning as a chore rather than a joy?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Do we see learning as a burden rather than a privilege?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not just a good attitude to have in life but necessary in the kind of economy Singaporeans will face in the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A good example of what could be done is what is already being done at SMU.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We could broaden what is being done at SMU.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At SMU, disruption is built into part of the syllabus through the way the core curriculum is designed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The core curriculum has three pillars: capabilities, communities and civilisations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under "capabilities", students pick up skills, such as numeracy and management lessons, to navigate the modern world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Internships are integrated with the other pillars, with a work-study scheme available so students can take up longer internships and earn credits at the same time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under "communities", students discover Singapore's Asian context through courses under the areas of economy and society, technology and society, cultures of the modern world and community service.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is something other schools could consider so that their students will not be theorists only but be able to handle both theory and practical, having the dexterity to apply strong foundations of theory into new real-world applications.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although there are some in Singapore who disagree with the use of the phrase "climate change" as they are of the view that the climate is and always has been changing, allow me to just use the phrase to point out some trends we should be concerned with, particularly relating to the rise in sea levels.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, sea levels have risen and ice in the ocean has been melting and physics will say that there will be an increase in sea levels.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, you have three minutes more.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I will take two, Sir, leaving one spare.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In my speech, Sir, I compared Singapore to a steady ship in the ocean.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As a country, we have weathered storms together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance Heng Swee Keat wrote on his Facebook page the day before he delivered the speech, "we	would not	have	been	able	to	act	quickly	and decisively if not for our deep Reserves.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I do not mean only our financial Reserves...

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is our Singapore way –	responding as one people, tirelessly safeguarding our country’s Reserves and future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is for these reasons that I stand in support of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But unity in the context of a democracy, along with the Fourth Generation (4G) leadership seeking to engender a Singapore Together movement, must also encounter varied, diverse, edgy and even contradictory views in the effort to find common cause.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is that process of embracing diversity and accommodating political differences that gives meaning to a democracy of deeds for the 21st century and not for a one-party Parliament of decades past.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My colleagues in the Workers' Party (WP) and I thank all Singaporeans for sharing their views and coming to us to bring up issues to Parliament over this term of Government, particularly, those that Government Members of Parliament (MPs) cannot be expected to raise, not out of an inability of their own but because of the nature of politics and political contestation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: WP MPs agree with the Government when we have to, disagree where we must, in the knowledge that we endeavour for the best outcomes for Singapore and for a unity of purpose when politics must take a backseat, like during this current COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My speech will be divided into three parts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will first speak of the geopolitical environment and the response of some businesses to the Budget announcements.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Next, I will talk about our fiscal position, with some points on our revenue and expenditure position before finally concluding with my views on the enhanced SkillsFuture Credits and the climate change-related announcements.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In his 2018 Budget speech, the Finance Minister outlined three major shifts in the coming decade: the shift in global economic weight to Asia; the emergence of new technologies that will change the way we live, work and play; and finally, ageing – themes which were repeated in the Minister's 2019 Budget speech as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The United States (US) Attorney General William Barr's speech at the Department of Justice earlier this month captured the mood of the times ahead, at least from Washington's perspective.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In reminiscing about the days of the Cold War, Barr remarked, "Russia wants to conquer the world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is going to be more challenging to deal with." American policy towards China is on a very different course and with a bifurcation of the world looking like an almost foregone conclusion, not just a technological decoupling, but with differences in values and norms at the heart of things.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More so than before, shaky US-China relations are threatening to force invidious choices upon Singapore, choices which the political leadership not just within the People's Action Party (PAP) but all political parties and citizens in Singapore would have to negotiate with greater judiciousness and sensibility without compromising an absolute commitment and loyalty to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, this circumspection does not just extend to the superpowers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We must also resist the urge to engage in gloating when our closest economic partners like Malaysia and competitors like Hong Kong negotiate their own unique political circumstances; circumstances which are historically apart, completely different and, in many cases, take place in a more complex and significantly larger country many times our population size.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, I understand that Chamber Members are also continuing the work on longer-term efforts at internationalisation and bringing businesses up to speed with new initiatives, particularly training and growth opportunities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They are our private hire bus companies and drivers who are bearing the brunt of cancelled trips and tours arising from the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are the bus drivers who bring our residents to Malaysia for durian trips and even National Servicemen around Singapore for local tours or training.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand that an industry briefing was held on 21 February by the Singapore Tourism Board on a relief package for travel agents and tour operators.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, I hope the Government reconsider this and extend some support by way of a one-month or partial waiver of the levies for companies that have no choice but to hire foreign manpower, on the condition that these companies consciously seek to increase their local headcount, by way of job redesign going forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some conditional support and consideration for them in these difficult times may provide greater impetus on all our companies overly reliant on foreign manpower today to make a greater effort to hire locals, including senior citizens, and even those on a part-time basis, tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One hard truth that we do not hear in this House, notwithstanding greater demands on expenditure, is that the current Government has had the privilege of far more budgetary elbow room, both political and fiscal, than any previous government in Singapore's history.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Compared to 2015 when the NIRC component of the Government's revenue was about $9 billion, today, the figure is almost double.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the last Budget, the Finance Minister provided a lengthy reply on why the dollar value of the Reserves could not be disclosed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the answer remains unsatisfactory, particularly when the same argument could apply to the overwhelming majority of other democratic societies, who nonetheless err on the side of fiscal scrutiny and accountability.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At last year's Budget, I brought along a Business Times article that saw Singaporeans calling for a greater discussion on the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These calls for greater transparency are not out of place and they will continue in years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They run in parallel with the Singapore Together spirit, with Singaporeans taking ownership, exploring fiscal solutions, seeking to co-create not just today's Singapore but a sustainable and equitable tomorrow that future generations of Singaporeans will inherit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Government share more details on these plans, as this year's Budget does not communicate the results of the Government studies on the borrowing or debt-financing framework and their fiscal consequences on future Budgets?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This year's Budget also saw the Finance Minister once again making reference to the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) project, an initiative that seeks to ensure companies are taxed where substantive economic activities are performed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Finance Minister first raised BEPS in his 2017 Budget speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Then the House was informed that the Government was in consultation with businesses on scheme refinement and implementation of the relevant standards.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What has been the results of these consultations from three years ago?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: BEPS was raised again in the Finance Minister's speech this year and the Minister shared that there are discussions to revise international tax rules and that Singapore was actively participating in them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, reference to BEPS this year was in the context of a subpoint of another sentence, which warned there were uncertainties and downside risks to the Government's revenue position, a matter which should be of interest to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have a query with respect to BEPS.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before that, it is useful to recap the Government's argument on proposals by Singaporeans to raise taxes of higher income earners, who do enjoy the safety and security offered by Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The concern was that high net-worth individuals would be able to structure and move their assets to avoid higher tax obligations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is the impact of BEPS on this prospect and the Government's assessment of the impact of BEPS' developments on our tax policies?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is there an upside, nonetheless, by way of other taxes on the ultra-rich to maintain our progressive tax system?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What are the best and worst case scenarios to the developments in BEPS on our revenue position?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At this year's Budget, the Finance Minister said that the Government put off the rise in GST after considering the state of the economy, but more critically, I quote, "...after reviewing our revenue and expenditure projections".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Finance Minister's position then was that one did not need to have information on everything to make a decision on anything.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But from the Minister's speech this year and the announcement not to raise GST next year, it is obvious that the Government relies on revenue and expenditure projections to make these decisions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would the Government make public these projections so that Singaporeans can critically evaluate the necessity of a GST hike?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe this openness would contribute to a more substantive conversation and understanding of our fiscal tradeoffs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This can only advance and mature conversations that take place in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The third segment of my speech is a short one, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I refer to the Government's call for special SkillsFuture Credit top-ups for Singaporeans between the ages of 40 and 60.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: WP supports this move, but urges the Government to track the use of these credits for this age group to job- and employability-related outcomes closely.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More generally, while SkillsFuture subsidised courses can range from, in the words of the Finance Minister, "cooking to coding", it does not bode well if taxpayers' money are expended on courses that are underweighted with regard to real improvements of skills, job prospects and employability of our workers, in view of the workplace disruptions to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We know from previous Parliamentary replies that there is an upper limit to certain entrepreneurial prospects in Singapore, such as the opening of cafes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, I expected some strong incentives or subsidies in this year's Budget on climate change outcomes, particularly in the aftermath of the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources' (MEWR's) efforts towards greater climate change awareness over the last few years, including designating one year as a year of climate action.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I would urge the Government to move more decisively to incentivise changing behavioural norms to reduce the overuse of plastic bags.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is also about the amount of waste we generate and dispose of which usually ends up in a plastic bag that is thrown down our bin chutes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A plastic bag charge is far from representing mere climate change symbolism.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is only a mere 15 years from now.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is a window to move more decisively and we should move fast.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, the Finance Minister is correct to say that many Singaporeans are coming up with and acting on ideas to make Singapore a better place on their own initiative.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For the first time in his Budget speech in this term of Government, the Minister has spoken about the democracy of deeds.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But whatever deeds our people underwrite, they take place within the context of our democracy, a democracy where alternative views, criticisms and disagreements shape the outcomes that give meaning to the phrase one united people – united in a vision for a better and more confident Singapore, no matter what our political beliefs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is like that anthem that was referred to in this House, during the course of this Budget Debate, "You Will Never Walk Alone".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But how many of us know that it is not just the anthem of one club but others, too, like Glasgow Celtic, Borussia Dortmund and many others?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As long as our people – youths, businesses, individuals – engage the issues of the day civilly in our democracy and treat their fellow Singaporeans and foreigners within our midst with dignity and empathy, and endeavour for a more caring society, the best years of Singapore – a Singapore for all – are ahead of us.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I tell them it is an occupational hazard because I am a chartered accountant by training.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But, I have found over the years, in practice, that numbers give us the most precise and clearest indication of one's financial position.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Year on year, we hope for increases in our operating revenue amid very challenging global competition.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: For example, our tax collections can increase if our companies do well and pay more corporate taxes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: At the same time, we also hope for more revenue from our NIRC.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our NIRC only became possible because of the prudence and wise investment decisions made by our earlier generation of leaders.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Against this backdrop, our estimated expenditure is expected to increase much larger because we need to fund our healthcare needs and infrastructure developments, like our Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) lines, to bring a better life for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I even filed a Parliamentary Question for that.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In my discussions with the Ministry of Health (MOH), they informed me that there is no more space in Potong Pasir estate because it is all built up.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But MOH is building Kallang polyclinic, which is connected to Kwong Wai Shiu hospital.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I see Dr Yaacob Ibrahim had a thumbs-up because that is in his Jalan Besar constituency.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, that is also good for Potong Pasir residents because that is one MRT station away.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, I think I found some space for MOH.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The residents of Bidadari are moving in and I think there should be some space in Bidadari estate to build a polyclinic for our Potong Pasir residents.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Only because the Government had accumulated sufficient Budget surpluses during this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As we have read in recent international media of other jurisdictions, similarly announcing support packages in their respective economies, I doubt you will find a jurisdiction that can say that they are able to fund such support packages in the manner that we have.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: During previous Budget Debates in this term of Government, I am sure Members of this House will also recollect repeated calls for more spending of the surpluses or the use of more income derived from our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There was even a suggestion that the Government had a political agenda behind more prudent spending in the early years of a term of Government.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Had the Government done as what was popularly asked – spend more in the good years – then, this year, we could very well have had to dip into our Reserves in order to introduce first-instance measures to support Singaporeans as a result of the COVID-19 virus outbreak.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I used the term "first-instance" because I worry that we may not have seen the eye of this particular storm.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Even as we speak, we continue to see worrying signs of the COVID-19 virus outbreak seriously affecting many countries, such as Japan, South Korea, Italy, Iran and many others.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We can anticipate further adverse headwinds against Singapore's globally interconnected economy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We could very well require even further measures from the Government to support and assist Singaporeans in the days ahead.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And I am sure I am not alone when I say that I am glad we did so for the past five years and, indeed, for many terms of Government before.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premises, Sir, I would invite our Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister to share with us the Government's intentions and plans to further support Singaporeans and businesses in the event that the situation is drawn out over a prolonged period of time.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I had been a part of the team that was trying to figure out some of the schemes and programmes to be rolled out each Budget and I am now on the other side of the fence as a beneficiary of some of the programmes and schemes themselves.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When I left the Ministry in the middle of 2017, I had wanted to set up my own ventures and businesses and I chose the most difficult path to do so.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I chose businesses and ventures of a Business-to-consumer (B2C) nature, which is to create a consumer product, a consumer brand, starting from zero and I wanted to see if I could do it with the environment that Singapore offers, with all the different measures, grants and schemes that the Ministry offers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, it has been a very good two-and-a-half years, but with a lot of grinding, a lot of pain and also a lot of risks taken.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But at the same time, I felt assured because I know that Singapore's business environment is one of ease of access as well as one that you could approach and give feedback, where you could actually have help and assistance.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But, of course, many in the business circle would say, "Well, you had been an officeholder, you were a Member of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I know many fall by the wayside and, out of 10, probably nine will fail.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am just lucky to be able to do so.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would not deny that some grants and programmes were made available for me or my company to be able to tap on them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But at the same time, it is very much dependent on ourselves, as business people, to do so, to be able to come up with solutions with what the market needs and what the consumer wants and we can build a successful business from there.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They cannot be the most critical function or most critical part of the business.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I know that many businesses apply for those grants and schemes, hoping for additional cash flow.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is very clear that we have the facility and resources to handle some of these challenges.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But, without which, we will find it a struggle to manage.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is like running the day-to-day business in every other way; you would want to have the reserves in order to handle some of these rainy days.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How the grants are rolled out is extremely important.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A smart allocation of these resources and what kind of outcomes that we can get, those are the first things.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And those schemes must be targeted to help, to be able to do so.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some people say, "Raise as much capital as you can if you are a startup so that you have millions and millions", but you make losses.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If you are a unicorn, it is okay to make losses and you raise a lot of money.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am pretty traditional in some sense, maybe a Teochew businessman type, which is that all businesses still have to be profitable.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: You can raise a lot of money, you can make a lot of losses, but no end to come, you would not see the tipping point.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, you will hone your skills in fundraising but not hone your skills in building the business.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is success an exiting of the business when you gain or what?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that success in business, to me, is about building a business with a social conscience.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The product or services that you provide must have some social impact in order to make it very meaningful but, at the same time, commercially viable.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, whatever Reserves and schemes we have are to be able to create the environment for some risk-taking, embracing failures, so that our people do not give up.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I think that is the most difficult part in terms of culture.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But you can see our Government is so pro-business.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Every which way, when there is a crisis, it will come up with more and more schemes.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: You see a comprehensive slew of schemes and measures.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sometimes, I wonder, so many of them, I am also confused.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I was also a culprit – creating those schemes and programmes as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But at the end of the day, it is with good intention.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The question is whether we are cushioning and detaching businesses from reality.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would they be more competitive when they go overseas?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have both business-to-business (B2B) and B2C businesses, especially B2C business, dealing with consumers who are facing demand issues because the whole environment has been affected.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, there are a few things that go through my mind when it comes to COVID-19 – the crisis itself, how it affects businesses.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: First, when I review my own businesses, all SMEs should ask ourselves whether we have the capital and resources like cash that can last us for the next two to three months if we are in the worst-case scenario – no demand, no revenue or minimal revenue.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But I also know that, on the ground, sometimes it is difficult because the banks are not changing their risk assessment to let you have access to the capital.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The first thing is to ask ourselves whether we have enough; second, maybe look for big companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I am glad that Minister Chan Chun Sing, in one of the dialogues, said that big companies should help small companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But big companies have their own objectives, too.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unless a small company has value for the big companies, it is very hard to have a big company wanting to help a small company.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Maybe an exit through the big company – let the big company acquire your small company or you just close it down, move on and move along.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, I had wanted to recruit this talent for a long time.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But because of COVID-19, his company retrenched him.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, he was willing to lower his salary and, suddenly, I have a great talent for information technology (IT) in my company today and we are growing.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He is glad that he joined a growing company.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But he was willing to be able to say "I joined the company.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let us grow it together", which was an opportunity.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Whilst I know the Government tells us, "Let us train our workers, people and executives".

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Well, also look out for some of this access to talents.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, it is not all about retrenchment but about growing, too.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, this COVID-19 is not exactly all gloom and doom for many companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Maybe during this time, there are a few things that you have to do.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A lot of times, when it comes to this kind of crisis, we will look up to the Government to see what schemes to apply.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I was telling my staff and my team this morning I do not think we want to do that.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We lower our price and we have to expand our market.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
